children.translated_text: "In order" indicates that in winter there is slight dryness, slight bitter taste, and slight debility; likewise in spring, moderate dryness, astringent taste, and moderate debility; and likewise in summer, extreme dryness, pungent taste, and great debility.

children.text: yadyapi ca kaṣāyo raso rūkṣatamaḥ kaṭukaśca rūkṣataraḥ yaduktaṃ raukṣyāt kaṣāyo rūkṣāṇāṃ pravaro madhyamaḥ kaṭuḥ ityādi raukṣyaprakarṣaśca grīṣme madhyabalaṃ ca raukṣyaṃ vasante tathāpi vāyvagniguṇabāhulyāt kaṭukasya vāyvagniguṇabahule grīṣmakāla evotpattiḥ pavanapṛthivyutkarṣavati tu vasante pavanapṛthivyutkarṣajanyasya kaṣāyasyotpattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And although the astringent taste is the driest and the pungent is drier, as has been said, "Because of dryness, astringent is foremost among dry things, and pungent is middling," and so on, and although the highest degree of dryness occurs in summer while dryness is moderate in spring, nevertheless, because the qualities of wind and fire are abundant, pungent arises precisely in the summer season, which has abundant wind-and-fire qualities; but in spring, where wind and earth predominate, the astringent taste arises, since it is produced by predominance of wind and earth.

children.text: yaduktaṃ vāyvagniguṇabhūyiṣṭhatvāt kaṭukaḥ pavanapṛthivyatirekāt kaṣāyaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: As has been said: "Because wind-and-fire qualities are predominant, there is pungent taste; because of an excess of wind and earth, there is astringent taste."
And the predominance of earth and the other elements, caused by the special influence of a particular time, is to be inferred from the observed effect.

children.text: abhivardhayanta iti vacanādyathāsvakāle tiktādīnāmabhivṛddhiḥ sūcyate tena na tadaikarasatvam ||
children.translated_text: From the word "increasing," the increase of bitter and the other tastes in their own respective times is indicated; therefore there is not a condition of only that one taste.

children.text: atra ca kramavad raukṣyotpattitiktādyutpattī api daurbalyotpattau kāraṇaṃ yato raukṣyamutpādayanta iti tiktakaṣāyakaṭukān abhivardhayanta iti ca hetugarbhaviśeṣaṇadvayaṃ kṛtvā daurbalyam āvahantītyuktam ||
children.translated_text: And here the orderly production of dryness and also the production of bitter and the other tastes are causes in the production of debility, because, after making the two qualifying expressions "producing dryness" and "increasing bitter, astringent, and pungent tastes" into implied reasons, it is said that they bring about debility.
The passage beginning with "the rains" and so on.
The particle <s>tu</s> excludes the prima facie objection.

children.text: dakṣiṇābhimukhe dakṣiṇāśāṃ gantumudyata evārke tena viṣuvadudayopalakṣitamadhyadeśād uttareṇa vartamāno'pi raviryadaiva dakṣiṇāśāṃ gantumudyato bhavati tadaiva kṣīyamāṇabalo bhavati uttarāśāgamanaprakarṣāhitabalaprakarṣatayā tu stokastokakramāpacīyamānabalo'pi tathā durbalo na lakṣyate ||
children.translated_text: "Facing south" means that, when the sun is just ready to go toward the southern direction, then, even though the sun is still situated north of the middle region marked by the equinoctial rising, as soon as it is ready to go south it has waning strength. But because the great strength acquired through the increase of its northward movement is diminishing only little by little, it is not perceived as being so weak.
The same is to be explained also with regard to <s>uttarāyaṇa</s>.

children.text: kālaḥ pūrvaṃ vyākhyātaḥ mārga iha dakṣiṇābhimukhaḥ meghasya vāto meghavātaḥ varṣaṇaṃ varṣaḥ etairabhihatapratāpe'rka iti sambandhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Kāla</s> has been explained earlier. Here <s>mārga</s> means facing south; the wind belonging to a cloud is cloud-wind; <s>varṣa</s> means raining. The construction is: the sun whose heat has been checked by these.

children.text: vātastviha meghasambandhāhitaśaityo'rkatāpaparipanthī bhavati śaśino'vyāhatabalatvaṃ sūryasya paripanthino'bhihatapratāpatvād anuguṇamedhavātavarṣaṇayogācca ||
children.translated_text: Here, however, the wind, having acquired coolness from its connection with clouds, opposes the heat of the sun. The moon's strength is unobstructed because the sun, its opponent, has had its heat checked, and because there is contact with favorable clouds, wind, and rain.
"In the world" means among what is stationary and moving.

children.text: atra ca pṛthivyagnibhūyiṣṭhatvādamlaḥ salilāgnibhūyiṣṭhatvāllavaṇa ityuktaṃ tat kathaṃ saumye visarge tayoścāgneyayorutpāda iti na vācyam yato balaprakarṣavato 'rkasya kṣīyamāṇabalasyāpi viṣuvaparyantaṃ balavattvamastyeveti vyutpāditameva ||
children.translated_text: And here it has been said that sour taste exists because earth and fire are predominant, and salty taste because water and fire are predominant. Therefore one should not object, "How can those two fiery tastes arise in moist <s>visarga</s>?" For it has already been explained that the sun, though its strength is waning, remains strong up to the equinox because it previously possessed an excessive degree of strength.

children.text: samprati śiśirādau balahrāsaḥ pratipādito varṣādau ca balotkarṣas tatra śiśire durbalā varṣāsu balavantaḥ prāṇino bhavantītyādidurgrahaṃ niṣeddhum āha ādāvante cetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Now the decrease of strength beginning with winter and the increase of strength beginning with the rains have been stated. In order to reject the difficult conclusion that beings are weak in winter and strong in the rains, he says, "At the beginning and at the end," and so on.

children.text: visargasyādau varṣāsu ādānasyānte grīṣme daurbalyaṃ prakarṣaṃ prāptaṃ nirdiśediti sambandhaḥ tathā madhye visargasya śaradi ādānasya madhye vasante madhyaṃ nātikṣīṇaṃ nātivṛddhaṃ balaṃ vinirdiśediti yojyaṃ tathānte visargasya hemante agre ca prathame ādānasya śiśire śreṣṭhaṃ balaṃ vinirdiśediti yojanā ||
children.translated_text: The construction is that at the beginning of <s>visarga</s>, in the rainy season, and at the end of <s>ādāna</s>, in summer, debility should be indicated as having reached its highest degree. Likewise, in the middle of <s>visarga</s>, in autumn, and in the middle of <s>ādāna</s>, in spring, strength should be indicated as moderate, neither greatly diminished nor greatly increased. Likewise, at the end of <s>visarga</s>, in early winter, and at the beginning of <s>ādāna</s>, in late winter, the best strength should be indicated.

children.text: evaṃ manyate visargaprakarṣāhitabalaprakarṣaḥ puruṣa ādānasyādau śiśire stokakṣīyamāṇabalo'pi balavān bhavati yathā pauṣamāsāntāhitavṛddhiprakarṣā niśā māghaphālgunayoḥ kṣīyamāṇāpi divasānmahatyeva bhavati ||
children.translated_text: This is the idea: a person whose strength has been made very high by the intensity of <s>visarga</s>, although his strength is slightly waning at the beginning of <s>ādāna</s>, in winter, remains strong, just as night, having acquired great increase up to the end of the month <s>Pauṣa</s>, remains longer than the day in <s>Māgha</s> and <s>Phālguna</s> even while it is waning.

children.text: anena nyāyena varṣāsu daurbalyaṃ vasantaśaradośca madhyamaṃ balaṃ boddhavyam ||
children.translated_text: By this same reasoning, debility in the rainy season and moderate strength in spring and autumn should be understood.

children.text: evaṃ kālarturasadehabalakāraṇatvam arkādīnāṃ vyavasthāpitaṃ doṣakāraṇatvaṃ tvagre ṛtuvidhānanirdeśe'bhidhāsyate ||
children.translated_text: Thus the status of the sun and the others as causes of time, season, taste, and bodily strength has been established. Their status as causes of the <s>doṣas</s> will be stated later in the instruction on seasonal regimen.
He sums up the bases with the passage beginning "thus" and so on.

children.text: vikārāṇāṃ hetavo bhavantīti sambandhaḥ tathā samayogayuktāḥ samyagyogayuktāḥ prakṛtihetavo bhavantīti yojyaṃ prakṛtiḥ ārogyam ||
children.translated_text: The construction is that they become causes of disorders. Likewise, when joined with proper conjunction, they become causes of normal condition. <s>Prakṛti</s> means health.

children.text: pūrvādhyāye rogāḥ svarūpamārgabāhyakāraṇabheṣajair abhihitāḥ upayuktajñānās tatkāraṇavātādayo bahuvācyatvān noktāḥ ataḥ samprati pṛthakprakaraṇe te 'bhidhīyante vātakalākalīye tatrāpi prādhānyād vāyureva prathamamucyate
children.translated_text: In the preceding chapter, diseases were described in terms of their own nature, pathways, external causes, and remedies. Their causes, <s>vāta</s> and the rest, though knowledge of them is useful, were not stated because much would have had to be said. Therefore now, in a separate section, they are being explained, in the <s>Vātakalākalīya</s>; and there too, because of its primacy, wind alone is stated first.

children.text: kalā guṇaḥ yaduktaṃ ṣoḍaśakalam iti akalā guṇaviruddho doṣaḥ tena vātakalākalīyo vātaguṇadoṣīya ityarthaḥ yadi vā kalā sūkṣmo bhāgas tasyāpi kalā kalākalā tasyāpi sūkṣmo bhāga ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Kalā</s> means a quality, as in the statement, 'possessed of sixteen kalās.' <s>Akalā</s> means a defect opposed to a quality. Thus <s>Vātakalākalīya</s> means 'that which concerns the qualities and defects of <s>vāta</s>.' Or else <s>kalā</s> means a subtle part; <s>kalākalā</s> means even the kalā of that, that is, an even subtler part.

Here the statement of the qualities of <s>vāta</s> and the others in the form of the words of many seers is meant to show the agreement of many seers, and also to establish that the treatise is furnished with traditional authority as a principle of the system.
'Non-aggregate' means without a collection of parts, unlike <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>.
'Unstable' means having motion as its nature.
'Not to be reached' should be understood as because of its motion and also because its parts are not compact.

children.text: rūkṣādayo bhāvapradhānāḥ tena rūkṣatvādayo guṇā mantavyāḥ
children.translated_text: The words beginning with 'dry' chiefly denote states; therefore the qualities such as dryness are to be understood.

children.text: dāruṇatvaṃ calatvaṃ calatvāt evaṃ dīrghaṃjīvitīyoktaṃ calatvamuktaṃ bhavati yadi vā dāruṇatvaṃ śoṣaṇatvātkāṭhinyaṃ karotīti
children.translated_text: Harshness is mobility; thus, because of mobility, the mobility stated in the <s>Dīrghaṃjīvitīya</s> is expressed. Or else harshness, because it dries, produces hardness.
'<s>Kumāraśiras</s>' is a qualifier of <s>Bharadvāja</s>, meant to exclude <s>Bharadvāja</s>, the teacher of <s>Ātreya</s>.

children.text: evamprabhāvairiti prabhāvād raukṣyādikārakair dhāvanajāgaraṇādibhiḥ prabhāvābhidhānaṃ ca karmaṇāṃ nirguṇatvāt
children.translated_text: 'By effects of such power' means by things that, through their particular power, produce dryness and the like, such as running, staying awake, and so on. The mention of 'power' is because actions have no qualities.
'When repeatedly practiced' means when employed again and again.
'Of bodies' means of the parts of the body.
'Making porous' means making openings.
'A support' means a place having similar qualities.
'Being nourished' means being accumulated.
The opposite of harsh is soft; the opposite of porous is dense.
'Not adhering' means not remaining fixed, that is, having parts that are wasting away.

children.text: etenaitaduktaṃ bhavati yadyapi vāyunā vātakāraṇānāṃ vātaśamanānāṃ vā tathā sambandho nāsti tathāpi śarīrasambaddhais tair vātasya śarīracāriṇaḥ sambandho bhavati tataśca vātasya samānaguṇayogādvṛddhir viparītaguṇayogācca hrāsa upapanna eveti ||
children.translated_text: By this the following is said: although wind has no direct relation in that way with the causes that produce <s>vāta</s>, or with those that pacify <s>vāta</s>, nevertheless those things, when connected with the body, have a relation with <s>vāta</s> as it moves in the body. Therefore the increase of <s>vāta</s> through conjunction with similar qualities, and its decrease through conjunction with opposite qualities, are indeed reasonable.

children.text: śarīrāśarīracarasyeti vātasvarūpakathanaṃ tena śarīreṣu carata iti bahiḥ śarīrebhyo veti ca punaruktaṃ na bhavati ||
children.translated_text: 'Moving in bodies and outside bodies' is a statement of the nature of <s>vāta</s>; therefore saying both 'moving in bodies' and 'outside bodies' is not repetitive.
Here, by saying 'parts,' he shows that complete statement is impossible because the elaboration would be extensive.
'Having established' means having set forth.

Among the actions of <s>vāta</s>, speech and the like are perceptible; the prompting of the mind and the like are inferable; and the shaping of the embryo and the like are known from authoritative teaching.

children.text: tantraṃ śarīraṃ yad uktaṃ tantrayantreṣu bhinneṣu tamo'ntyaṃ pravivikṣatām iti tadeva yantraṃ yadi vā tantrasya yantraṃ saṃdhayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Tantra</s> means the body, as stated: 'when the tantras and yantras are broken, final darkness enters those who wish to enter.' That same thing is the <s>yantra</s>. Or else the <s>yantra</s> of the <s>tantra</s> is the joints.
'Having the nature of <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest' means having <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest as its own form.

children.text: ceṣṭāviśeṣaṇam uccāvacānāṃ vividhānām ityarthaḥ kiṃvā śubhāśubhānāmityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This is a qualification of activity: 'high and low' means varied; or else it means auspicious and inauspicious.

children.text: niyantā anīpsite viṣaye pravartamānasya manasaḥ praṇetā ca manasa evepsite 'rthe ||
children.translated_text: 'Controller' means the guide of the mind when it is proceeding toward an undesired object; and 'director' means the guide of the very same mind toward a desired object.

children.text: udyojakaḥ prerakaḥ kiṃvā udyogakāraka iti pāṭhaḥ so 'pyabhinnārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Instigator' means impeller. Or there is the reading 'producer of effort'; that too has the same meaning.

children.text: abhivoḍhevābhivoḍhā sarvendriyārthagrāhakatvena taccāsya vāyumayena sparśanendriyeṇa sarvendriyāṇāṃ vyāpakatvāt pūrvādhyāyapratipāditena nyāyena boddhavyam ||
children.translated_text: 'Carrier,' or 'the one who carries,' means because it apprehends all objects of the senses. This should be understood according to the principle explained in the preceding chapter: because, through its wind-made tactile sense, it pervades all the senses.
'Arranger' means maker of a collection, that is, maker of structure.

children.text: prakṛtiḥ kāraṇaṃ śabdakāraṇatvaṃ ca vāyor nityam ākāśānupraveśāt uktaṃ hi khādīnyabhidhāya teṣāmekaguṇaḥ pūrvo guṇavṛddhiḥ pare pare iti ||
children.translated_text: 'Source' means cause. The fact that wind is the cause of sound is due to its constant penetration by space. For it has been said, after naming space and the other elements: 'The earlier has one quality; in each later one there is an increase of qualities.'

children.text: tathā punaruktaṃ khādīnyabhidhāya viṣṭaṃ hy aparaṃ pareṇa iti ||
children.translated_text: And again, after naming space and the other elements, it has been repeated: 'For the later is pervaded by the earlier.'

children.text: śravaṇamūlatvaṃ vāyoḥ karṇaśaṣkulīracanāviśeṣe vyāpriyamāṇatvāt mūlaṃ pradhānakāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: Wind is the root of hearing because it operates in the particular formation of the conch of the ear. 'Root' means principal cause.
'Zeal' means the mind's effort in actions.
'Womb' means the cause of manifestation.
'Dryer of the doṣas' means dryer of the bodily moisture.
'Divider' means maker; and this occurs at the time of the production of the body.
The word <s>bhūta</s> denotes its own form.
The division is '<s>upaghātāya</s>.'

children.text: garbhāniti vikṛtim āpādayatyatikālaṃ dhārayatītyanena ca sambadhyate ||
children.translated_text: 'Embryos' is connected with 'it brings them to deformation' and also with 'it carries them beyond the proper time.'
The arrangement of motion of the sun and the others by continuity, without interruption, is the continuous arrangement of motion.
'Of streams' means of rivers.
'Division' means a distinguishing characteristic.

children.text: dhātūnāmiti pṛthivyādīnāṃ dhātavaḥ kāryadravyāṇi prastarādīni mānaṃ parimāṇaṃ saṃsthānamākṛtiḥ tayorvyaktirabhivyaktiḥ tatra kāraṇamiti yāvat ||
children.translated_text: 'Of the elements' means of earth and the others. <s>Dhātus</s> are produced substances such as stones. Measure is dimension; configuration is shape. The manifestation of those two means, in effect, the cause of their manifestation.
The cultivation of a seed, such as rice, is its power to generate a sprout.

children.text: avikledaḥ pākakālād arvāg aviklinnatvam upaśoṣaṇaṃ ca pākena yavādīnāmārdrāṇāmeva avikledopaśoṣaṇe śasyānāmeva ||
children.translated_text: 'Non-wetting' means remaining unmoistened before the time of ripening, and also drying up. In the case of barley and the like, which are moist, non-wetting and drying through ripening apply specifically to crops.

children.text: avaikārikavikāreṇa sarvasminneva jagati prakṛtirūpe kāraṇatvaṃ brūte ||
children.translated_text: By 'a modification without abnormal change,' he states causality in the form of the nature of everything in the entire world.
<s>Śikharin</s> means mountain.
<s>Anokaha</s> means tree.
Upward rolling is <s>udvartana</s>.
<s>Pratisaraṇa</s> is movement in the opposite direction.

children.text: visarjanaṃ visargaḥ sa ca pṛthaṅnīhārādibhiḥ sambadhyate nīhāraḥ śiśirasamūhaḥ nirhrādo meghaṃ vinā garjitam aśaniḥ vajrabhedo'gniḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Visarjana</s> is <s>visarga</s> (release), and it is connected separately with such things as mist. <s>Nīhāra</s> is a mass of cold; <s>nirhrāda</s> is thunder without a cloud; <s>aśani</s> is fire, a splitting thunderbolt.
<s>Asaṃghāta</s> is non-production, or else non-accumulation.
<s>Upasarga</s> is the appearance of pestilence and the like.
In the passage beginning 'clouds and sun,' <s>visarga</s> means creation.

children.text: vāyur iha devatārūpo'bhipretaḥ tena tasya bhūtalacaturyugāntakarānilakaraṇam aviruddham evaṃ yadanyad apy anupapadyamānaṃ vāyos tadapi devatārūpatvenaiva samādheyam ||
children.translated_text: Here wind is intended in the form of a deity. Therefore its being the cause of the wind that ends the four-yuga cycle on the earth is quite consistent. In the same way, whatever else is also not logically fitting in regard to wind should be resolved precisely by taking it as having the form of a deity.

children.text: samprati sāmānyena punaḥ kupitākupitasya vāyoḥ svarūpamucyate sa hi bhagavānityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, in general, the nature of wind, whether aggravated or not aggravated, is again stated in the passage beginning 'for that blessed one'.
<s>Prabhava</s> means cause.
<s>Avyaya</s> means imperishable.
It is to be connected with the following word, 'of beings'.
The distinctions of death, <s>Yama</s>, and the like are to be known from scripture.

children.text: sarvatantrāṇāṃ sarvakarmaṇāṃ tantraśabdaḥ karmavacano'pyasti yaduktaṃ vastistantrāṇāṃ karmaṇāmityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For all <s>tantras</s>, that is, for all actions; the word <s>tantra</s> also denotes action, as has been said. The meaning is 'for the actions of the enema-procedures'.

children.text: pittāntargata iti vacanena śarīre jvālādiyuktavahniniṣedhena pittoṣmarūpasya vahneḥ sadbhāvaṃ darśayati na tu pittādabhedaṃ pitte nāgnimāndyasya grahaṇyadhyāye vakṣyamāṇatvāt tathā pittaharasya sarpiṣo'gnivardhanatvenoktatvāt ||
children.translated_text: By the statement 'included in pitta', while denying in the body a fire furnished with flame and the like, he shows the existence of fire in the form of pitta-heat, but not its non-difference from pitta; for weakness of <s>agni</s> in pitta will be mentioned in the chapter on <s>grahaṇī</s>, and ghee, which alleviates pitta, is likewise said to increase <s>agni</s>.

children.text: paktimapaktimiti avikṛtivikṛtibhedena pācakasyāgneḥ karma darśanādarśane netragatasyālocakasya ūṣmaṇo mātrāmātratvaṃ varṇabhedau ca tvaggatasya bhrājakasya bhayaśauryādayo hṛdayasthasya sādhakasya rañjakasya tu bahiḥsphuṭakāryādarśanād udāharaṇaṃ na kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: By saying 'digestion and non-digestion', he indicates the function of the digestive fire according to the distinction between its normal and abnormal states. For the heat of the visual fire located in the eye, there are seeing and non-seeing; for the illuminative fire located in the skin, there are due measure and lack of due measure and differences of complexion; for the accomplishing fire located in the heart, there are fear, courage, and the like. But no example is given for the coloring fire, because an externally manifest effect is not seen.
<s>Soma</s> is the deity of water, or else the moon.

children.text: pūrvaṃ sāmānyena vātādijanyā gadā uktāḥ sampratyavaśiṣṭān kevalavātādijanyānabhidhātuṃ mahārogādhyāyo'bhidhīyate ||
children.translated_text: Previously, diseases produced by vāta and the other doṣas were stated in general. Now the chapter on major diseases is introduced in order to explain the remaining diseases produced by vāta and the others alone.
Although the adventitious disease has already been mentioned in the <s>Triśothīya</s>, it is mentioned again here in order to explain its signs and so forth specifically.
Here <s>prakṛti</s> means nature.

children.text: manaḥśarīraviśeṣāditi āgantorapi manaḥ śarīraṃ cādhiṣṭhānam evaṃ nijasyāpi āgantugrahaṇena ca mānaso'pi kāmādirgṛhyate
children.translated_text: In the phrase 'from a specific distinction of mind and body', even an adventitious disease has mind and body as its seat. In the same way, even in the case of an innate disease, by the mention of the adventitious, mental conditions such as desire are also included.

children.text: evaṃ caturvidhatvādi pratipādya punaḥ prakārāntareṇāparisaṃkhyeyatāṃ rogāṇāmāha vikārā ityādi
children.translated_text: Having thus taught their fourfoldness and so on, he again states, in another manner, that diseases cannot be enumerated, in the passage beginning 'disorders'.
'Again' means by another manner that is about to be stated.

children.text: prakṛtiḥ pratyāsannaṃ kāraṇaṃ vātādi adhiṣṭhānaṃ dūṣyaṃ liṅgāni lakṣaṇāni āyatanāni bāhyahetavo duṣṭāhārācārāḥ eṣāṃ vikalparūpo viśeṣo vikalpaviśeṣaḥ teṣāmaparisaṃkhyeyatvāditi
children.translated_text: <s>Prakṛti</s> is the proximate cause, such as vāta and the others. The seat is the vitiated substrate. The signs are the symptoms. The bases are external causes, namely corrupt food and conduct. The particular distinction in the form of the alternatives of these is the particular alternative; because these cannot be enumerated.

children.text: atra doṣāḥ saṃsargāṃśāṃśavikalpādibhirasaṃkhyeyāḥ dūṣyāstu śarīrāvayavā aṇuśaḥ parasparamelakena vibhajyamānā asaṃkhyeyāḥ liṅgāni kṛtsnavikāragatānyasaṃkhyeyānyeva āviṣkṛtāni tu tantre kathitāni hetavaścāvāntaraviśeṣādasaṃkhyeyāḥ pravyaktā eva
children.translated_text: Here the doṣas are innumerable through combinations, fractional parts, and fractional variations. The vitiated substrates, however, are the parts of the body, which become innumerable when divided minutely and through mutual combination. The signs that belong to all disorders are themselves innumerable; only the manifest ones have been stated in the treatise. And the causes too are clearly innumerable because of their subordinate distinctions.

children.text: kecit punaḥ eṣāṃ vikārāḥ iti paṭhanti sa tu pāṭho nānumatastāvat yadi ca syāttadā dehamanaḥpratyavamarśakam eṣām iti padaṃ bahuvacanaṃ tu manaḥśarīrayorbahutvavivakṣayā ||
children.translated_text: Some, however, read 'the disorders of these'. But that reading is not accepted. And if it were accepted, then the word 'of these' would refer back to body and mind; the plural would be intended because of the plurality of mind and body.
<s>Mukhāni</s> means causes, as in the expression 'approach to a menstruating woman and other causes of misfortune'.
'Impelling' means cause, because verbal roots have many meanings.
<s>Anubadhnanti</s> means they follow after.

children.text: na saṃdehamāpadyanta iti na saṃdehaviṣayatāmāpadyante miśrībhūtā api pratisvaṃ bhinnairlakṣaṇairbhedena jñāyanta ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'They do not fall into doubt' means that they do not become objects of doubt. Even when mixed together, they are individually recognized as distinct by their own separate signs; this is the meaning.
He states the distinguishing sign of adventitious and innate diseases in the passage beginning 'for an adventitious one'.

children.text: āganturutpannaḥ san vyathāpūrvamiti pīḍāṃ prathamaṃ kṛtvā paścāddoṣāṇāṃ vaiṣamyamiti doṣavaiṣamyalakṣaṇam uktaṃ svalakṣaṇakārakaṃ tu vaiṣamyamāgantorāditaḥprabhṛti vidyamānamapyakiṃcitkaramiti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: An adventitious disease, when arisen, first produces pain, as indicated by the phrase 'preceded by distress', and afterwards produces disequilibrium of the doṣas. The disequilibrium described as marked by doṣa-imbalance and producing its own symptoms is, however, present from the very beginning in an adventitious disease too, but it is ineffectual; this is the sense.

children.text: āgantunijayorbhedakaṃ lakṣaṇamabhidhāya nijavikārakarāṇāṃ vātādīnāṃ bhedajñānārthamāha teṣāmityādi
children.translated_text: Having stated the distinguishing sign of adventitious and innate diseases, he says 'of these' and so on in order to know the distinctions of vāta and the other factors that produce innate disorders.
The receptacle of feces is the colon.

children.text: yadyapi prāṇādibhedabhinnasya vāyoḥ pṛthageva sthānāni vakṣyati yathā sthānaṃ prāṇasya śīrṣoraḥkaṇṭhajihvāsyanāsikāḥ ityādi tathāpīdaṃ vaiśeṣikaṃ sthānaṃ jñeyaṃ yato'tra prāyo vātavikārā bhavanti bhūtāśca durjayāḥ atra ca vijite vāte sarvavātavikārāvajaya iti ||
children.translated_text: Although the separate locations of wind, divided into the forms called <s>prāṇa</s> and the rest, will be stated later, as in 'the locations of <s>prāṇa</s> are the head, chest, throat, tongue, mouth, and nose,' still this should be known as its specific location, because vāta disorders mostly arise here and, once arisen, are difficult to conquer. And when vāta is conquered here, all vāta disorders are conquered.
<s>Lasīkā</s> is the slimy part of water.

children.text: pittasthāneṣu āmāśaya iti āmāśayādhobhāgaḥ śleṣmasthāneṣvāmāśaya āmāśayordhvabhāgaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among the locations of pitta, 'stomach' means the lower part of the stomach; among the locations of phlegm, 'stomach' means the upper part of the stomach.

children.text: sāmānyajā iti vātādibhiḥ pratyekaṃ militaiśca ye janyante ||
children.translated_text: Those born generally are the disorders that are produced by vāta and the other doṣas individually and also when combined.

children.text: nānātmajā iti ye vātādibhir doṣāntarāsaṃpṛktair janyante ||
children.translated_text: Those born from a single source are the disorders produced by vāta and the other doṣas when unmixed with another doṣa.
<s>Vipādikā</s> is cracking of the hands and feet.
<s>Pādabhraṃśa</s> is the falling of the foot somewhere other than the place that is the object of setting the foot down.
<s>Supti</s> is inactivity of the two feet, or insensibility to touch.
<s>Vātakhuḍḍatā</s> is commonly known as <s>cāluka</s>.
By the word <s>gṛdhrasī</s>, the pain of <s>gṛdhrasī</s> is meant.
And by <s>ūrustambha</s>, mere stiffening of the thighs is meant, insofar as it is produced by <s>vāta</s>.
In the same way, in the cases of pain in the ear and in the eye, only the pain itself is meant.
Even in diarrhea caused by <s>vāta</s>, the breaking up of feces is caused by <s>vāta</s>.

children.text: evaṃ ca na gṛdhrasyādīnāṃ sāmānyajatvaṃ yathoktāṃśasya kevalavātajanyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Thus conditions such as <s>gṛdhrasī</s> are not produced by a general cause, because the specified portion, as stated, is produced by <s>vāta</s> alone.
<s>Udarāveṣṭa</s>, abdominal constriction, is like an enclosing of the abdomen.
<s>Aśabdaśravaṇa</s> is hearing sound even when there is no sound.
<s>Uccaiḥśruti</s> is hearing only a high pitch, while a slight sound is not heard at all.
<s>Bādhirya</s> is the non-hearing of sound altogether.
<s>Timira</s>, however, is only <s>vāta</s>-born; the connection there with another <s>doṣa</s> is in the form of a secondary association.

children.text: ekāṅgarogaḥ sarvāṅgarogaśceti jvarādiṣu uṣṇatvaśītatvādīnāṃ kadācid ekāṅgavyāpakatvenaikāṅgarogaḥ teṣāmeva kadācit sarvāṅgavyāpakatvena sarvāṅgarogaḥ doṣāntarasambandhe'pi vyādhyavyāptī vātakṛte eva vāyunā yatra nīyante tatra varṣanti meghavat iti vacanāt ||
children.translated_text: There is one-limb disease and whole-body disease: in fevers and the like, heat, cold, and so on are sometimes pervasive in one limb, and so there is one-limb disease; at other times these same qualities pervade the whole body, and so there is whole-body disease. Even when another <s>doṣa</s> is associated, the pervasions of disease are produced by <s>vāta</s> alone, in accordance with the statement, 'wherever they are led by the wind, there they rain, like clouds.'
Likewise, <s>bhrama</s>, when <s>vātika</s>, has the form of bewilderment of memory.

children.text: atra kasyacidaṅgasya pādādeḥ śūlādayo'bhihitā na hastādīnāṃ tatra ye'bhihitāste pradhānabhūtāḥ prāyobhāvitvena anuktāstu vātavikārāṇām aparisaṃkhyeyatvena grāhyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here pains and the like of some limb, such as the foot, have been stated, but not those of the hands and so forth. Among them, those that have been stated are principal because they generally occur; those not stated are to be understood because the disorders of <s>vāta</s> cannot be exhaustively enumerated.
In the passage beginning 'this belongs to <s>vāyu</s>,' 'this belongs to <s>vāyu</s>' means its own form, its intrinsic nature.
'Unchanging' means established innately, not produced by some other limiting condition.
'And of action' means of the action of deranged <s>vāyu</s>.
'Its own characteristic' means its particular characteristic.

children.text: atrāpyapariṇāmīti sambadhyate apariṇāmīti pittaśleṣmasambandhanirapekṣaṃ na tu śarīrāvayavānapekṣamiti yataḥ brūte taṃ taṃ śarīrāvayavamāviśataḥ iti ata eva ca sraṃsādīnāṃ śarīrāvayavāpekṣatvena na sarvadā bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here too 'unchanging' is to be connected. 'Unchanging' means independent of association with <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s>, not independent of the bodily parts, because he says, 'as it enters this or that bodily part.' For this very reason, since displacement and the others depend on bodily parts, they do not occur at all times.
And in this same way, the intrinsic nature and the rest of <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s> also are to be explained.
'Incorporeality' means invisibility.
'Because it is of such a kind' is to be construed as 'because <s>vāyu</s> is furnished with roughness and the other qualities.'
<s>Sraṃsa</s> is a slight movement from one's own place, whereas <s>bhraṃśa</s> is movement to a distant place.
<s>Vyāsa</s> is spreading out.
<s>Harṣa</s>, horripilation or tingling, is produced because <s>vāyu</s> is unstable, or else by its specific power.
<s>Varta</s> is making something circular.
<s>Cāla</s> is tremor.
Taste and color are produced by <s>vāyu</s> through its specific power, even though <s>vāyu</s> itself is devoid of taste and color.
Because it has come up in the present topic, he states the therapeutic rule in the passage beginning 'that with sweet,' and so on.
'Right from the beginning' means very quickly.
'Purely pathological' means productive of all disorders.

children.text: saṃgrahe saṃgraha iti catvāro rogā ityādisaṃkṣepoktiḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the summary, 'summary' refers to the concise statement beginning 'there are four diseases,' and so on.
'Nature' refers to the passage beginning 'again it is twofold,' and so on.
'Place' refers to the passage beginning 'and their substratum is twofold,' and so on.

children.text: vikārāśca mukhaṃ ca vikāramukhaṃ tatra vikārāḥ punaḥ ityādinā vikārāḥ mukhāni ityādinā mukham ||
children.translated_text: The disorders and the mouths of disorder are the 'disorder-mouth'; there, the disorders are taught in the passage beginning 'the disorders again,' and the mouth is taught in the passage beginning 'the mouths,' and so on.
In the passage beginning 'but of the two,' and so on, there is impelling.
'Freedom from doubt' refers to the passage beginning 'and not mutually,' and so on.
'In all,' and so on, refers to secondary association.
The statement that all are <s>nānātmaja</s> means that they are said to be produced by a <s>doṣa</s> not mixed with another <s>doṣa</s>.

After stating one part of what is wholesome and unwholesome, the <s>Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya</s>, which teaches taste, potency, and digestive transformation, is explained in order to know the wholesomeness and unwholesomeness of substances as a whole.

children.text: tatrāpi vipākādīnāmapi rasenaiva prāyo lakṣaṇīyatvādrasaprakaraṇam ādau kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: There also, because digestive transformation and the others are generally to be characterized by taste itself, the section on taste has been placed first.
The prima facie view is first set forth through the opinions of sages, and the established conclusion is then fixed for the instruction of the student.

children.text: rasenāhāraviniścayo rasāhāraviniścayaḥ kiṃvā ayaṃ rasaviniścayaḥ tathā paraṃ cāto vipākānām ityādirāhāraviniścayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Determination of food by taste is <s>rasāhāraviniścaya</s>; or else this is the determination of taste, and the following passage beginning 'and next, concerning the digestive transformations' is the determination of food.
The passage beginning 'there is one only,' and so on.
In 'of the objects of the senses,' the genitive is used for specification.

children.text: anyatamam iti ekam anyaśabdo hy ayamekavacanaḥ yathānyo dakṣiṇena gato 'nya uttareṇa eka ityarthaḥ tam appratyayaśca svārthikaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Any one' means one. For this word <s>anya</s> is singular, as in, 'one went to the south, another to the north'; the meaning is 'one.' And the suffix <s>tamap</s> is used in its own sense.
'Pertaining to the tongue' means grasped by the tongue.
Even the absence of taste is perceived by the tongue; therefore he says 'an existent thing.'

children.text: udakādananya iti rasodakayor ekatvakhyāpanārthaṃ pūrvapakṣatvād aduṣṭam ||
children.translated_text: 'Not different from water' is not faulty because, as a prima facie view, it is meant to declare the identity of taste and water.
And this prima facie view is theirs according to the doctrine of <s>Kapila</s>.

children.text: hi rasatanmātraṃ gandhatanmātram ityādivacanena guṇāvyatiriktaṃ dravyamiti bruvate ||
children.translated_text: For, with statements such as 'the subtle element of taste, the subtle element of smell,' they say that substance is not distinct from quality.
'To be cut down' means causing depletion.
'To be pacified' means nourishing.

children.text: sādhāraṇa ityāgneyasaumyasāmānyād ubhayor api laṅghanabṛṃhaṇayoḥ kartā parasparavirodhādakartā vā ||
children.translated_text: 'Common' means that, because of the commonality of both fiery and lunar natures, it may perform both depletion and nourishment; or, because these are mutually opposed, it may perform neither.

children.text: svāduriti abhīṣṭaḥ hita iti āyatāv anapakārī ||
children.translated_text: 'Sweet' means desired; 'wholesome' means not harmful in the long run.

children.text: āśrīyata ityāśrayo dravyaṃ guṇāḥ snigdhagurvādayaḥ karma dhātuvardhanakṣapaṇādi saṃsvādaḥ rasānām avāntarabhedaḥ eṣāṃ viśeṣāṇāṃ bhedānām ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Substrate" is so called because something rests upon it; it is the substance. The qualities are oiliness, heaviness, and the like. Action is such things as increasing and diminishing the bodily tissues. <s>Saṃsvāda</s> is a subsidiary distinction among tastes. "Of these distinctions" means "of these differences."

children.text: tatra dravyabhedād ādhārabhedenāśritasyāpi rasasya bhedo bhavati āśrayo hi kāraṇaṃ kāraṇabhedācca kāryabhedo 'vaśyaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, because substances differ, that is, because supports differ, even the taste that rests on them differs. For the support is a cause, and when the cause differs, the effect necessarily differs.
Likewise, differences in qualities such as heaviness and differences in actions are produced by taste itself.

children.text: tataś ca kāryabhedādavaśyaṃ kāraṇabheda iti pūrvapakṣābhiprāyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Consequently, from a difference in effect there is necessarily a difference in cause: this is the intention of the prima facie view.

children.text: saṃsvādabhedastu ekasyām api madhurajātāv ikṣukṣīraguḍādigataḥ pratyakṣameva bhedo dṛśyate sa tu saṃsvādabhedaḥ svasaṃvedya eva yaduktam ikṣukṣīraguḍādīnāṃ mādhuryasyāntaraṃ mahat ||
children.translated_text: But a difference of <s>saṃsvāda</s> is directly seen even within a single class of sweetness, as in sugarcane, milk, jaggery, and the like. That difference of savor is known only by one's own experience, as has been said: the difference in the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, jaggery, and so on is great.
Even so, that difference cannot be described even by <s>Sarasvatī</s>.
He states the settled conclusion by the statement of <s>Punarvasu</s>, in the passage beginning "There are only six," and so on.
He states the arrangement, mentioned in the prima facie view, concerning the unity and so forth of taste, in the passage beginning "Of those six," and so on.

children.text: yoniḥ ādhārakāraṇaṃ kāryakāraṇayośca bhedāt siddha udakādrasabhedaḥ pratyakṣa eveti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Source" means the supporting cause. And because effect and cause are distinct, the difference of taste from water and the like is established and directly perceptible: this is the sense.

children.text: kṣitivyatiriktam udakameva yathā rasayonistathā rasanārtho rasastasya ityādau vivṛtameva dīrghaṃjīvitīye ||
children.translated_text: How water alone, apart from earth, is the source of taste, and how taste is the object of the organ of taste, has already been explained in the <s>Dīrghaṃjīvitīya</s> and related passages.

children.text: tayormiśrībhāvāditi karmaṇor amūrtayor miśrībhāvānupapattau tadādhārayor dravyayor miśrībhāvāditi boddhavyam ||
children.translated_text: In the phrase "because of the mixture of the two," since mixture is impossible for the two incorporeal actions, it should be understood as the mixture of the two substances that are their supports.
"Common" means possessing a common effect.
"Inclination" means desire.

children.text: tena yo yamicchati sa tasya svādurasvāduritara iti puruṣāpekṣau dharmau na rasabhedakāryāv ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, whatever a person desires is tasty for him, and what he does not desire is otherwise. These two properties depend on the person and are not effects that distinguish taste.

children.text: pañcamahābhūtetyādau tuśabdo 'vadhāraṇe tena āśrayā eva na rasā ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the passage beginning "the five great elements," the particle <s>tu</s> is restrictive. Therefore the substrates alone are meant, not the tastes.

children.text: kiṃbhūtā bhaumādayo bhūtavikārā āśrayā ityāha prakṛtivikṛtivicāradeśakālavaśā iti vaśaśabdo 'dhīnārthaḥ sa ca prakṛtyādibhiḥ pratyekaṃ yojyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: What sort of element-modifications, beginning with the earthy, are the substrates? He answers: they are dependent on nature, modification, preparation, place, and time. The word "dependent" means "subject to," and it is to be connected separately with nature and the other factors.

children.text: tatra prakṛtivaśā yathā mudgāḥ kaṣāyā madhurāśca santaḥ prakṛtyā laghavaḥ etaddhi lāghavaṃ na rasavaśaṃ tathāhi sati kaṣāyamadhuratvād gurutvaṃ syāt vikṛtivaśaṃ ca vrīher lājānāṃ laghutvaṃ tathā saktusiddhapiṇḍakānāṃ ca gurutvaṃ vicāraṇā vicāro dravyāntarasaṃyoga ityarthaḥ tena vicāraṇāvaśaṃ yathā madhusarpiṣī saṃyukte viṣaṃ tathā viṣaṃ cāgadasaṃyuktaṃ svakāryavyatiriktakāryakāri deśo dvividho bhūmir āturaśca tatra bhūmau śvetakāpotī valmīkādhirūḍhā viṣaharī tathā himavati bheṣajāni mahāguṇāni bhavanti śarīradeśe yathā sakthimāṃsād gurutaraṃ skandhakroḍaśiraspadām ityādi kālavaśaṃ tu yathā mūlakamadhikṛtyoktaṃ tadbālaṃ doṣaharaṃ vṛddhaṃ tridoṣaṃ tathā yathartupuṣpaphalam ādadīta ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Among these, dependence on nature is as follows: mung beans, though astringent and sweet, are by nature light; this lightness is not dependent on taste, for if it were, they would be heavy because they are astringent and sweet. Dependence on modification is the lightness of parched grains made from rice, and likewise the heaviness of balls prepared from roasted flour. "Preparation" means treatment, that is, conjunction with another substance. Thus, by dependence on preparation, honey and ghee when combined become poison; likewise poison combined with an antidote produces an effect other than its own. Place is twofold: land and the patient. With respect to land, white <s>kāpotī</s> growing on an anthill counteracts poison; likewise medicines in the Himalaya have great virtues. With respect to bodily location, the flesh of the shoulder, flank, head, and feet is heavier than thigh flesh, and so on. Dependence on time is as stated with reference to radish: when young it removes <s>doṣas</s>, but when old it has the three <s>doṣas</s>; likewise, one should take flowers and fruits according to the season, and so on.

children.text: atra caikaprakaraṇoktā ye 'nuktās te cakārāt svabhāvādiṣvevāntarbhāvanīyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: And here, whatever items are stated in the same section but not mentioned here are, because of the word "and," to be included under intrinsic nature and the other factors.

children.text: yaduktaṃ caraḥ śarīrāvayavāḥ svabhāvo dhātavaḥ kriyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: As has been said: conduct, bodily parts, intrinsic nature, tissues, and actions,

children.text: liṅgaṃ pramāṇaṃ saṃskāro mātrā cāsmin parīkṣyate iti ||
children.translated_text: as well as sign, measure, processing, and quantity, are examined in this matter.

children.text: tatra caraśarīrāvayavadhātūnāṃ deśena grahaṇaṃ mātrā vicāre praviśati śeṣaṃ svabhāve tathā rasavimāne vakṣyamāṇaṃ cātrāpraviṣṭam āhāraviśeṣāyatanam antarbhāvanīyaṃ yathāsambhavam ||
children.translated_text: There, conduct, bodily parts, and tissues are included under place; quantity enters under preparation; and the remainder comes under intrinsic nature. Also, the special bases of food that will be stated in the <s>Rasavimāna</s> but are not included here should be included as far as possible.

children.text: snigdharūkṣādyā ityatrādigrahaṇenānuktā api tīkṣṇamṛdvādayo na rasāḥ kiṃtu dravyaguṇāḥ pṛthageveti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: In "oily, dry, and so forth," by the inclusion of "and so forth" he shows that unmentioned qualities such as sharp and soft are not tastes, but separate qualities of substances.

children.text: kṣaraṇāt adhogamanakriyāyogāt kṣāro dravyaṃ nāsau rasaḥ rasasya hi niṣkriyasya kriyānupapannetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because it flows, that is, because it is connected with the action of downward movement, <s>kṣāra</s> is a substance, not a taste. For action is not possible in taste, which is inactive.

children.text: kṣaraṇaṃ ca kṣārasya pānīyayuktasyādhogamanena vadanti hi laukikāḥ kṣāraṃ srāvayāmaḥ iti śāstraṃ ca chittvā chittvāśayāt kṣāraḥ kṣaratvāt kṣārayatyadhaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: And people speak of the flowing of <s>kṣāra</s> when it moves downward after being mixed with water; ordinary people say, "We make the <s>kṣāra</s> drain." Scripture too says: "Having cut and cut, <s>kṣāra</s> from the receptacle, because it flows, makes things flow downward."

children.text: hetvantaram āha dravyaṃ tadanekarasotpannam iti anekarasebhyo muṣkakāpāmārgādibhya utpannam anekarasotpannaṃ yataś cānekarasotpannam ata evānekarasaṃ kāraṇaguṇānuvidhāyitvāt kāryaguṇasyeti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He gives another reason: "that substance is produced from many tastes." It is produced from many taste-bearing sources such as <s>muṣkaka</s> and <s>apāmārga</s>, and so it is produced from many tastes. And because it is produced from many tastes, it therefore has many tastes, since the quality of the effect follows the qualities of the causes: this is the sense.
He states precisely its possession of many tastes: "mostly pungent and salty."
By the word "mostly," he shows that there is connection with other, non-principal tastes.
He states another reason: "endowed with the objects of several senses."

children.text: kṣāro hi sparśena gandhena cānvitaḥ tena dravyaṃ rase hi guṇe na sparśo nāpi gandha iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For <s>kṣāra</s> is endowed with touch and smell. Therefore it is a substance, since in taste, which is a quality, there is neither touch nor smell: this is the sense.

children.text: hetvantaramāha karaṇābhinirvṛttamiti karaṇena bhasmaparisrāvaṇādinābhinirvṛttaṃ kṛtam ityarthaḥ na raso 'nena prakāreṇa kriyata iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He states another reason: "produced by an instrument." That is, it is produced, or made, by an instrument or procedure such as the filtering of ash; taste is not made in this manner: this is the sense.
He rejects the position that there is an unmanifest taste with the passage beginning, "the becoming unmanifest," and so on.

children.text: avyaktībhāva ityabhūtatadbhāve cvipratyayena rasānāṃ madhurādīnāṃ vyaktānām eva kvacidādhāre 'vyaktatvaṃ nānyo madhurādibhyo 'vyaktarasa ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Becoming unmanifest" means, by the suffix <s>cvi</s> in the sense of becoming what it was not, that tastes such as sweet, which are themselves manifest, have unmanifestness in some substrate. The meaning is that there is no unmanifest taste other than sweet and the rest.
"Of tastes" means of the six, sweet and the rest.
The passage beginning, "in the original state," and so on.
"In the original state" means in the cause, that is, in water.

children.text: avyaktatvaṃ ca rasasāmānyamātropalabdhir madhurādiviśeṣaśūnyā sā ca jale bhavati yata uktaṃ jalaguṇakathane suśrute vyaktarasatā rasadoṣaḥ iti ihāpi ca avyaktarasaṃ ca iti vakṣyati loke'pi cāvyaktarasaṃ dravyamāsvādya vaktāro vadanti jalasyevāsya raso na kaścin madhurādir vyakta iti ||
children.translated_text: And unmanifestness is the apprehension of only taste in general, devoid of specific distinctions such as sweet. This occurs in water, since, when describing the qualities of water, <s>Suśruta</s> says, "having manifest taste is a defect of taste." Here too he will say, "and unmanifest in taste." In ordinary life also, after tasting a substance with unmanifest taste, speakers say, "Like water, this has no taste such as sweet that is manifest."
And the non-apprehension of a specific taste such as sweet is due to its not having become manifest.

children.text: yathā dūrād avijñāyamānaviśeṣavarṇe vastuni rūpasāmānyapratītir bhavati na śuklatvādiviśeṣabuddhiḥ tathānurase 'vyaktībhāvo bhavati pradhānaṃ vyaktaṃ rasamanugato 'vyaktatvenetyanurasaḥ yathā veṇuyave madhure kaṣāyo 'nurasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as, in an object whose specific color is not recognized from afar, there is an apprehension of color in general but no cognition of a specific feature such as whiteness, so in a secondary taste there is a becoming unmanifest. A secondary taste is so called because, following after the principal manifest taste, it is unmanifest; for example, in bamboo-rice, which is sweet, the astringent taste is the secondary taste.

children.text: yaduktaṃ rūkṣaḥ kaṣāyānuraso madhuraḥ kaphapittahā iti ||
children.translated_text: For it has been said: "Sweet, dry, with an astringent secondary taste, removes <s>kapha</s> and <s>pitta</s>."

children.text: anurasasamanvita iti sarvānurasayukte yathā viṣe vacanaṃ hi uṣṇam anirdeśyarasam ityādi ||
children.translated_text: "Accompanied by secondary tastes" means joined with all secondary tastes, as in the statement about poison: "hot and of indescribable taste," and so on.

children.text: kiṃvā aṇurasasamanvite iti pāṭhas tena aṇurasenaikena maricena śarkarāpānake kaṭutvam avyaktaṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: Or else the reading is "accompanied by a minute taste." By that, through one minute taste, as when one black pepper is in a sugar drink, pungency would be unmanifest.
He faults the position that tastes are innumerable with the passage beginning, "not," and so on.

children.text: teṣāmiti rasānām aparisaṃkhyeyatvaṃ na yuktam āśrayādīnāṃ bhāvānāmiti āśrayaguṇakarmasaṃsvādānām viśeṣāparisaṃkhyeyatvāditi āśrayādibhedasyāparisaṃkhyeyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: "Their" means the tastes. It is not proper that they should be innumerable because of the things consisting in substrates and so on; that is, because the specific distinctions of substrates, qualities, actions, and savors are innumerable, since the divisions of substrate and the rest are innumerable.
Here he states the reason with the passage beginning, "For even each single one," and so on.

children.text: eṣāmāśrayaguṇakarmasaṃsvādānāṃ viśeṣān ekaiko 'pi madhurādir āśrayate na ca tasmād āśrayādibhedād anyatvam āśritasya madhurāder bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Even each single taste, such as sweet, rests upon the specific distinctions of these substrates, qualities, actions, and savors; but because of that difference in substrate and so forth, the sweet taste and the rest, which rest upon them, do not become different entities.

children.text: evaṃ manyate yadyapi śālimudgaghṛtakṣīrādayo madhurasyāśrayā bhinnāḥ tathāpi tatra madhuratvajātyākrānta eka eva raso bhavati balākākṣīrakārpāsādiṣu śuklavarṇa iva ||
children.translated_text: He means this: although rice, mung beans, ghee, milk, and so on, as substrates of sweetness, are different, still there is one and the same taste there, pervaded by the class-character of sweetness, just as there is white color in cranes, milk, cotton, and the like.

children.text: tathā guṇānāṃ gurupicchilasnigdhādīnāmanyatve 'pi karmaṇāṃ vā rasādivardhanāyurjananavarṇakaratvādīnāṃ bhinnatve satyapi na madhurarasasyānyatvaṃ yata eka eva madhuras tattadguṇayukto bhavati tatkarmakārī ceti ko virodhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, even though qualities such as heaviness, sliminess, and oiliness are different, or even though actions such as increasing <s>rasa</s> and the other bodily constituents, producing longevity, and improving complexion are different, the sweet taste does not become different; for one and the same sweet taste is joined with those respective qualities and performs those respective actions. What contradiction is there?

children.text: tathā madhurasyāvāntarāsvādabhede 'pi madhuratvajātyanatikramaḥ kṛṣṇavarṇāvāntarabhede yathā kṛṣṇatvānatikramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Similarly, even when sweetness has a difference of subordinate savors, it does not transgress the class-character of sweetness, just as, when black color has subordinate differences, there is no transgression of blackness.

children.text: nanu maivaṃ bhavatv aparisaṃkhyeyatvaṃ rasānāṃ parasparasaṃyogāt tu ya āsvādaviśeṣaḥ sa kāryaviśeṣakaro 'pi na hi yanmadhurāmlena kriyate tanmadhureṇa vāmlena vā śakyam atastena parasparasaṃyogenāparisaṃkhyeyatvaṃ bhaviṣyatītyāha parasparetyādi ||
children.translated_text: But one may object: let it be so; let there be no innumerability of tastes. Yet because of the mutual combination of tastes, the specific savor produced is also a producer of a specific effect. For what is done by sweet combined with sour cannot be done by sweet alone or by sour alone. Therefore, through that mutual combination, there will be innumerability. To this he replies with the passage beginning, "mutually," and so on.

children.text: saṃsṛṣṭam iti bhāve ktaḥ tena parasparasaṃsargabhūyiṣṭhatvād eṣāṃ madhurādīnām abhinirvṛtterna guṇaprakṛtīnām asaṃkhyeyatvam iti yojanā ayamarthaḥ yadyapi rasāḥ parasparasaṃsargeṇātibhūyasā yuktāḥ santo 'bhinirvṛttā dvirasādau dravye bhavanti tathāpi na teṣāṃ guṇā gurulaghvādayaḥ prakṛtayo vā madhurādīnāṃ yā yā āyuṣyatvarasābhivardhakatvādyās tā asaṃkhyeyā bhavanti kiṃtu ya eva madhurādīnāṃ pratyekaṃ guṇāḥ prakṛtayaśca uddiṣṭāsta eva miśrā bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: "Combined" has the affix <s>kta</s> in the abstract sense. Thus the construction is: because these tastes such as sweet are for the most part produced through mutual association, the qualities and natures are not innumerable. The meaning is this: although tastes, being very greatly joined by mutual association, come into being in a substance possessing two tastes and so on, still their qualities, such as heaviness and lightness, or their natures, namely those of sweet and the rest, such as promoting longevity and increasing <s>rasa</s>, do not become innumerable. Rather, the very same qualities and natures assigned separately to sweet and the other tastes become mixed.

children.text: kiṃvā guṇaprakṛtīnāmiti madhurādiṣaḍguṇasvarūpāṇām ityarthaḥ tena rasasya rasāntarasaṃsarge doṣāṇāmiva doṣāntarasaṃsarge rasānāṃ nāparisaṃkhyeyatvam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or else "of qualities and natures" means of the six forms of qualities, sweet and the rest. Therefore, when one taste is associated with another taste, there is no innumerability of tastes, just as, when one <s>doṣa</s> is associated with another <s>doṣa</s>, the <s>doṣas</s> do not become innumerable.

children.text: prakṛtiśabdena karma vocyate tena guṇakarmaṇām ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By the word "nature," action is meant; therefore the meaning is "of qualities and actions."
Even the specific subordinate savor of sweet and the other tastes should be understood as caused by mutual association.

children.text: yata eva heto rasānāṃ saṃsṛṣṭānāṃ nānye guṇakarmaṇī bhavataḥ ata eva saṃsṛṣṭānāṃ rasānāṃ pṛthakkarma śāstrāntare 'pi noktam ityāha tasmād ityādi ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason, because combined tastes do not have different qualities and actions, the separate action of combined tastes is not stated even in another treatise. He says this with the passage beginning, "therefore," and so on.

children.text: karmaśabdeneha gauravalāghavādikārakā gurutvādayo rasaraktādijananādayaś cāpi boddhavyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here, by the word "action," one should understand both heaviness and the like, which cause heaviness, lightness, and so forth, and also the production of <s>rasa</s>, blood, and the other bodily constituents.

children.text: na kevalam anyaśāstrakārai rasānāṃ saṃsṛṣṭānāṃ karma nopadiṣṭaṃ kiṃtu vayamapi nopadekṣyāma ityāha taccaivetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Not only have other authors of treatises not taught the action of combined tastes, but we too will not teach it; he says this with the passage beginning, "and that very," and so on.
"That very cause" means the fact that, even in mutual association, the tastes have no additional qualities or actions.
Distinctness by definition is definitional distinctness.

children.text: tatra lakṣyate yena tallakṣaṇam atastu madhuro rasaḥ ityādinā granthena tathā snehanaprīṇanahlādana ityādinā ca yadvācyaṃ tat sarvaṃ gṛhyate ||
children.translated_text: In this context, a definition is that by which something is characterized. Therefore, by the passage beginning 'the sweet <s>rasa</s> (taste)' and likewise by the passage beginning 'uncting, nourishing, gladdening,' everything that is to be denoted by those words is included.

children.text: kiṃvā lakṣaṇaśabdena madhuro rasa ityādigranthavācyaṃ lakṣaṇam ucyate pṛthaktvaṃ ca rasabhedajñānārthaṃ yad vakṣyati snehanaprīṇana ityādi tad gṛhyate ||
children.translated_text: Or else, by the word 'definition' is meant the defining mark denoted by the passage beginning 'the sweet <s>rasa</s>.' And by 'separateness' is included what he will state, beginning 'uncting and nourishing,' for the sake of knowing the distinctions among tastes.
'But later,' and so on.

children.text: raseṣu vācyeṣu dravyabhedam abhipretya pratipādanīyatayā parigṛhya rasānāṃ dravyajñānādhīnajñānatvād dravyābhidhānam agre kṛtam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: With regard to the tastes that are to be described, the statement of substances is made first because their difference as substances is intended, because they are taken as what is to be taught, and because knowledge of tastes depends on knowledge of substances. This is the meaning.

children.text: kiṃciditi āyurvedopayogidravyasvarūpaṃ na sarvam aprasaṅgadoṣād iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Somewhat' means the nature of substances useful for Ayurveda, not all substances, because otherwise there would be the fault of irrelevance. This is the intention.
'Every substance' means an effect-substance.
'In this matter' means in this topic.

children.text: dravāntā iti vacanena pūrvoktān viṃśatiguṇān āha ||
children.translated_text: By the statement 'ending with fluid,' he indicates the twenty qualities mentioned earlier.

children.text: atra ca paratvāparatvādīnām ihānabhidhānena cikitsāyāṃ paratvādīnām aprādhānyaṃ darśayati ye 'pi tatrāpi yuktisaṃyogaparimāṇasaṃskārābhyāsā atyarthacikitsopayogino 'pi na te pārthivādidravyāṇāṃ śabdādivat sāṃsiddhikāḥ kiṃ tarhy ādheyāḥ ata iha naisargikaguṇakathane noktāḥ ||
children.translated_text: And here, by not mentioning priority, posteriority, and the like, he shows that in therapy priority and the others are not principal. Even though, in therapy too, reasoning, conjunction, measure, processing, and habituation are extremely useful, they are not innate in substances made of earth and the other elements in the way that sound and the rest are. Rather, they are superimposed. Therefore they have not been stated here in the discussion of natural qualities.
'It has been stated' means in the <s>Apāmārgataṇḍulīya</s>.
And this is said because of its predominance; therefore strengthening and the other effects too should be understood.

children.text: bahulaśabdo gurvādibhiḥ pratyekaṃ sambadhyate kiṃvā gandhenaiva yato gandhaguṇabahulā pṛthivyeva bhavati ata eva dravyāntaralakṣaṇe 'pi vaiśeṣikaguṇo 'nta eva paṭhyate rasaguṇabahulāni ityādi tena tatrāpi rasādibhir eva bahulaśabdo yojyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The word 'abundant' is connected with heavy and the other qualities individually. Or else it is connected only with smell, because earth alone is abundant in the quality of smell. For this very reason, even in the definition of another substance, the distinctive quality alone is recited at the end, as in 'those abundant in the quality of taste,' and so forth. Therefore there too the word 'abundant' should be joined precisely with taste and the others.
Although all effect-substances are made of the five elements, their being earthy and so on should be understood by the predominance of earth and the other elements.
'Massiveness' means hardness; 'stability' means immovability.
'Binding' means mutual joining; 'refreshment' means satisfaction of the body and senses.
'Subtle' means following the subtle channels.

children.text: prabhā varṇaprakāśinī dīptiḥ yaduktaṃ varṇamākrāmati chāyā prabhā varṇaprakāśikā ityādi ||
children.translated_text: 'Radiance' is brilliance that illuminates color. As has been said: shadow overlays color; radiance illuminates color, and so on.
'Movement' means motion; that is the sense.
'Porosity' means abundance of holes.

children.text: atrākāśabāhulyaṃ dravyasya pṛthivyādibhūtāntarālpatvena bhūrivyaktākāśatvena ca jñeyaṃ yadeva bhūriśuṣiraṃ tannābhasaṃ kiṃvā ākāśaguṇabahulatvena nābhasaṃ dravyam ityucyate ||
children.translated_text: Here abundance of ether in a substance should be understood through the smallness of the other elements such as earth and through a great manifestation of ether. That which has many cavities is etherial. Or else, because of abundance in the qualities of ether, a substance is called etherial.

children.text: aneneti pratiniyatadravyaguṇopadeśena yat pārthivādi dravyaṃ yadguṇaṃ tadguṇe dehe saṃpādye tad bheṣajaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By this, that is, by the instruction about substances and qualities that are fixed in each case, the meaning is that an earthy or other substance becomes a medicine when that same quality is to be produced in the body.

children.text: tacca pārthivādi dravyaṃ na sarvathā na ca sarvasmin vyādhau bheṣajamityāha tāṃ tāṃ yuktim ityādi ||
children.translated_text: And that earthy or other substance is not a medicine in every respect or in every disease. He says this with the words beginning 'that particular application.'

children.text: yuktim iti upāyam arthamiti prayojanam abhipretyeti adhikṛtya tena kenacidupāyena kvacit prayojane kiṃcid dravyamauṣadhaṃ bhavati na sarvatra ||
children.translated_text: 'Application' means a means; 'object' means a purpose; 'having regard to' means taking as the topic. Therefore some substance becomes a medicine by some particular means, for some particular purpose, in some particular case, not everywhere.

children.text: tena yaducyate vairodhikānāṃ sarvadāpathyatvena nānauṣadhaṃ dravyam iti vaco virodhi tanna bhavati vairodhikāni hi saṃyogasaṃskāradeśakālādyapekṣāṇi bhavanti vairodhikasaṃyogādyabhāve tu pathyānyapi kvacit syuḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, when it is said that, because incompatible things are always unwholesome, the statement 'there is no substance that is not medicine' is contradictory, that is not so. For incompatible things depend on conjunction, processing, place, time, and so forth; but in the absence of an incompatible conjunction and the like, they too may be wholesome in some case.

children.text: yānyapi sarvadāpi svabhāvādeva viṣamandakādīnyapathyāni tānyapy upāyayuktāni kvacit pathyāni bhavanti yathā udare viṣasya tilaṃ dadyāt ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Even those things, such as poison and mandaka, that are always unwholesome by their very nature may become wholesome somewhere when joined with an appropriate method, as in the statement, 'In abdominal disease one should give a sesame-seed measure of poison,' and so on.

children.text: yattu tṛṇapāṃśuprabhṛtīni nopayujyante ato na tāni bheṣajānītyucyate tanna teṣāmapi bheṣajasvedādyupāyatvena bheṣajatvāt ||
children.translated_text: But the claim that grass, dust, and the like are not used, and therefore they are not medicines, is not correct, because they too have the status of medicine as means for medicinal sweating and the like.

children.text: pārthivādidravyāṇāṃ gurukharādiguṇayogād bheṣajatvam uktaṃ tena guṇaprabhāvādeva bheṣajaṃ syāditi śaṅkāṃ nirasyann āha na tu kevalam ityādi ||
children.translated_text: It has been said that earthy and other substances have the status of medicine because they are connected with qualities such as heaviness and roughness. Rejecting the doubt that a thing might be a medicine through the power of qualities alone, he says 'but not merely,' and so on.

children.text: dravyaprabhāvād yathā dantyā virecakatvaṃ tathā maṇīnāṃ viṣādihantṛtvam ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Through the power of substance, for example, <s>dantī</s> has purgative capacity, and jewels have the capacity to counteract poison and the like.

children.text: guṇaprabhāvādyathā jvare tiktako rasaḥ śīte 'gnir ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Through the power of qualities, for example, bitter taste is useful in fever, fire in cold, and so on.

children.text: dravyaguṇaprabhāvād yathā kṛṣṇājinasyoparīti atrāpi kṛṣṇatvaṃ guṇo'jinaṃ ca dravyamabhipretaṃ yathā vā maṇḍalair jātarūpasya tasyā eva payaḥ śṛtam tatra maṇḍalaguṇayuktasyaiva jātarūpasya kārmukatvam ||
children.translated_text: Through the power of substance and quality together, as in the case of sitting on a black antelope skin. There too blackness is intended as the quality, and the skin as the substance. Or again, as in 'the same milk boiled with disks of gold'; there the efficacy belongs only to gold furnished with the quality of disk-form.
How do they act? He answers with the words beginning 'in each and every case.'

children.text: tāṃ tāṃ yuktimāsādyeti tāṃ tāṃ yojanāṃ prāpya ||
children.translated_text: 'Having obtained that particular application' means having reached that particular arrangement.

children.text: yat kurvantītyādāv udāharaṇaṃ yathā śirovirecanadravyāṇi yacchirovirecanaṃ kurvanti tac chirovirecanaṃ karma yenoṣṇatvādikāraṇena śirovirecanaṃ kurvanti tadvīryaṃ vīryaṃ śaktiḥ sā ca dravyasya guṇasya vā yatra śirovirecanaṃ kurvanti tadadhikaraṇaṃ śiraḥ nānyatrādhikaraṇe śirovirecanadravyaṃ prabhavatītyarthaḥ yadeti vasantādau śirogauravādiyukte ca kāle etenākāle śīte śirovirecanaṃ stabdhatvānna kārmukaṃ kiṃtu svakāla eva yathā yena prakāreṇa pradhamanāvapīḍanādinā tathā prasāritāṅgamuttānaṃ śayane saṃstarāstṛte ||
children.translated_text: In the example beginning 'what they do': for instance, the substances for <s>śirovirecana</s> (head-clearing therapy) perform head-clearing; that is the action called <s>śirovirecana</s>. That by reason of which, such as heat and the like, they perform head-clearing is their <s>vīrya</s> (potency). <s>Vīrya</s> means power, and that may belong to a substance or to a quality. The place where they perform head-clearing, the locus, is the head. The meaning is that a head-clearing substance does not operate in another locus. 'When' means at a time such as spring, or at a time accompanied by heaviness of the head and the like. By this it is indicated that head-clearing in the wrong season, in cold weather, is not effective because of stiffness, but only in its proper season. 'How' means by whatever method, such as blowing or squeezing into the nostrils. Thus, with the limbs extended, lying face-up on a bed covered with bedding,

children.text: īṣat pralambaśirasaṃ saṃveśya cāvṛtekṣaṇam ityādinā vidhinā kurvanti sa upāyaḥ yat sādhayanti śirogauravaśūlādyuparamaṃ tat phalaṃ phalam uddeśyam ||
children.translated_text: and, according to the rule beginning 'having seated him with the head slightly hanging down and with the eyes covered,' they perform it. That is the means. What they accomplish, namely the cessation of heaviness of the head, pain, and the like, is the result. The result is the intended aim.

children.text: karma kāryaṃ sādhanam uddeśyaṃ phalaṃ sādhyaṃ yathā yāganiṣpādyo dharmaḥ kāryatayā karma tajjanyastu svargādir uddeśyaḥ phalam evaṃ vamanādiṣvapi karmādhikaraṇādyunneyam ||
children.translated_text: Action is what is to be done, the instrument is what accomplishes, and the intended aim is the result, what is to be accomplished. For example, the <s>dharma</s> produced by sacrifice is the action in the sense of what is to be done, while heaven and the like produced by it are the intended aim, the result. In the same way, in emesis and the other procedures too, the action, locus, and so forth are to be inferred.

children.text: samprati dravyam abhidhāya vikṛtānāṃ rasānām eva bhedam āha bhedaś caiṣām ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, having stated substance, he gives the divisions specifically of altered tastes in the passage beginning 'and their division'.

children.text: prabhāvaśabdo dravyadeśakālaiḥ pratyekaṃ yujyate tatra dravyaprabhāvād yathā somaguṇātirekān madhuraḥ ityādi deśaprabhāvād yathā himavati drākṣādāḍimādīni madhurāṇi bhavantyanyatrāmlānītyādi kālaprabhāvādyathā bālāmraṃ sakaṣāyaṃ taruṇamamlaṃ pakvaṃ madhuraṃ tathā hemante oṣadhyo madhurā varṣāsv amlā ityādi ||
children.translated_text: The word <s>prabhāva</s> is connected individually with substance, place, and time. There, from the influence of substance, for example, 'because of an excess of <s>soma</s>-qualities it is sweet,' and so on. From the influence of place, for example, grapes, pomegranates, and the like in the Himalaya are sweet, but elsewhere sour, and so on. From the influence of time, for example, an unripe mango is somewhat astringent, a young one is sour, and a ripe one is sweet; likewise herbs are sweet in winter and sour in the rainy season, and so on.

children.text: agnisaṃyogādayo ye 'nye rasahetavas te 'pi kāle dravye vāntarbhāvanīyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Other causes of taste, such as contact with fire, should also be included under time or substance.
He states the division in the passage beginning 'sweet'.

children.text: tatra svādoramlādiyogāt pañca śeṣair iti āditvenopayuktād anyaiḥ tenāmlasya lavaṇādiyogāc catvāri evaṃ lavaṇasya kaṭvādiyogāt trīṇi kaṭukasya tiktakaṣāyayogād dve tiktasya kaṣāyayogād ekam evaṃ pañcadaśa dvirasāni ||
children.translated_text: There, because sweet combines with sour and the others, there are five with the remaining tastes. The word 'and so on' indicates the others beyond the one already taken; therefore, by the combination of sour with salt and the others there are four, similarly by the combination of salt with pungent and the others there are three, by the combination of pungent with bitter and astringent there are two, and by the combination of bitter with astringent there is one. Thus there are fifteen two-taste combinations.
He states the three-taste combination in the passage beginning 'separately'.

children.text: madhurasyāmlādirasacatuṣṭayena pṛthag ityekaikaśo yuktasya śeṣairlavaṇādibhir yogo bhavati tatra madhurasyāmlayuktasya śeṣalavaṇādiyogāc catvāri tathā madhurasya lavaṇayuktasya kaṭvādiyogāt trīṇi tathā kaṭuyuktasya tiktādiyogād dve tathā tiktayuktasya kaṣāyayogād ekam evaṃ madhureṇādisthitena daśa ||
children.translated_text: Sweet, joined separately, that is one by one, with the four tastes beginning with sour, is then combined with the remaining tastes, namely salt and the others. There, when sweet has been joined with sour, through combination with the remaining tastes beginning with salt there are four. Likewise, when sweet has been joined with salt, through combination with pungent and the others there are three; likewise, when joined with pungent, through combination with bitter and the others there are two; likewise, when joined with bitter, through combination with astringent there is one. Thus, with sweet standing first, there are ten.

children.text: evamamlasyādisthitasya lavaṇayuktasya kaṭvādiyogāt trīṇi tathā kaṭukayuktasya śeṣābhyāṃ yogād dve evaṃ tiktayuktasya kaṣāyayogād ekam evam amlasya ṣaṭ ||
children.translated_text: In the same way, with sour standing first, when it is joined with salt, through combination with pungent and the others there are three; likewise, when joined with pungent, through combination with the two remaining tastes there are two; and when joined with bitter, through combination with astringent there is one. Thus sour has six.

children.text: anenaiva nyāyena lavaṇasya trīṇi kaṭoś caikameva evaṃ militvā trirasāni viṃśatiḥ ||
children.translated_text: By this very principle, salt has three and pungent only one. Thus, when combined, the three-taste combinations are twenty.

children.text: catūrase svādvamlāv ādisthitau lavaṇādibhir ekaikaśyena yuktau śeṣaiḥ kaṭvādibhir yogāt ṣaḍ bhavanti ||
children.translated_text: In the four-taste combinations, sweet and sour, standing first, are joined one by one with salt and the others, and, through combination with the remaining tastes beginning with pungent, there are six.

children.text: svādulavaṇau sahitau ādisthitau kaṭvādibhiriti kaṭutiktābhyāṃ pṛthagyuktau śeṣair iti tiktakaṣāyābhyāṃ teneha bahuvacanaṃ jātau boddhavyam evaṃ trīṇi ||
children.translated_text: Sweet and salt, together and standing first, are joined separately with pungent and bitter in the phrase 'with pungent and the others'; and with the remaining tastes, namely bitter and astringent. Therefore the plural here should be understood generically. Thus there are three.
By 'sweet and pungent likewise,' there is one combination in the form sweet-pungent-bitter-astringent.
In the passage beginning 'with pungent and the others' too, the plural is generic.

children.text: amlalavaṇau saṃyuktau kaṭunā sahitau śeṣābhyāṃ yogād dve tathāmlalavaṇau tiktayuktau śeṣayogād ekam ||
children.translated_text: Sour and salt, combined and joined with pungent, give two through combination with the remaining two; likewise sour and salt joined with bitter give one through combination with the remaining taste.
By 'sour and pungent likewise,' there is one combination in the form sour-pungent-bitter-astringent.
And by the passage beginning 'but they are joined,' there is one.
Thus there are fifteen four-taste combinations.
'By exclusion' means by omission.

children.text: atra ca rasānāṃ guṇatvenaikasmin dravye samavāyo yogaśabdenocyate ||
children.translated_text: And here, since tastes are qualities, their inherence in a single substance is denoted by the word 'combination'.

children.text: rasasaṃsargasya prakārāntareṇāsaṃkhyeyatām āha triṣaṣṭiḥ syād ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states the innumerability of taste-combination in another way in the passage beginning 'there would be sixty-three'.
<s>Anurasa</s> (secondary taste) will be explained later.

children.text: atra ca triṣaṣṭyātmakarase rasānurasakalpanā nāsti kevale madhurādau tadabhāvāt tena yathāsambhavaṃ saptapañcāśatsaṃyogaviṣayaṃ rasānurasakalpanaṃ jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: And here, in the taste-set consisting of sixty-three, there is no construction of primary taste and secondary taste, because that is absent in the single tastes such as sweet alone. Therefore the construction of taste and secondary taste should be understood, as far as applicable, as pertaining to the fifty-seven combinations.
Or else, even in a single taste there is certainly a secondary taste, though it is not separately describable.

children.text: prakārāntareṇāpy asaṃkhyeyatām āha rasās taratamābhyām ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states their innumerability also in another way in the passage beginning 'tastes, by degrees of more and less'.
The sense is that tastes become innumerable through distinctions such as sweet, sweeter, sweetest, and so on.

children.text: kiṃvā rasānurasatvenaiva yāsaṃkhyeyatā tatraivāyaṃ hetuḥ rasās taratamābhyāmityādiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or else, the reason stated here, in the passage beginning 'tastes, by degrees of more and less,' applies precisely to that innumerability which exists through taste and secondary taste.

children.text: evamasaṃkhyeyatve'pi triṣaṣṭividhaiva kalpanā cikitsāvyavahārārtham ihācāryaiḥ kalpitetyāha saṃyogā ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Thus, although they are innumerable, the teachers have here construed them as only sixty-three kinds for the sake of medical practice; he states this in the passage beginning 'the combinations'.

children.text: tatra yogyatvād iti tatra svasthāturahitacikitsāprayoge 'natisaṃkṣepavistararūpatayā hitatvād ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, in the phrase "because it is suitable," the meaning is: because, in the application of treatment beneficial to the healthy and the sick, it is useful by being neither too brief nor too extended.
He states that very application of treatment with the passage beginning "in some cases."
Here, by the inclusion implied in "and so on," unmentioned factors such as place, time, and strength are also included.

children.text: etadeva saṃyuktāsaṃyuktarasakalpanaṃ bhinnarasadravyamelakād vānekarasaikadravyaprayogād ekarasadravyaprayogādvā bhavatīti darśayannāha dravyāṇītyādi ||
children.translated_text: Showing that this very formulation of combined and uncombined <s>rasas</s> (tastes) may arise either from the mixing of substances with different tastes, from the use of one substance with many tastes, or from the use of a substance with one taste, he says, "substances," and so on.

children.text: dvirasādīni utpattisiddhadvirasatrirasādīni dvirasaṃ yathā kaṣāyamadhuro mudgaḥ trirasaṃ yathā madhurāmlakaṣāyaṃ ca viṣṭambhi guru śītalam ||
children.translated_text: "Two-tasted and so on" means those that are established by their origin as having two tastes, three tastes, and so forth. An example of two tastes is <s>mudga</s>, which is astringent and sweet. An example of three tastes is: "sweet, sour, and astringent, obstructive, heavy, and cooling."

children.text: pittaśleṣmaharaṃ bhavyam ityādi catūrasas tilaḥ yad uktaṃ snigdhoṣṇamadhuras tiktaḥ kaṣāyaḥ kaṭukas tilaḥ pañcarasaṃ tv āmalakaṃ harītakī ca śivā pañcarasā ityādivacanāt vyaktaṣaḍrasaṃ tu dravyam ihānuktaṃ viṣaṃ tv avyaktaṣaḍrasasaṃyuktaṃ hārīte tv eṇamāṃsaṃ vyaktaṣaḍrasasaṃyuktam uktam ||
children.translated_text: "It removes <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s> and is beneficial," and similar statements apply. <s>Tila</s> has four tastes, as has been said: "sesame is oily, hot, sweet, bitter, astringent, and pungent." <s>Āmalaka</s> and <s>harītakī</s> have five tastes, according to statements such as "the auspicious <s>harītakī</s> has five tastes." A substance with six manifest tastes is not mentioned here. Poison, however, is joined with six unmanifest tastes; and in <s>Hārīta</s>, the flesh of the antelope is said to be joined with six manifest tastes.
Thus, through the combination of substances having two tastes and so on, there is use of two tastes and so forth.

children.text: tathā saṃyuktāṃśca rasāniti ekaikarasādidravyamelakāt saṃyuktān rasān ekaikaśaḥ kalpayanti prayojayanti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, in "and combined tastes," they formulate and apply combined tastes one by one from the mixing of substances having one taste each and the like.

children.text: gadān pratīti prādhānyena tena svasthavṛtte 'pi boddhavyaṃ kiṃvā dvirasādibhedo gada eva svasthe tu sarvarasaprayoga eva yaduktaṃ samasarvarasaṃ sātmyaṃ samadhātoḥ praśasyate iti ||
children.translated_text: "With regard to diseases" means principally so; therefore it should also be understood in the regimen for the healthy. Or else, the distinction into two tastes and so on applies only in disease, while for the healthy there is simply the use of all tastes, as it has been said: "A balanced use of all tastes is praised as wholesome for one whose bodily constituents are balanced."

children.text: evaṃ ca vyākhyāne sati kvacideko rasa ityādinā samamasya na paunaruktyam ||
children.translated_text: And when the explanation is made in this way, there is no repetition between this passage and the statement beginning "in some cases one taste."

children.text: kiṃvā kvacid eko rasaḥ ityādinā svamatam uktam atraivārthe dravyāṇi dvirasādīni ityādinācāryāntarasammatiṃ darśayati ata evānyācāryāntarābhiprāyeṇa kalpayantītyuktaṃ tena na paunaruktyam ||
children.translated_text: Or else, by "in some cases one taste" and so on, his own view is stated; while on the same matter, by "substances having two tastes and so on," he shows the agreement of other teachers. For this very reason it is said, "they formulate," according to the intention of other teachers; therefore there is no repetition.
He states the result of knowing <s>rasa</s> with the passage beginning "who might be."

children.text: atra rasavikalpajñānādeva vyādhihetudravyajñānaṃ kṛtsnamavaruddhaṃ rasajñānenaiva prāyaḥ sakaladravyaguṇasya vakṣyamāṇatvāt ||
