children.translated_text: Here, from the knowledge of the variations of taste alone, the knowledge of disease-causes and substances is entirely included, because nearly all the qualities of substances will be taught precisely through knowledge of taste.

children.text: doṣavikalpajñānācca liṅgajñānaṃ yāvaddhi liṅgaṃ tat sarvaṃ doṣavikalpasambaddham ||
children.translated_text: And from knowledge of the variations of <s>doṣas</s>, there is knowledge of signs; for whatever is a sign is all connected with a particular variation of the <s>doṣas</s>.

children.text: rasadoṣavikalpajñānāt tu bheṣajajñānaṃ yato rasataḥ svarūpajñānaṃ bheṣajadravyasya doṣataśca bheṣajaprayogaviṣayavijñānam ||
children.translated_text: But from knowledge of the variations of taste and <s>doṣa</s>, there is knowledge of medicines, because through taste there is knowledge of the essential nature of a medicinal substance, and through <s>doṣa</s> there is knowledge of the field in which the medicine is to be applied.

children.text: kiṃvā rasavikalpāc ca tathā doṣavikalpāc ca hetvādijñānaṃ pṛthageva vaktavyaṃ rasabhedāddhi tatkāryaṃ liṅgamapi jñāyate hetubheṣajavijñānaṃ tu ||
children.translated_text: Or else, from the variation of taste and likewise from the variation of <s>doṣa</s>, knowledge of causes and the rest should be stated separately. For from the difference of taste, even its effect, namely the sign, is known; but knowledge of causes and medicines is another matter.

children.text: rasabhedavijñānādeva vaktavyaṃ yato rasabhedavad dravyameva vikārāṇāṃ heturbheṣajaṃ ca bhavatīti evaṃ doṣabhedaṃ jñātvā ca tasya samānaṃ hetuṃ pratyeti doṣavirodhi ca dravyaṃ bheṣajamiti ||
children.translated_text: This should be stated from the knowledge of taste-distinctions alone, since it is precisely a substance possessing a particular distinction of taste that becomes both the cause of disorders and their medicine. And having known the distinction of <s>doṣa</s>, one recognizes a cause similar to it, and a substance opposed to the <s>doṣa</s> as the medicine.

children.text: tad yuktam uktaṃ na sa muhyedvikārāṇāṃ hetuliṅgopaśāntiṣviti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore it has rightly been said: "He would not be confused regarding the causes, signs, and pacification of disorders."
He states the previously mentioned definition of <s>rasa</s> and <s>anurasa</s> with the passage beginning "manifest."

children.text: śuṣkasya ceti cakārād ārdrasya ca ādau ceti cakārādante ca tena śuṣkasya vārdrasya vā prathamajihvāsambandhe vāsvādānte vā yo vyaktatvena madhuro 'yam amlo 'yam ityādinā vikalpena gṛhyate sa vyaktaḥ yas tūktāvasthācatuṣṭaye 'pi vyakto nopalabhyate kiṃ tarhy avyapadeśyatayā chāyāmātreṇa kāryadarśanena vā mīyate so 'nurasa iti vākyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In "and of the dry," by the particle "and" the moist is also included; and in "at the beginning," by the particle "and" the end is also included. Thus, whether a thing is dry or moist, and whether at the first contact with the tongue or at the end of tasting, that which is grasped manifestly by a determination such as "this is sweet" or "this is sour" is manifest taste. But that which is not perceived as manifest in any of those four conditions, but is measured only as inexpressible, by a mere trace or by seeing its effect, is <s>anurasa</s> (aftertaste). This is the meaning of the sentence.

children.text: yataśca madhurādaya eva vyaktatvāvyaktatvābhyāṃ rasānurasarūpāḥ ato'vyakto nāma saptamo raso nāsti ||
children.translated_text: And since the sweet and the other tastes themselves, by being manifest or unmanifest, take the form of <s>rasa</s> and <s>anurasa</s>, there is no seventh taste called "unmanifest."

children.text: ayaṃ cārthaḥ pūrvaṃ pratiṣiddho 'pyanuguṇaspaṣṭahetuprāptyā punar niṣidhyate ||
children.translated_text: Although this point was already refuted earlier, it is refuted again because a favorable and clear reason has now been obtained.

children.text: anye tv āhuḥ śuṣkasya cetyanena yasya dravyasya śuṣkasya cārdrasya copayogaḥ tatra śuṣkāvasthāyāṃ yo 'vyaktaḥ sa rasa ucyate yastvārdrāvasthāyāṃ vyaktaḥ san śuṣkāvasthāyāṃ nānuyāti nāsau rasaḥ kiṃtv anurasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Others, however, say: by the phrase "and of the dry," where a given substance is used both dry and moist, that which is unmanifest in the dry state is called its taste; but that which, though manifest in the moist state, does not persist in the dry state is not its taste, but rather <s>anurasa</s>.

children.text: yathā pippalyā ārdrāyā madhuro raso vyaktaḥ śuṣkāyāstu pippalyāḥ kaṭukaḥ tena kaṭuka eva rasaḥ pippalyāḥ madhurastvanurasaḥ yastu drākṣādīnām ārdrāvasthāyāṃ śuṣkāvasthāyāṃ ca madhura eva tatra vipratipattirapi nāsti tena tatra madhura eva rasaḥ nityārdraprayojyānāṃ tu kāñjikatakrādīnāmādau vyakto ya upalabhyate rasaḥ anu copalabhyate yaḥ so 'nuraso yuktas tiktatvādiḥ tathā ārdrāvasthāyāṃ śuṣkāvasthāviparīto yaḥ pippalyā iva madhuraḥ so 'nurasa iti ||
children.translated_text: For example, in fresh <s>pippalī</s> the sweet taste is manifest, but in dried <s>pippalī</s> the pungent taste is manifest. Therefore pungent alone is the taste of <s>pippalī</s>, while sweet is its <s>anurasa</s>. But in the case of grapes and the like, where the taste is sweet both in the fresh state and in the dry state, there is no disagreement; therefore there the taste is simply sweet. For things that are always to be used moist, such as <s>kāñjika</s> and <s>takra</s>, the taste perceived manifestly at first is taste, and what is perceived afterward is properly <s>anurasa</s>, such as bitterness. Likewise, when in the moist state there is a taste opposite to that in the dry state, as the sweetness in <s>pippalī</s>, that is <s>anurasa</s>.

children.text: kiṃtv ārdrāpi pippalī madhurarasaiveti paśyāmaḥ yato vakṣyati śleṣmalā madhurā cārdrā gurvī snigdhā ca pippalī iti madhurasya tatrānurasatve gurutvaśleṣmakartṛtvāny anupapannāni tena ārdrā pippalī vyaktamadhurarasaiva śuṣkā tu madhurānuraseti yuktam ||
children.translated_text: But we see that even fresh <s>pippalī</s> is precisely sweet in taste, since he will say, 'Fresh <s>pippalī</s> is phlegm-producing, sweet, heavy, and unctuous.' If sweetness there were only a secondary taste, heaviness and the production of phlegm would not make sense. Therefore it is reasonable that fresh <s>pippalī</s> has a manifest sweet taste, while dried <s>pippalī</s> has sweetness as a secondary taste.

children.text: samprati pūrvoktagurvādiguṇātiriktān paratvāparatvādīn daśa guṇān rasadharmatvenopadeṣṭavyān āha paretyādi ||
children.translated_text: Now he states the ten qualities, beginning with superiority and inferiority, which are additional to the previously mentioned qualities such as heaviness and are to be taught as properties of taste, in the passage beginning 'superior'.
That superiority is predominance, and inferiority is non-predominance.
Its explanation is in the passage beginning 'place and time'.

children.text: tatra deśo maruḥ paraḥ anūpo 'paraḥ kālo visargaḥ paraḥ ādānamaparaḥ vayastaruṇaṃ param aparam itaran mānaṃ ca śarīrasya yathā vakṣyamāṇaṃ śarīre paraṃ tato'nyadaparaṃ pākavīryarasāstu ye yasya yoginaste taṃ prati parāḥ ayaugikās tv aparāḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, with respect to place, arid land is superior and marshy land inferior; with respect to time, the period of release is superior and the period of taking-up is inferior; with respect to age, youth is superior and the other age is inferior. The measure of the body, as will be stated, is superior when it is in the body, and anything other than that is inferior. As for digestion, potency, and taste, those that are suitable for a given thing are superior in relation to it, while those that are unsuitable are inferior.
By the word 'and so on', constitution, strength, and the like are included.

children.text: kiṃvā paratvāparatve vaiśeṣikokte jñeye tatra deśāpekṣayā saṃnikṛṣṭadeśasambandhinam apekṣya vidūradeśasambandhini paratvaṃ saṃnikṛṣṭadeśasambandhini cāparatvaṃ bhavati evaṃ saṃnikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭakālāpekṣayā ca sthavire paratvaṃ yūni cāparatvaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Or else, superiority and inferiority should be understood as stated in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> system. There, in relation to something connected with a nearby place, superiority belongs to what is connected with a distant place, and inferiority belongs to what is connected with the nearby place. Likewise, with regard to near and remote times, superiority belongs to the old person and inferiority to the young person.

children.text: vayaḥprabhṛtiṣu paratvāparatvaṃ yathāsambhavaṃ kāladeśakṛtam evehopayogād upacaritam apyabhihitaṃ yato na guṇe mānādau guṇāntarasambhavaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In matters such as age, superiority and inferiority are, as applicable, precisely due to time and place; here, because of their usefulness, they are stated even figuratively, since in a quality such as measure there is no possibility of another quality inhering in it.

children.text: yuktiścetyādau yojanā doṣādyapekṣayā bheṣajasya samīcīnakalpanā ata evoktaṃ yā tu yujyate yā kalpanā yaugikī bhavati sā tu yuktir ucyate ayaugikī tu kalpanāpi satī yuktir nocyate putro 'pyaputravat ||
children.translated_text: In 'and suitability', the construction is that <s>yukti</s> (suitability) is the proper arrangement of a medicine with reference to the doṣas and the like. Therefore it has been said: that arrangement which is fitted and becomes suitable is called <s>yukti</s>; an unsuitable arrangement, though it is an arrangement, is not called <s>yukti</s>, just as even a son may be like no son.
This <s>yukti</s>, though included under conjunction, measure, processing, and the like, is stated separately because it is extremely useful.
He defines number in the passage beginning 'number'.
Here calculation means one, two, three, and so on.
He describes conjunction in the passage beginning 'joining'.

children.text: saheti militānāṃ dravyāṇāṃ yogaḥ prāptirityarthaḥ sahetyanenehākiṃcitkaraṃ parasparasaṃyogaṃ nirākaroti ||
children.translated_text: 'Together' means that conjunction is the joining, that is, the coming together, of substances that have been combined. By the word 'together' he here excludes a mutual conjunction that accomplishes nothing.
He states its divisions in the passage beginning 'twofold-action'.

children.text: tatra dvaṃdvakarmajo yathā yudhyamānayor meṣayoḥ sarvakarmajo yathā bhāṇḍe prakṣipyamāṇānāṃ māṣāṇāṃ bahulamāṣakriyā yogajaḥ ekakarmajo yathā vṛkṣavāyasayoḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, conjunction produced by the action of both is like that of two rams fighting; conjunction produced by the action of all is like that of black gram grains being thrown into a vessel, where there is much action of the grains; conjunction produced through union and by the action of one is like that of a tree and a crow.
With the word 'impermanent', he shows the impermanence of conjunction, because it is produced by action.
He describes separation in the passage beginning 'but separation'.
Separation is division, the act of dividing.

children.text: vibhaktimeva vivṛṇoti viyoga iti saṃyogasya vigamo viyogaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He explains separation itself: in 'disjunction', disjunction is the disappearance of conjunction.

children.text: tat kiṃ saṃyogābhāva eva viyoga ityāha bhāgaśo graha iti ||
children.translated_text: Is disjunction, then, merely the absence of conjunction? He answers: 'apprehension part by part'.

children.text: vibhāgaśo vibhaktatvena grahaṇaṃ yato bhavatīti bhāvaḥ tena vibhaktirityeṣā bhāvarūpā pratītir na saṃyogābhāvamātraṃ bhavati kiṃtarhi bhāvarūpavibhāgaguṇayuktā ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The sense is: because apprehension occurs in terms of division, as something divided. Therefore this awareness called separation is a positive entity, not merely the absence of conjunction. Rather, it is endowed with the positive quality of division.

children.text: pṛthaktvaṃ tu idaṃ dravyaṃ paṭalakṣaṇaṃ ghaṭāt pṛthag ityādikā buddhiryato bhavati tat pṛthaktvaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Distinctness is that from which there arises a cognition such as, 'This substance characterized as a cloth is distinct from a pot.'
The teacher states that in three forms in the passage beginning 'distinctness'.

children.text: tatra yat sarvathāsaṃyujyamānayoriva meruhimācalayoḥ pṛthaktvam etadasaṃyoga ityanenoktam ||
children.translated_text: There, the distinctness of things that are entirely unconnected, as of <s>Meru</s> and the <s>Himālaya</s>, is stated by the word 'non-conjunction'.

children.text: tathā saṃyujyamānānāmapi pṛthaktvaṃ vijātīyānāṃ mahiṣavarāhādīnāṃ tadāha vailakṣaṇyamityādi ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, even among things that are conjoined, there is the distinctness of heterogeneous things such as buffaloes and boars. He states that in the passage beginning 'dissimilarity'.
The meaning is: distinctness among heterogeneous things is characterized by their being endowed with distinguishing marks.

children.text: tathaikajātīyānāmapy avilakṣaṇānāṃ māṣāṇāṃ pṛthaktvaṃ bhavatītyāha anekateti ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, even among things of one class and without differentiating marks, such as black gram grains, there is distinctness. He says this with the word 'manyness'.

children.text: ekajātīyeṣu hi saṃyukteṣu na vailakṣaṇyaṃ nāpyasaṃyogaḥ atha cānekatā pṛthaktvarūpā bhavatīti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For among conjoined things of one class there is neither dissimilarity nor non-conjunction, and yet manyness exists as a form of distinctness. This is the sense.

children.text: kiṃvā pṛthaktvaṃ guṇāntaramicchan lokavyavahārārtham asaṃyogavailakṣaṇyānekatārūpameva yathodāhṛtaṃ pṛthaktvaṃ darśayati ||
children.translated_text: Or else, while accepting distinctness as another quality for the sake of ordinary usage, he shows distinctness, just as illustrated, precisely in the forms of non-conjunction, dissimilarity, and manyness.
Measure is what is to be measured by a <s>prastha</s>, an <s>āḍhaka</s>, a scale, and the like.

children.text: karaṇaṃ guṇāntarādhāyakatvaṃ saṃskaraṇamityarthaḥ yadvakṣyati saṃskāro hi guṇāntarādhānamucyate iti ||
children.translated_text: Making is the capacity to add another quality; the meaning is processing. He will say: 'For processing is called the addition of another quality.'
Habit is the repeated practice of a state, such as the use of <s>ṣaṣṭika</s> rice, and of exercise and the like.

children.text: abhyasanameva lokaprasiddhābhyāṃ paryāyābhyāṃ vivṛṇoti śīlanaṃ satatakriyeti yaṃ lokāḥ śīlanasatatakriyābhyām abhidadhati so 'bhyāsa iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He explains repeated practice itself by two synonyms well known in ordinary speech, 'cultivation' and 'constant performance'. The sense is: what people call cultivation and constant performance is habit.

children.text: ayaṃ ca saṃyogasaṃskāraviśeṣarūpo 'pi viśeṣeṇa cikitsopayuktatvāt pṛthagucyate ||
children.translated_text: And this, though it is a particular form of conjunction and processing, is stated separately because it is especially useful in treatment.

children.text: na yathāvat pravartata iti vacanena śabdādiṣu ca gurvādiṣu ca parādīnāmaprādhānyaṃ sūcayati ||
children.translated_text: By the statement 'does not operate properly', he indicates that the qualities beginning with superiority are not principal among sound and the others, nor among heaviness and the other qualities.

children.text: samprati rasānāṃ parasparasaṃyogo guṇa uktaḥ tathāgre ca snigdhatvādirguṇo vācyaḥ sa ca guṇarūparase na sambhavatīti yathā rasānāṃ guṇanirdeśo boddhavyas tadāha guṇā ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now the mutual combination of tastes has been stated as a quality, and further on the quality beginning with unctuousness is to be stated. Since that does not occur in taste as a quality-form, he says the words beginning 'qualities' to show how the statement of qualities belonging to tastes is to be understood.

children.text: guṇā guṇāśrayā noktā iti dīrghaṃjīvitīye samavāyī tu niśceṣṭaḥ kāraṇaṃ guṇaḥ ityanena ||
children.translated_text: In the <s>Dīrghaṃjīvitīya</s>, qualities are not stated apart from their supports as qualities, by the statement, 'But a quality is an inactive inherent cause.'

children.text: rasaguṇāniti rase snigdhādīn guṇān nirdiṣṭān tad rasādhāradravyaguṇān eva vidyāt ||
children.translated_text: 'The qualities of tastes' means: one should understand the qualities such as unctuousness, stated with reference to taste, as precisely the qualities of the substances that support those tastes.

children.text: nanu yadi dravyaguṇā eva te tat kimiti rasaguṇatvenocyanta ityāha karturityādi karturiti tantrakartuḥ ||
children.translated_text: But if they are simply qualities of substances, why are they called qualities of tastes? He answers with the words beginning 'of the maker.' 'Of the maker' means of the author of the treatise.

children.text: abhiprāyā iti tatra tatropacāreṇa tathā sāmānyaśabdādiprayogeṇa tantrakaraṇabuddhayaḥ sāmānyaśabdopacārādiprayogaś ca prakaraṇādivaśād eva sphuṭatvāt tathā prayojanavaśāc ca kriyate ||
children.translated_text: 'Intentions' means the authorial understandings in various places, through figurative usage and through the use of generic terms and the like. The use of figurative expression, generic terms, and so on is made because the meaning is clear through context and the like, and also because of the intended purpose.

children.text: tacca prakaraṇādi ataśca prakṛtaṃ buddhvā ityādau darśayiṣyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And that context and the like we shall explain under the passage beginning 'therefore, having understood what is under discussion.'

children.text: iha ca dravyaguṇānāṃ raseṣu yadupacaraṇaṃ tasyāyamabhiprāyo yat madhurādinirdeśenaiva snigdhaśītādiguṇā api prāyo madhurādyavyabhicāriṇo dravye nirdiṣṭā bhavantīti na madhuratvaṃ nirdiśya snigdhatvādipratipādanaṃ punaḥ pṛthak kriyata iti ||
children.translated_text: Here, in the figurative attribution of the qualities of substances to tastes, the intention is this: by the very statement of sweet and the other tastes, qualities such as unctuousness and coldness, which mostly do not deviate from sweet and the rest, are also stated in the substance. Therefore, after stating sweetness, the presentation of unctuousness and the like is not made again separately.

children.text: abhiprāyapṛthaktve sati yathā grantho boddhavyas tadāha ataś cetyādi ||
children.translated_text: When there is a distinction of intention, he states how the text is to be understood with the words beginning 'and therefore.'

children.text: tatra prakṛtaṃ buddhvā yathā kṣārāḥ kṣīraṃ phalaṃ puṣpam ityatrodbhidagaṇasya prakṛtatvāt kṣīramiti snuhyādikṣīram eva kṣīraśabdena vadet ||
children.translated_text: There, 'having understood what is under discussion' is illustrated as follows: in 'alkalis, milk, fruit, and flower,' since the group of exuding plants is under discussion, by the word 'milk' one should mean only the milky sap of <s>snuhī</s> and similar plants.

children.text: deśāntaraṃ buddhveti yathā śirasi śodhane 'bhidhīyamāne krimivyādhau iti tacchirogatakrimivyādhāv eva bhavati ||
children.translated_text: 'Having understood another place' is illustrated as follows: when purification of the head is being discussed, the phrase 'in worm disease' applies only to worm disease located in that head.

children.text: kālāntare yathā vamanakāle 'bhihitaṃ pratigrahāṃś copahārayed iti tatra pratigrahaśabdena pātramucyate na tu grahaṇaṃ pratigrahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: With respect to another time, for example, when at the time of emesis it is said, 'and one should bring up the receptacles,' there the word 'receptacle' means a vessel, not the act of receiving.

children.text: tantrakartur abhiprāyān iti yathoktaṃ raseṣu guṇāropaṇe tad boddhavyam ||
children.translated_text: 'From the intention of the author of the treatise' should be understood as in the previously stated attribution of qualities to tastes.
'Means' means the methods of the science, in the form of <s>tantrayukti</s> (interpretive devices).
'Meaning' means the thing to be expressed.

children.text: yadyapi prakṛtādayo 'pi tantrakartur abhiprāyā eva tathāpi yatra prakṛtatvādi na sphuṭaṃ pratīyate tatra tantrakartur abhiprāyatvena boddhavyam ||
children.translated_text: Although context and the others too are in fact intentions of the author of the treatise, still, where being the topic and the like are not clearly perceived, the matter should be understood by taking it as the author's intention.
'The six divisions' means the six divisions beginning with sweet.

children.text: ṣaṭ pañcabhūtaprabhavā iti pañcabhūtaprabhavāḥ santo yathoktena prakāreṇa somaguṇātirekāt ityādinā yathā ṣaṭ saṃkhyātāḥ ṣaṭsaṃkhyāparicchinnā bhavanti tathā vakṣyāmīti yojanā ||
children.translated_text: 'The six arise from the five elements' should be construed thus: while they arise from the five elements, we shall explain how, in the manner stated by 'because of an excess of soma-quality' and so on, they become numbered as six, that is, delimited by the number six.

children.text: samprati rasānām ādikāraṇameva tāvad āha saumyā ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now he first states the primary cause of tastes with the words beginning 'watery.'
'Watery' means having <s>Soma</s> as their deity.

children.text: bhraśyamānā iti vadatā bhūmisambandhavyatirekeṇāntarīkṣeritaiḥ pṛthivyādiparamāṇvādibhiḥ sambandho rasārambhako bhavatīti darśyate ||
children.translated_text: By saying 'falling down,' he shows that, apart from connection with the earth, connection with earth and the other atoms impelled in the atmosphere is what initiates taste.
'Forms' means manifest individual states.
'They satisfy' means they satiate, or else they generate.
'The tastes become manifest' means they come into individual manifestation.

children.text: atra cāntarīkṣamudakaṃ rasakāraṇatve pradhānatvāduktaṃ tena kṣitistham api sthāvarajaṅgamotpattau rasakāraṇaṃ bhavatyeva ||
children.translated_text: And here atmospheric water is mentioned because of its predominance as a cause of taste. Therefore water situated in the earth too certainly becomes a cause of taste in the production of stationary and moving beings.

children.text: somaguṇātirekāditi atirekaśabdena sarveṣveva raseṣu sarvabhūtasāṃnidhyam asti kvacit tu kasyacid bhūtaguṇasyātirekād rasaviśeṣe bhavatīti darśayati etacca madhuraṃ prati abguṇātiriktatvaṃ viśeṣotpattau kāraṇatvena jñeyaṃ yaccādhārakāraṇatvam apāṃ tat sarvasādhāraṇam ||
children.translated_text: 'Because of an excess of soma-quality': by the word 'excess' he shows that in all tastes there is a presence of all the elements, but that because of an excess of some elemental quality in some case, a particular taste arises. And this excess of the qualities of water with respect to sweetness should be known as a cause in the arising of that specific taste; but the supporting causality of the waters is common to all.
In this way, in the case of salt taste too, the causality of water should be understood.

children.text: lavaṇastu suśrute pṛthivyagnyatirekāt paṭhitaḥ asmiṃś ca virodhe kāryavirodho nāstyeva ||
children.translated_text: But in <s>Suśruta</s>, salt is taught as arising from an excess of earth and fire; and in this disagreement there is no contradiction in the effect at all.

children.text: nanu uṣṇaśītābhyāmagnisalilābhyāṃ kṛtasya lavaṇasyāpy uṣṇaśītatvena bhavitavyaṃ tal lavaṇaṃ katham uṣṇaṃ bhavati naivaṃ yato bhūtānām ayaṃ svabhāvo yat kenacit prakāreṇa saṃniviṣṭāḥ kaṃcid guṇam ārabhante na sarvam ||
children.translated_text: Objection: Since salt is produced by fire and water, which are hot and cold, salt too ought to possess both heat and coldness. How then is salt hot? Not so, because this is the nature of the elements: when arranged in some particular way, they initiate some particular quality, not every quality.

children.text: yathā makuṣṭhake 'dbhir madhuro rasaḥ kriyate na snehaḥ tathā saindhave vahnināpi noṣṇatvam ārabhyate ||
children.translated_text: For example, in <s>makuṣṭhaka</s>, a sweet taste is produced by waters, but not oiliness; similarly in rock salt, even by fire, heat is not initiated.

children.text: ayaṃ ca bhūtānāṃ saṃniveśo 'dṛṣṭaprabhāvakṛta eva sa ca saṃniveśaḥ kāryadarśanenonneyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And this arrangement of the elements is indeed produced by the power of unseen factors, and that arrangement is to be inferred from the observation of its effect.

children.text: tena yatra kāryaṃ dṛśyate tatra kalpyate yathā lavaṇe uṣṇatvād agnir viṣyanditvācca jalamanumīyate ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, where an effect is seen, there it is postulated; for example, in salt, fire is inferred from heat, and water from its liquefying property.
This matter is also knowable from authoritative tradition; here the conjectures of people such as ourselves do not extend.

children.text: etena yaducyate toyavat pṛthivyādayo'pi kimiti pṛthagrasāntaraṃ na kurvanti tathā toyavātādisaṃyogādibhyaḥ kimiti rasāntarāṇi notpadyanta iti tadapi bhūtasvabhāvāparyanuyogād eva pratyuktam ||
children.translated_text: By this, even the objection that is stated, 'Why do earth and the other elements, like water, not separately produce another taste? And why do other tastes not arise from conjunctions with water, wind, and so on?' has also been answered simply on the ground that the inherent nature of the elements is not open to further challenge.

children.text: iha ca kāraṇatvaṃ bhūtānāṃ rasasya madhuratvādiviśeṣa eva nimittakāraṇarūpam ucyate tena nīrasānām api hi dahanādīnāṃ kāraṇatvamupapannam eva vyutpāditam ||
children.translated_text: Here the causality of the elements in relation to <s>rasa</s> (taste) is stated as an instrumental cause only with respect to particular forms such as sweetness and the rest. Therefore the causality even of tasteless things such as fire has indeed been duly explained.
Establishing the distinction of tastes by an example, he says 'in this way,' and so on.

children.text: rasānāṃ ṣaṭtvaṃ mahābhūtānāṃ nyūnātirekaviśeṣāt somaguṇātirekapṛthivyagnyatirekādeḥ ṣaḍutpādakāraṇādupapannaṃ ṣaḍbhyaḥ kāraṇebhyaḥ ṣaṭ kāryāṇi bhavantīti yuktameveti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The sixfoldness of tastes is appropriate because of the particular deficiency and excess of the <s>mahābhūtas</s> (great elements), since there are six producing causes, such as an excess of <s>soma</s>-qualities and an excess of earth and fire. The intention is that it is quite reasonable for six effects to arise from six causes.

children.text: bhūtānāṃ yathā nānāvarṇākṛtiviśeṣā mahābhūtānāṃ nyūnātirekaviśeṣāt tathā rasānām apīti ||
children.translated_text: Just as, among the elements, there are various particular colors and shapes because of particular deficiencies and excesses of the great elements, so it is also with tastes.

children.text: bhūtānāṃ yathoktānām atirekaviśeṣahetum āha ṣaḍṛtukatvād ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states the cause for the particular excess of the elements already described with the words beginning 'because there are six seasons.'

children.text: ṣaḍṛtukatvena kālo nānāhemantādirūpatayā kaṃcidbhūtaviśeṣaṃ kvacidvardhayati sa cātmakāryaṃ rasaṃ puṣṭaṃ karoti yathā hemantakāle somaguṇātireko bhavati śiśire vāyvākāśātirekaḥ evaṃ tasyāśitīyoktarasotpādakrameṇa vasantādāv api bhūtotkarṣo jñeyaḥ ṣaḍṛtukācceti cakāreṇāhorātrakṛto 'pi bhūtotkarṣo jñeyaḥ tathādṛṣṭakṛtaś ca tena hemantādāv api rasāntarotpādaḥ kvacidvastuny upapanno bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Because time consists of six seasons, in the various forms beginning with winter it increases some particular element in some place, and that element makes its own effect, the taste, well nourished. For example, in the winter season there is an excess of <s>soma</s>-qualities, and in the cool season there is an excess of wind and ether. In this same way, by the order of taste-production stated in the chapter on food and drink, the predominance of elements in spring and the other seasons should also be understood. And from the phrase 'from the six-seasoned year,' the word 'and' indicates that a predominance of elements caused by day and night should also be understood, and likewise one caused by unseen factors. Thus even in winter and the other seasons the production of another taste in some substance is reasonable.

children.text: yadyapi ca ṛtubhede'pi bhūtotkarṣaviśeṣa eva kāraṇaṃ yaduktaṃ tāv etāv arkavāyū ityādi tathāpi bījāṅkurakāryakāraṇabhāvavat saṃsārānāditayaiva bhūtaviśeṣartvoḥ kāryakāraṇabhāvo vācyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Although, even when seasons differ, the particular predominance of elements alone is the cause, as was stated in the passage beginning 'these two, the sun and wind,' still, just as in the causal relation between seed and sprout, because the world-process is beginningless, the causal relation between particular elements and seasons must also be stated.
He states another property of tastes caused by particular elements with the words beginning 'there.'
'Generally' means not in every case.
'Tastes' means substances furnished with tastes.

children.text: plavanatvāditi gatimattvāt yadyapi gatiradho'pi syāt tathāpi laghutvaparigatagatir iha vāyor ūrdhvam eva gamanaṃ karoti yathā śālmalītulānām ||
children.translated_text: 'Because of floating' means because of mobility. Although motion may also be downward, here motion qualified by lightness makes wind move upward, as in the case of silk-cotton fibers.

children.text: hetvantaram āha ūrdhvajvalanatvāc cāgneriti agner apyūrdhvagatitvād ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He states another reason: 'and because fire flames upward.' The meaning is: because fire too has upward motion.
'Going to a low place' means precisely going downward.

children.text: yathādravyamiti yadyasya rasasya dravyam ādhāras tadanatikrameṇa ||
children.translated_text: 'According to the substance' means without transgressing the substance that is the support of each particular taste.

children.text: etena rasānāṃ guṇakarmaṇī rasādhāre dravye boddhavye iti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By this he shows that the qualities and actions of tastes are to be understood in the substance that is the support of the taste.
There, with the words beginning 'there.'

children.text: madhura ādāv ucyate praśastāyuṣyādiguṇatayā prāyaḥ prāṇipriyatayā ca ||
children.translated_text: Sweet is mentioned first because of its excellent qualities such as promoting life, and because it is generally dear to living beings.
The six senses, together with the mind.
'Life-restoring' means restoring life to one who has fainted from injury and the like.
'Promoting longevity' means causing an increase of lifespan.

children.text: kṣīṇasya saṃdhānakaro dhātupoṣakatvena kiṃvā kṣīṇaścāsau kṣataśceti tena kṣīṇakṣatasya uraḥkṣataṃ saṃdadhāti ||
children.translated_text: It joins together what is wasted because it nourishes the bodily tissues; or, 'wasted and wounded' means one who is both wasted and wounded, and thus it heals the chest wound of one who is wasted and wounded.
The statement of the quality of being desired by bees and the like is useful for recognizing conditions such as <s>prameha</s> (urinary disorder).

children.text: yaduktaṃ mūtre 'bhidhāvanti pipīlikāśca iti tathā riṣṭe vakṣyati yasmin gṛdhnanti makṣikāḥ iti anena ca madhuratvaṃ jñāyate ||
children.translated_text: As it has been said, 'ants run toward the urine'; and likewise in the section on fatal signs he will say, 'on which flies settle greedily.' By this, sweetness is known.

children.text: akṣyāmayenaivābhiṣyande labdhe viśeṣopādānārthaṃ punarvacanaṃ kiṃvā abhiṣyando nāsādiṣvapi jñeyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since <s>abhiṣyanda</s> (congestive discharge) is already obtained under disease of the eye, the repetition is for the sake of a specific mention; or else <s>abhiṣyanda</s> should be understood also in the nose and other parts.
Because it satisfies the heart, it is heart-pleasing.

children.text: bhuktam apakarṣayatīti sārayati kledayati tathā jarayati bhuktameva ||
children.translated_text: Because it draws down what has been eaten, it moves it onward, moistens it, and also digests that very food.

children.text: avamūtritaṃ mūtraviṣairjantubhiḥ parisarpitaṃ ca sparśaviśeṣaiḥ kāraṇḍādibhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Urinated upon' means affected by creatures through urinary poisons, and 'crawled over' means affected by particular contacts from creatures such as kāraṇḍas and the like.
'Expansive' means cutting through moisture.
'Moving downward' means having the nature of flowing down.

children.text: sarvarasapratyanīkabhūta iti yatra mātrātirikto lavaṇo bhavati tatra nānyo rasa upalakṣyate ||
children.translated_text: 'Opposed to all tastes' means that where salty taste is present in excessive measure, no other taste is perceived.
'Joined with food' means that it is always used in food.
'It deludes' means it causes mental disturbance.
'It causes fainting' means it causes loss of consciousness.

children.text: vipākasya prabhāvo vipākaprabhāvaḥ vipākaśca kaṭūnāṃ kaṭureva rasasya vīryasya ca prabhāvo rasavīryaprabhāvaḥ ayaṃ ca vakṣyamāṇe sarvatra hetuḥ ||
children.translated_text: The effect of <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive transformation) is the effect of <s>vipāka</s>; and the <s>vipāka</s> of pungent substances is itself pungent. The effect of taste and potency is the effect of taste and <s>vīrya</s> (potency). This is the cause everywhere in what is about to be stated.
The direct mention of the feet and the other parts is because disorders of wind mostly occur precisely there.

children.text: atra ca vipākaprabhāvādikathanam udāharaṇārthaṃ tena madhurādiṣu vipākādikāryam unneyam ||
children.translated_text: Here the statement about the effect of <s>vipāka</s> and so forth is by way of example. Therefore the effects of <s>vipāka</s> and the like should be inferred in the sweet and other tastes as well.
'It weakens' means it produces a loss of exhilaration.
'Pain-causing' means causing pain in a wound.
Because it consumes the moisture of the body, it is absorptive.
In 'cold and not light,' because of the coalescence of the letter 'a,' the meaning is 'not light.'
'It restrains' means it makes things bound.
'Separately' means one by one, by measure.
'As one' means having made them one, that is, by measure as an aggregate.
'By measure' means through a measured amount.
And that unification should be understood as occurring with two, three, and all the tastes, and so on.
'Of the inner world' means of the whole class of living beings.
'Otherwise' means not according to measure.

children.text: samprati rasadvāreṇaiva dravyāṇāṃ vīryam āha śītamityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now he states the <s>vīrya</s> (potency) of substances precisely through the channel of <s>rasa</s> (taste), in the passage beginning "cold."

children.text: yaddravyaṃ rase pāke ca madhuraṃ tacchītaṃ vīryeṇa jñeyaṃ tathā tayoriti rasapākayor yadamlaṃ dravyaṃ taduṣṇaṃ vīryeṇa tathā yacca dravyaṃ tayoriti rasapākayoḥ kaṭukam uktaṃ taccoṣṇaṃ vīryeṇa bhavati iti śeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The substance which is sweet in taste and in digestive transformation should be known as cold in potency. Likewise, "in both" means in taste and digestive transformation: a substance that is sour in those two is hot in potency. And the substance that is said to be pungent in those two, namely taste and digestive transformation, is also hot in potency; this is the remainder to be supplied.

children.text: kiṃvā yaccoṣṇaṃ kaṭukaṃ tayoḥ iti pāṭhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or the reading may be, "and whatever is hot and pungent in those two."

children.text: tatra yadrasato madhuraṃ tad vīryataḥ śītamiti vaktavye yad rasapākayor iti karoti tan madhurarasocitapākasyaiva madhuradravyasya śītavīryatāprāptyartham evam amlakaṭukayor api vācyam ||
children.translated_text: There, where one might simply say, "whatever is sweet in taste is cold in potency," he says "whatever is sweet in taste and digestive transformation" in order to establish cold potency only for a sweet substance whose digestive transformation is appropriate to the sweet taste. The same should also be stated for sour and pungent.

children.text: teṣām iti madhurapākādīnāṃ rasopadeśeneti rasamātrakathanenaiva yato vipāko 'pi rasata eva prāyo jñāyate yad vakṣyati kaṭutiktakaṣāyāṇāṃ vipākaḥ prāyaśaḥ kaṭur ityādi ||
children.translated_text: "Of these" means of such things as sweet digestive transformation. "By the instruction of taste" means by the mere statement of taste, because digestive transformation too is generally known from taste itself, as he will state: "The digestive transformation of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances is generally pungent," and so on.
And he says that this is not so everywhere, in the passage beginning "by potency."

children.text: vīryato'viparītānāṃ rasadvārā vīryajñānaṃ na tu rasaviruddhavīryāṇāṃ mahāpañcamūlādīnāṃ na kevalaṃ rasena kiṃ tarhi pākataśca ya upadekṣyate guṇasaṃgrahaḥ śukrahā baddhaviṇmūtro vipāko vātalaḥ kaṭuḥ ityādinā sa ca vīryato 'viruddhānāṃ vijñeyaḥ yadi tatra vīryaṃ virodhi bhavati tadā vipāko'pi yathoktaguṇakarī na syāt ||
children.translated_text: For substances whose potency is not contrary, knowledge of potency comes through taste; but not for those whose potency conflicts with taste, such as <s>mahāpañcamūla</s> and the like. Nor is it known merely from taste; rather, also from digestive transformation. The collection of qualities that will be taught with statements such as "pungent digestive transformation injures semen, binds feces and urine, and promotes <s>vāta</s>" should be understood for substances whose potency is not contrary. If the potency there is contrary, then the digestive transformation too would not produce the stated qualities.

children.text: kiṃvā pākataścāviparītānāṃ rasopadeśena guṇasaṃgrahaḥ śītoṣṇalakṣaṇo nirdeśyaḥ yasyāstu pippalyāḥ kaṭukāyā api viparītamadhurapākitvaṃ na tatra kaṭu rasatvenoṣṇatvam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or, by the instruction of taste, the collection of qualities characterized by cold and hot is to be indicated for things whose digestive transformation is also not contrary. But in the case of <s>pippalī</s>, though it is pungent, there is a contrary sweet digestive transformation; therefore hotness is not established there merely because it is pungent in taste. This is the meaning.

children.text: asmiṃśca pakṣe upadekṣyate iti yathā payaḥ ityādinā sambadhyate ||
children.translated_text: And in this interpretation, "will be taught" is connected with the passage beginning "as milk."
He states those very substances whose potency and digestive transformation are not contrary, in the passage beginning "as milk."
For substances beginning with milk are to be taught, in the account of the qualities of substances, as having non-contradictory potency and digestive transformation.

children.text: samprati yatra viruddhavīryatvena rasenoṣṇatvādi na nirdeśyaṃ tad āha madhuram ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, where hotness and the like should not be indicated from taste because the potency is contrary, he states this in the passage beginning "sweet."

children.text: kiṃcit kaṣāyaṃ coṣṇaṃ tiktaṃ coṣṇam iti yojanā kaṣāyatiktalavaṇānām udāharaṇam asūtritānām api prakaraṇāt kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: The construction is: "some astringent is also hot, and some bitter is also hot." The examples of astringent, bitter, and salty things are given from the context, even though they were not stated in the root text.
Here <s>mahatpañcamūla</s> is the pentad of roots beginning with <s>bilva</s>.

children.text: etacca tiktasya kaṣāyasya coṣṇatāyām udāharaṇam abjānūpāmiṣaṃ tu madhurasyoṣṇavīryatve ||
children.translated_text: And this is an example of heat in something bitter and astringent. But meat from water-born and marsh-dwelling animals is an example of something sweet having hot potency.

children.text: vīryaprasaṅgād anyam apyamlādīnāṃ viruddhaguṇam āha kiṃcid ityādi ||
children.translated_text: In connection with potency, he also states another quality of sour and the other tastes that is contrary, in the passage beginning "some."

children.text: abhayāyām ato'nyatheti abhayāyāṃ kaṣāyo raso bhedanaś coṣṇaś cetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "In <s>abhayā</s> it is otherwise than this" means that in <s>abhayā</s> the taste is astringent, but it is purgative and hot.
"Because of dryness," and so on.

children.text: raukṣyeṇa kaṣāya uttama iti rūkṣatamaḥ tikto rūkṣaḥ kaṭustu madhyo rūkṣataraḥ evam anyatrāpi ||
children.translated_text: "The astringent is highest in dryness" means that it is the driest; the bitter is dry; but the pungent is in the middle, that is, drier. The same applies elsewhere too.
"And the pungent is last" means that it is inferior.
Likewise, "and salt is last" means that it is inferior.
"Salt is inferior" means in heaviness.

children.text: amlāt kaṭur ityādau amlātkaṭurlaghuḥ tataḥ kaṭukād uttamāt tikto laghutvenottamottamaḥ uttamāt kaṭukāduttama uttamottamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In the statement "pungent is lighter than sour," and so on, pungent is light in relation to sour. Then bitter is higher than pungent, which is already superior, in respect of lightness; being higher than the superior pungent, it is the very highest.
He states the opinion of some, in the passage beginning "some."
Accepting the opinion of some by the manner of his wording, he says "in heaviness," and so on.

children.text: etena gaurave lāghave cāvaratvaṃ lavaṇasya svīkurvan gaurave 'vara ityanenāmlakaṭutiktebhyo gurutvaṃ svīkaroti lavaṇasya lāghave cāvara ityanenāmlādapi laghuno 'lpaṃ lāghavaṃ lavaṇasya svīkaroti ||
children.translated_text: By this, while accepting the inferiority of salt in both heaviness and lightness, by the phrase "inferior in heaviness" he accepts that salt is heavier than sour, pungent, and bitter; and by the phrase "inferior in lightness" he accepts that salt has little lightness, even less than sour.

children.text: na ca vācyam amle pṛthivī kāraṇaṃ lavaṇe tu toyaṃ tataḥ pṛthivyapekṣayā toyajanyasya lavaṇasyaiva lāghavamucitamiti yato na niveśena gauravalāghave śakyete 'vadhārayituṃ tathāhi toyātirekakṛto madhuraḥ pṛthivyatirekakṛtāt kaṣāyādgururbhavati ||
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said: "Earth is the cause in sour, but water in salt; therefore salt, being produced from water, should properly be lighter than what depends on earth." For heaviness and lightness cannot be determined by composition. Thus a sweet thing produced by an excess of water is heavier than an astringent thing produced by an excess of earth.
Now, because digestive transformation too has the form of a taste, he states its definition in the passage beginning "the later."
By the word "generally" he shows that substances such as <s>pippalī</s> and <s>kulattha</s> have digestive transformations not conforming to their tastes.

children.text: kaṭukādiśabdena ca tadādhāraṃ dravyamucyate yato na rasāḥ pacyante kiṃtu dravyam eva ||
children.translated_text: And by the word "pungent" and the like, the substance that is the substrate of that taste is meant, because tastes are not digested; rather, only the substance is digested.
"Salt likewise" means that salt too generally has a sweet digestive transformation.

children.text: vipākalakṣaṇaṃ tu jaṭharāgniyogād āhārasya niṣṭhākāle yo guṇa utpadyate sa vipākaḥ vacanaṃ hi
children.translated_text: But the definition of digestive transformation is this: the quality that arises in food at the final stage through conjunction with the gastric fire is <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive transformation). For there is a statement:
"The other taste that arises through conjunction with the gastric fire,
at the end of the transformation of food, is called <s>vipāka</s>."

children.text: samprati vakṣyamāṇavipākalakṣaṇe madhurāmlapākayor vātamūtrapurīṣān avarodhakatve tathā kaṭorvipākasya vātamūtrapurīṣavibandhakatve hetum āha madhura ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, in the definition of digestive transformation about to be stated, he gives the reason why sweet and sour digestive transformations do not obstruct <s>vāta</s>, urine, and feces, and likewise why pungent digestive transformation obstructs <s>vāta</s>, urine, and feces, in the passage beginning "sweet."

children.text: atra madhurāmlalavaṇā niṣṭhāpākaṃ gatā api santaḥ snehaguṇayogād vātapurīṣāṇāṃ visargaṃ sukhena kurvantīti vākyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here the meaning of the sentence is that sweet, sour, and salty substances, even when they have reached the final digestive transformation, because they possess the quality of oiliness, easily bring about the release of <s>vāta</s> and feces.
Therefore this characteristic is common to the sweet and sour <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive transformation).
Likewise, in the case of pungent, bitter, and astringent substances too, the meaning of the sentence applies even in the reverse way.

children.text: samprati vipākalakṣaṇaṃ hetuvyutpāditaṃ śukrahatvādiviśeṣayuktaṃ vaktum āha śukrahetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, in order to state the definition of <s>vipāka</s>, derived by reasoning and furnished with distinctions such as injuring semen, he says the passage beginning "injuring semen."
"Other than this" means light.

children.text: samprati yathoktavipākalakṣaṇānāṃ dravyabhede kvacidalpatvaṃ kvacinmadhyatvaṃ kvacic cotkṛṣṭatvaṃ yathā bhavati tad āha vipāketyādi ||
children.translated_text: Now he states how, according to differences among substances, the previously stated characteristics of <s>vipāka</s> may be slight in one case, middling in another, and predominant in another, in the passage beginning "of <s>vipāka</s>."

children.text: vipākalakṣaṇasyālpamadhyabhūyiṣṭhatām upalakṣayet prati prati dravyāṇāṃ guṇavaiśeṣyāddhetor ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: One should observe the slightness, middling degree, and predominance of the characteristic of <s>vipāka</s> in each individual substance, because of the particular excellence of its qualities; this is the meaning.

children.text: etena dravyeṣu yad guṇavaiśeṣyaṃ madhuratvamadhurataratvamadhuratamatvādi tato hetor vipākānāmalpatvādayo viśeṣā bhavantītyuktaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: By this it is said that the distinctions of slightness and the like in <s>vipāka</s> arise from that cause, namely the particular excellence of qualities in substances, such as sweetness, greater sweetness, and greatest sweetness.

children.text: atra kecidbruvate pratirasaṃ pāko bhavati yathā madhurādīnāṃ ṣaṇṇāṃ ṣaṇmadhurādayaḥ pākā iti kecid bruvate balavatāṃ rasānāmabalavanto rasā vaśatāṃ yānti tataś cānavasthitaḥ pākaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here some say that there is a digestive transformation corresponding to each <s>rasa</s> (taste), as, for the six tastes beginning with sweet, there are six transformations beginning with sweet. Others say that weaker tastes come under the control of stronger tastes, and consequently digestive transformation is indeterminate.

children.text: tatraitaddvitayamapi pāke vyavasthākaraṇam anādṛtya suśrutena dvividhaḥ pāko madhuraḥ kaṭuś cāṅgīkṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this matter, disregarding both of these theories as a basis for fixing digestive transformation, <s>Suśruta</s> accepted a twofold <s>pāka</s> (digestive transformation), sweet and pungent.

children.text: dvaividhyaṃ ca pañcabhūtātmake dravye gurubhūtapṛthivītoyātirekānmadhuraḥ pāko bhavati śeṣalaghubhūtātirekāt tu kaṭukaḥ pāko bhavati yaduktaṃ dravyeṣu pacyamāneṣu yeṣv ambupṛthivīguṇāḥ ||
children.translated_text: And the twofoldness is this: in a substance made of the five elements, a sweet <s>pāka</s> arises from an excess of the heavy elements earth and water, while a pungent <s>pāka</s> arises from an excess of the remaining light elements. As it has been said: "Among substances being digested, those in which the qualities of water and earth
come forth in excess: there the <s>pāka</s> is called sweet.
But among those being digested in which the qualities of fire, wind, and space
come forth in excess: there the <s>pāka</s> is called pungent."

children.text: pratirasapāke tathānavasthitapāke ca dravyaṃ rasaguṇenaiva tulyaṃ pākāvasthāyāmapi bhavati tena na kaścidviśeṣo vipākena tatra bodhyata iti suśrutena tatpakṣadvayam upekṣitamiti sādhu kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: In the theory of a separate transformation for each taste, and also in the theory of indeterminate transformation, the substance remains exactly equal to its taste-quality even in the state of digestive transformation; therefore no distinction at all is made known there by <s>vipāka</s>. Thus <s>Suśruta</s> did well to set aside those two positions.

children.text: tṛtīyāmlapākanirāsastu doṣam āvahati yato vrīhikulatthādīnām amlapākatayā pittakartṛtvamupalabhyate atha manyase vrīhyāder uṣṇavīryatvena tatra pittakartṛtvaṃ tanna madhurasya vrīhestanmate madhuravipākasyoṣṇavīryatāyām api satyāṃ na pittakartṛtvamupapadyate rasavipākābhyām ekasya vīryasya bādhanīyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: But the rejection of a third, sour <s>pāka</s> brings a fault, because rice, horse gram, and the like are observed to produce <s>pitta</s> by having a sour <s>pāka</s>. If you think that in rice and the like the production of <s>pitta</s> is due to hot <s>vīrya</s> (potency), that is not so; for in that view, even when sweet rice, which has a sweet <s>vipāka</s>, has hot potency, production of <s>pitta</s> is not reasonable, since a single potency must be overridden by both taste and <s>vipāka</s>.

children.text: kiṃca amlapākatvād vrīhyādeḥ pittamamlaguṇamutpadyate yadi tu tad uṣṇavīryatākṛtaṃ syāttadā kaṭuguṇabhūyiṣṭhaṃ pittaṃ syāt dṛśyate ca vrīhibhakṣaṇād amlodgārādināmlaguṇabhūyiṣṭhataiveti ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, because rice and the like have a sour <s>pāka</s>, <s>pitta</s> possessing a sour quality is produced. But if that were caused by hot potency, then the <s>pitta</s> would be predominantly pungent in quality; and yet, from eating rice, through sour belching and the like, predominance of the sour quality alone is observed.

children.text: kiṃca pṛthivīsomaguṇātirekān madhuraḥ pāko bhavati vāyvagnyākāśātirekācca kaṭur bhavatīti pakṣe yadā vyāmiśraguṇātirekatā bhavati tadā somāgnyātmakasyāmlasyotpādaḥ kathaṃ pratikṣepaṇīyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, on the view that sweet <s>pāka</s> arises from an excess of the qualities of earth and <s>Soma</s>, and pungent <s>pāka</s> from an excess of wind, fire, and space, when there is an excess of mixed qualities, how can the production of sourness, which has the nature of <s>Soma</s> and fire, be denied?

children.text: athavā tantrakārayoḥ kim anayor anena vacanamātravirodhena kartavyaṃ yato yadamlapākaṃ carako brūte tatsuśrutena vīryoṣṇam iti kṛtvā samādhīyate tena na kaścid dravyaguṇe virodhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or else, what need have the two system-makers for this mere verbal contradiction between them? For what <s>Caraka</s> calls sour <s>pāka</s> is resolved by <s>Suśruta</s> by treating it as hot in potency; therefore there is no contradiction in the qualities of substances.

children.text: yattu suśrute'mlapākanirāsārthaṃ dūṣaṇam ucyate pittaṃ hi vidagdham amlatām upaiti ityādinā tadanabhyupagamādeva nirastam ||
children.translated_text: But the criticism stated in <s>Suśruta</s> for rejecting sour <s>pāka</s>, beginning "for <s>pitta</s>, when vitiated, becomes sour," is dismissed simply because that is not accepted.

children.text: nanu lavaṇasya madhurapākitve pittaraktādikartṛtvam anupapannaṃ tathā tiktakaṣāyayoḥ kaṭupākitve pittahantṛtvamanupapannaṃ naivaṃ satyapi lavaṇasya madhurapākitve tatra lavaṇarasa uṣṇaṃ ca vīryaṃ yadasti tena tat pittaraktādikārakaṃ vipākastu tatra pittaraktaharaṇalakṣaṇe kārye bādhitaḥ san sṛṣṭaviṇmūtra ityādinā lakṣaṇena lakṣyata eva ||
children.translated_text: Objection: if salt has a sweet <s>pāka</s>, its production of <s>pitta</s>, blood, and the like is not reasonable; likewise, if bitter and astringent substances have pungent <s>pāka</s>, their destruction of <s>pitta</s> is not reasonable. Not so. Even though salt has a sweet <s>pāka</s>, the salty taste and the hot potency that exist there make it productive of <s>pitta</s>, blood, and the like. But <s>vipāka</s>, though overridden there in the action characterized by removing <s>pitta</s> and blood, is still indicated by the characteristic beginning "it releases feces and urine."

children.text: etena yaducyate lavaṇe madhuro vipākaścedrasavīryābhyāṃ bādhitaḥ san svakāryakaro na bhavati tatkiṃ tenopadiṣṭeneti tannirastaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: By this, the claim that if salt has a sweet <s>vipāka</s>, then, being overridden by taste and potency, it does not perform its own action and so there is no point in teaching it, is refuted.

children.text: yato'styeva sṛṣṭaviṇmūtratādinā tatra lavaṇe madhuravipākitvaṃ lakṣaṇīyam ||
children.translated_text: For in salt, the fact that it has sweet <s>vipāka</s> is indeed to be inferred from such things as release of feces and urine.
By this line of reasoning, the prima facie objection and its answer are also supplied for bitter and astringent substances.

children.text: anye tv etaddoṣabhayāl lavaṇo'pyamlaṃ pacyata iti vyākhyānayanti lavaṇastathetyatra tathāśabdena viprakṛṣṭasyāmlamityasya karṣaṇāditi ||
children.translated_text: Others, out of fear of this fault, explain that salt too is digested as sour, because in the phrase "salt likewise," the word "likewise" draws in the remote word "sour."

children.text: tanna kaṭvādīnāṃ kaṭurvipāko'mlo'mlasya śeṣayor madhuraḥ iti jatūkarṇavacanāt ||
children.translated_text: That is not so, because of the statement of <s>Jatūkarṇa</s>: "The <s>vipāka</s> of pungent and the others is pungent, that of sour is sour, and that of the remaining two is sweet."

children.text: naca vācyaṃ kasmāt traya eva vipākā bhavanti na punastiktādayo'pīti yato bhūtasvabhāva evaiṣaḥ yena madhurādayas traya eva bhavanti bhūtasvabhāvāś cāparyanuyojyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nor should it be said, "Why are there only three <s>vipāka</s>s, and not also bitter and the others?" For this is simply the nature of the elements, by which only the three beginning with sweet arise; and the natures of the elements are not open to further questioning.

children.text: nanu yaśca rasaviparītaḥ pāko yathā lavaṇasya madhuraḥ tiktakaṣāyayoś ca kaṭuḥ sa ucyatāṃ yastu samānaguṇo madhurasya madhuro'mlasyāmlaḥ kaṭukasya vā kaṭukaḥ tatkathane kiṃ prayojanaṃ yato rasaguṇair eva tatra vipākaguṇo'pi jñāsyate ||
children.translated_text: But, one may object: let that <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive transformation) which is contrary to the <s>rasa</s> (taste) be stated, as the sweet transformation of salt and the pungent transformation of bitter and astringent things. But when it has the same quality, namely the sweet transformation of a sweet substance, the sour of a sour substance, or the pungent of a pungent substance, what is the use of stating it, since in that case the quality of the <s>vipāka</s> too will be known from the qualities of the taste itself?

children.text: naivaṃ yena lavaṇādivad visadṛśarasāntarotpādaśaṅkānirārāsārtham api tatrānuguṇo'pi vipāko vaktavya eva vipākajaśca rasa āhārapariṇāmānte bhavati prākṛtastu raso vipākaviruddhaḥ pariṇāmakālaṃ varjayitvā jñeyaḥ tena pippalyāḥ kaṭukarasatvam ādau kaṇṭhasthaśleṣmakṣapaṇamukhaśodhanādikartṛtvena saprayojanaṃ madhuravipākatvaṃ tu pariṇāmena vṛṣyatvādijñāpanena saprayojanam ||
children.translated_text: Not so. For even there, even though the <s>vipāka</s> is conformable, it must indeed be stated, in order to remove the suspicion that some different taste might arise, as in salt and the rest. And the taste produced by <s>vipāka</s> occurs at the end of the transformation of food; but the natural taste, when opposed to <s>vipāka</s>, should be known apart from the time of transformation. Therefore, in <s>pippalī</s>, its pungent taste is meaningful at first, because it removes phlegm situated in the throat and cleanses the mouth and so on; but its having a sweet <s>vipāka</s> is meaningful because it makes known, through transformation, such effects as being aphrodisiac.

children.text: tathā yatra vipākasya rasāḥ samānaguṇatayānuguṇā bhavanti tatra balavat kāryaṃ bhavati viparyaye tu durbalam iti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, where the tastes are conformable to the <s>vipāka</s> by having the same qualities, there the effect is strong; but in the opposite case it should be known to be weak.

children.text: etacca pākatrayaṃ dravyaniyataṃ tena grahaṇyadhyāye vakṣyamāṇāhārāvasthāpākādbhinnam eva tatra hy aviśeṣeṇa sarveṣāmeva rasānām avasthāvaśāt trayaḥ pākā vācyāḥ annasya bhuktamātrasya ṣaḍrasasya prapākataḥ ityādinā granthena ||
children.translated_text: And this threefold transformation is fixed according to the substance. Therefore it is quite different from the transformations of food in its stages that will be described in the chapter on <s>grahaṇī</s>; for there, without distinction, three transformations are to be stated for all tastes because of the condition of the stage, in the text beginning, "Of the six-tasted food just eaten, from its cooking," and so on.
He states the definition of <s>vīrya</s> (potency) according to the opinion of some, in the passage beginning "soft," and so on.
And this twofold opinion of some proceeds by giving priority to the conventional technical designation <s>vīrya</s>.

children.text: vaidyake hi rasavipākaprabhāvavyatirikte prabhūtakāryakāriṇi guṇe vīryamiti saṃjñā tenāṣṭavidhavīryavādimate picchilaviśadādayo guṇā na rasādiviparītaṃ kāryaṃ prāyaḥ kurvanti tena teṣāṃ rasādyupadeśenaiva grahaṇaṃ mṛdvādīnāṃ tu rasādyabhibhāvakatvamasti yathā pippalyāṃ kaṭurasakāryaṃ pittakopanamabhibhūya tadgate mṛduśītavīrye pittameva śamayatīti tathā kaṣāye tiktānurase mahati pañcamūle tatkāryaṃ vātakopanam abhibhūyoṣṇena vīryeṇa tadviruddhaṃ vātaśamanameva kriyate tathā madhure'pīkṣau śītavīryatvena vātavṛddhir ityādi ||
children.translated_text: For in medicine the name <s>vīrya</s> is applied to a quality, other than taste, <s>vipāka</s>, and special efficacy, that produces many effects. Therefore, according to the doctrine of eightfold <s>vīrya</s>, qualities such as slimy and clear generally do not perform an action contrary to taste and the rest; thus they are included merely through the teaching of taste and so forth. But qualities such as soft have the capacity to overpower taste and the rest. For example, in <s>pippalī</s>, after overpowering the effect of pungent taste, namely the aggravation of bile, the soft and cold potency present in it actually pacifies bile. Likewise, in the great <s>pañcamūla</s>, which is astringent with a bitter secondary taste, after overpowering its effect, namely aggravation of wind, by its hot potency, the contrary effect, precisely the pacification of wind, is produced. Similarly, in sweet sugarcane too, because of cold potency, there is an increase of wind, and so on.

children.text: yaduktaṃ suśrute etāni khalu vīryāṇi svabalaguṇotkarṣād rasam abhibhūyātmakarma darśayanti ityādi ||
children.translated_text: This is what is said in <s>Suśruta</s>: "These potencies, because of the excellence of their own strength and quality, overpower taste and show their own action," and so on.

children.text: śītoṣṇavīryavādimataṃ tv agnīṣomīyatvāj jagataḥ śītoṣṇayoreva prādhānyājjñeyam ||
children.translated_text: But the view of those who maintain cold and hot potency alone should be understood from the fact that the world is made of fire and soma, and from the primacy of cold and hot alone.
And it has been said:
"Even though a substance has various natures, the two mighty principles, fire and soma,
it never at any time passes beyond, just as the manifest and unmanifest world does not."

children.text: etacca matadvayam apyācāryasya paribhāṣāsiddhamanumatameva yenottaratra rasavīryavipākānāṃ sāmānyaṃ yatra lakṣyate ityādau pāribhāṣikam eva vīryaṃ nirdekṣyati ||
children.translated_text: And both these opinions are accepted by the teacher as established by convention; for later, in the passage beginning "where the common feature of taste, potency, and <s>vipāka</s> is observed," he will point out potency precisely in the conventional technical sense.

children.text: pāribhāṣikavīryasaṃjñāparityāgena tu śaktiparyāyasya vīryasya lakṣaṇamāha vīryaṃ tv ityādi ||
children.translated_text: But, abandoning the conventional technical designation <s>vīrya</s>, he states the definition of <s>vīrya</s> in the sense of power, in the passage beginning "but potency," and so on.
"<s>Vīrya</s>" means power.

children.text: yeneti rasena vā vipākena vā prabhāvena vā gurvādiparādibhirvā guṇairyā kriyā tarpaṇahlādanaśamanādirūpā kriyate tasyāṃ kriyāyāṃ tad rasādi vīryam ||
children.translated_text: That by which, whether by taste, by <s>vipāka</s>, by special efficacy, or by qualities such as heavy and the rest or superior and the rest, an action such as nourishing, gladdening, or pacifying is performed: in that action, that taste and so on is <s>vīrya</s>.

children.text: ata evoktaṃ suśrute yena kurvanti tadvīryam iti ||
children.translated_text: For this very reason it is said in <s>Suśruta</s>: "That by which they act is <s>vīrya</s>."

children.text: atraiva lokaprasiddhām upapattim āha nāvīryam ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states, in this very connection, an argument well known in ordinary life, in the passage beginning "not without potency," and so on.
"Without potency" means powerless.
"Done by potency" means done by something possessing potency; that is, done by potency.

children.text: rasādīnāmekadravyaniviṣṭānāṃ bhedena nārthaṃ lakṣaṇamāha raso nipāta ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states the definition, according to their difference, of taste and the others that reside in a single substance, in the passage beginning "taste is contact," and so on.
"Contact" means conjunction with the tongue.

children.text: karmaniṣṭhayeti karmaṇo niṣṭhā niṣpattiḥ karmaniṣṭhā kriyāparisamāptiḥ rasopayoge sati yo 'ntyāhārapariṇāmakṛtaḥ karmaviśeṣaḥ kaphaśukrābhivṛddhyādilakṣaṇaḥ tena vipāko niścīyate ||
children.translated_text: "By establishment in action" means by the establishment, that is, the accomplishment, of the action. <s>Vipāka</s> is determined by that particular effect, produced by the final transformation of food when taste has been used, whose marks are such things as the increase of phlegm and semen.

children.text: adhīvāsaḥ sahāvasthānaṃ yāvad adhīvāsāditi yāvaccharīranivāsāt etacca vipākātpūrvaṃ nipātāccordhvaṃ jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: "Residence" means staying together. "So long as there is residence" means so long as there is residence in the body. And this should be understood after contact and before <s>vipāka</s>.

children.text: nipātācceti śarīrasaṃyogamātrāt tena kiṃcid vīryam adhīvāsād upalabhyate yathānūpamāṃsāder uṣṇatvaṃ kiṃcic ca nipātādeva labhyate yathā marīcādīnāṃ tīkṣṇatvādi kiṃcic ca nipātādhīvāsābhyāṃ yathā marīcādīnāmeva ||
children.translated_text: "And from contact" means merely from conjunction with the body. Therefore some potency is perceived from residence, as the heat of the meat of marsh-dwelling animals; some is obtained from contact itself, as the sharpness and the like of black pepper and similar substances; and some from both contact and residence, as in the case of black pepper and the like themselves.

children.text: etena rasaḥ pratyakṣeṇaiva vipākastu nityaparokṣaḥ tatkāryeṇānumīyate vīryaṃ tu kiṃcidanumānena yathā saindhavagataṃ śaityam ānūpamāṃsagataṃ vā auṣṇyaṃ kiṃcic ca vīryaṃ pratyakṣeṇaiva yathā rājikāgatam auṣṇyaṃ ghrāṇena picchilaviśadasnigdharūkṣādayaḥ cakṣuḥsparśanābhyāṃ niścīyanta iti vākyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By this the meaning of the sentence is as follows: taste is known by direct perception itself; <s>vipāka</s>, however, is always beyond direct perception and is inferred from its effect. As for <s>vīrya</s>, some is known by inference, such as the coldness present in rock salt or the heat present in the meat of marsh-dwelling animals; and some potency is known by direct perception itself, such as the heat present in mustard by the sense of smell, while slimy, clear, oily, dry, and similar qualities are determined by sight and touch.

children.text: etacca vīryaṃ sahajaṃ kṛtrimaṃ ca jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: And this <s>vīrya</s> should be understood as both natural and artificial.

children.text: etacca yathāsambhavaṃ gurulaghvādiṣu vīryeṣu lakṣaṇaṃ jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: And, as far as applicable, this definition should be understood for the potencies beginning with heavy and light.
"Of substances" means of the substances that are being used.
And that definition of <s>vīrya</s> (potency) concerns only <s>vīrya</s> in the technical sense.
He states the definition of <s>prabhāva</s> (specific efficacy) in the passage beginning "taste and potency."
"Commonality" means likeness.
"The distinction of actions" means such things as purgativeness, residing in <s>dantī</s> and the other substances.

children.text: sāmānyaṃ lakṣyata ityanena rasādikāryatvena yannāvadhārayituṃ śakyate kāryaṃ tat prabhāvakṛtam iti sūcayati ata evoktaṃprabhāvo 'cintya ucyate rasavīryavipākakāryatayācintya ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By saying "a commonality is indicated," he suggests that any effect which cannot be ascertained as an effect of taste and the rest is produced by <s>prabhāva</s>. For this very reason it is said, "<s>prabhāva</s> is called inconceivable," meaning that it is inconceivable as an effect of <s>rasa</s> (taste), <s>vīrya</s> (potency), and <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive transformation).

children.text: asyaiva durabhigamatvād udāharaṇāni bahūnyāha kaṭuka ityādinā ||
children.translated_text: Because this very thing is hard to understand, he gives many examples with the passage beginning "pungent."
"Likewise" means having qualities similar to those of <s>citraka</s>.
"It has been stated to counteract poison" refers to the statement beginning "therefore fang-poison is primary."

children.text: ūrdhvānulomikamiti yugapad ubhayabhāgaharaṃ kiṃvā ūrdhvaharaṃ tathānulomaharaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: "Moving upward and downward" means removing through both routes at once, or else removing upward and also carrying downward in the natural direction.
"The action which has a manifold nature" means actions such as removing poison and removing colic.

children.text: etaccodāharaṇamātraṃ tena jīvanamedhyādidravyasya rasādyacintyaṃ sarvaṃ prabhāva iti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: And this is only an example. Therefore everything in substances such as life-promoting and intellect-promoting drugs that is inconceivable in terms of taste and the rest should be understood as <s>prabhāva</s>.

children.text: prabhāvaśceha dravyaśaktir abhipretā sā ca dravyāṇāṃ sāmānyaviśeṣaḥ dantītvādiyuktā vyaktireva yataḥ śaktirhi svarūpameva bhāvānāṃ nātiriktaṃ kiṃciddharmāntaram evaṃ pradeśāntaroktaguṇaprabhāvādiṣvapi vācyam yathoktaṃ dravyāṇi hi dravyaprabhāvādguṇaprabhāvām ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Here <s>prabhāva</s> is intended as the power of a substance. And that is the common and particular nature of substances, namely the very individual thing qualified by being <s>dantī</s> and the like; for power is simply the own-form of things, not some additional separate property. The same should be said also of qualities, <s>prabhāva</s>, and so on mentioned in another place, as in the statement beginning "substances, because of the <s>prabhāva</s> of substances and the <s>prabhāva</s> of qualities."

children.text: na ca vācyaṃ dantyādiḥ svarūpata eva virecayati tena kimiti jalādyupahatā dantī na virecayatīti pratibandhakābhāvaviśiṣṭasyaiva prabhāvasya kāraṇatvāt jalopahatāyāṃ dantyāṃ jalopaghātaḥ pratibandhaka ityādyanusaraṇīyam ||
children.translated_text: Nor should one say, "<s>Dantī</s> and the like purge simply by their own nature; then why does <s>dantī</s> impaired by water not purge?" For only a <s>prabhāva</s> qualified by the absence of an obstruction is causal. In <s>dantī</s> impaired by water, injury by water is the obstruction; the explanation should be followed in this way.

children.text: naiyāyikaśaktivāde yā ca viṣasya viṣaghnatve upapattir uktā ūrdhvādhogāmitvavirodhalakṣaṇā sāntarbhāgatvāt prabhāvād eva bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And in the Naiyāyika doctrine of power, the rationale stated for poison's counteracting poison, characterized as a conflict between upward and downward movement, also occurs only from <s>prabhāva</s>, because it is included within it.
The same should be said even when earthiness and the like are mentioned in cases such as upward-and-downward movement.
"Vijñāna" means that by which something is known, that is, a defining mark.
"Dissolving" means becoming dissolved.
Because it causes flow, it is called "flow-producing."

children.text: vikāsīti hṛdayavikasanaśīla uktaṃ hi suśrute hṛdayaṃ pīḍayati iti ||
children.translated_text: "Expansive" means disposed to expand the heart. For it is stated in <s>Suśruta</s>, "it presses upon the heart."
Now, in order to explain incompatible food, he says "thus" and so on.

children.text: śarīradhātuvirodhaṃ kurvantīti vairodhikāḥ lakṣyate vairodhikamaneneti lakṣaṇaṃ vairodhikābhidhāyako grantha eva ||
children.translated_text: They are called "incompatible" because they create opposition to the bodily constituents. "That by which incompatibility is indicated" is the definition; it is the very passage denoting incompatibility.
The definition of incompatibility should be understood from the passage beginning "whatever, having caused any doṣa to flow out."

children.text: dehadhātupratyanīkabhūtānīti dehadhātūnāṃ rasādīnāṃ vātādīnāṃ ca prakṛtisthānāṃ pratyanīkasvarūpāṇi ||
children.translated_text: "Things contrary to the bodily constituents" means things whose own nature is contrary to the bodily constituents, namely <s>rasa</s> and the rest, and also to <s>vāta</s> and the rest when these are in their normal state.

children.text: virodhamāpadyanta iti dehadhātūnāṃ virodhamācaranti dūṣayantīti yāvat ||
children.translated_text: "They enter into opposition" means they act in opposition to the bodily constituents; that is, they vitiate them.

children.text: yathābhūtāni dravyāṇi dehadhātubhirvirodhamāpadyante tadāha parasparaviruddhāni kānicid ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states how substances come into opposition with the bodily constituents in the passage beginning "some are mutually opposed."

children.text: tatra parasparaguṇaviruddhāni yathā na matsyān payasābhyavaharet ubhayaṃ hy etad ityādinoktāni ||
children.translated_text: Among these, mutually opposed by qualities are those mentioned in passages such as "one should not eat fish with milk, for both of these," and so on.

children.text: saṃyogaviruddhaṃ yathā tadeva nikucaṃ pakvaṃ na māṣa ityādinoktaṃ yat saṃskārādiviruddhaguṇakathanaṃ vinā sāhityamātreṇa viruddham ucyate tat saṃyogaviruddham ||
children.translated_text: An incompatibility of combination is, for example, what is stated in the passage beginning "that same ripe <s>nikuca</s> fruit, not with <s>māṣa</s>." Whatever is called incompatible merely because of being together, without mention of qualities made incompatible by preparation and the like, is incompatibility of combination.

children.text: matsyapayasos tu yadyapi sahopayogo viruddhatvenoktaḥ tathāpyasau guṇaviruddhatvena kathita iti guṇavirodhakasyaivodāharaṇam
children.translated_text: Although the joint use of fish and milk is stated to be incompatible, that is described as an incompatibility of qualities; therefore it is indeed an example of quality-incompatibility.

children.text: virodhaśca viruddhaguṇatve satyapi kvacid eva dravyaprabhāvād bhavati tena ṣaḍrasāhāropayoge madhurāmlayor viruddhaśītoṣṇavīryayor virodho nodbhāvanīyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Incompatibility, even when qualities are mutually opposed, occurs only in certain cases because of the <s>prabhāva</s> of the substance. Therefore, when a diet containing all six tastes is used, no incompatibility should be raised between sweet and sour things whose cold and hot potencies are opposed.

children.text: saṃskārato viruddhaṃ yathā na kapotān sarṣapatailabhṛṣṭān ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Incompatibility by preparation is, for example, the statement beginning "not pigeons fried in mustard oil."
Place is twofold: land and the body.

children.text: tatra bhūmiviruddhaṃ yathā tadeva bhasmapāṃśuparidhvastam kiṃvā yat kiṃcidagocarabhṛtaṃ taddeśaviruddhaṃ śarīraviruddhaṃ yathā uṣṇārtasya madhu maraṇāya ||
children.translated_text: There, incompatibility with respect to land is, for example, that same thing covered with ash and dust; or whatever has grown in an unsuitable range is incompatible with respect to place. Incompatibility with respect to the body is, for example, honey for a person afflicted by heat, which leads to death.
Incompatibility with respect to time is, for example, stale <s>kākamācī</s>, which leads to death.
Incompatibility with respect to measure is, for example, honey and ghee in equal quantity, which leads to death.
By the word "and so on," incompatibilities related to <s>doṣa</s>, constitution, and the like are included.
Incompatibility by nature is, for example, poison.
"With reference to incompatibility" means having set forth incompatibility as the topic.

children.text: śītoṣṇatvāditi payaḥ śītam uṣṇavīryāśca matsyāḥ śeṣaṃ madhuratvādi samānam ||
children.translated_text: "Because of coldness and hotness" means that milk is cold, while fish are hot in potency; the rest, such as sweetness, is the same.
And this too is incompatible precisely because of the <s>prabhāva</s> of the substance.

children.text: sa punaḥ śakalī ityādinā nāndiniḥ iti khyāto matsya ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Again, by the passage beginning "<s>śakalī</s>," a fish known as <s>nāndinī</s> is meant.
Meat of domestic animals and the like are incompatible with any one of honey and the other substances.
"Kalamūkatā" means indistinctness of speech.

children.text: pauṣkarādīnāṃ madhupayobhyāṃ sahābhyavahāro viruddhaḥ pauṣkaraṃ puṣkaratratrarūpaṃ śākaṃ rohiṇī kaṭurohiṇī ||
children.translated_text: The eating of <s>pauṣkara</s> and the others together with honey and milk is incompatible. <s>Pauṣkara</s> is a vegetable in the form of <s>puṣkaratra</s>; <s>rohiṇī</s> is <s>kaṭurohiṇī</s>.
<s>Dhamanīpraticaya</s> is a knot-like swelling of the vessels.
<s>Jātuśāka</s> is bamboo-leaf vegetable.

children.text: vairodhikatvādityanena prakaraṇalabdhasyāpi vairodhikatvasya punarabhidhānaṃ sāmānyoktaṣāṇḍhyādivyādhikartṛtopadarśanārtham evamanyatrāpi sāmānye'pi vairodhikatvamātrābhidhāne vaktavyam
children.translated_text: By the phrase 'because it is incompatible,' the incompatibility already obtained from the context is stated again precisely in order to show that generally mentioned diseases such as impotence are caused by incompatibility. The same should be supplied elsewhere too, even where only incompatibility in general is stated.

children.text: tathāmletyādau amlagrahaṇena labdhānāpy amlāmrātakādīnām abhidhānaṃ viśeṣavirodhasūcanārtham ||
children.translated_text: Likewise, in the passage beginning 'with sour things,' the mention of sour <s>āmrātaka</s> and the like, though already obtained by the word 'sour,' is for indicating a specific incompatibility.

children.text: sarvagrahaṇenaiva dravādravāmle prāpte punardravādravavacanaṃ sarvaśabdasya dravādravāmlakārtsnyārthatāpratiṣedhārthaṃ bhavati hi prakaraṇād ekadeśe 'pi sarvavyapadeśaḥ yathā sarvān bhojayediti kiṃvā sarvagrahaṇam amlavipākānāṃ vrīhyādīnāṃ grahaṇārtham ||
children.translated_text: Although liquid and non-liquid sour things are already included by the word 'all,' the repeated statement 'liquid and non-liquid' is meant to prevent taking the word 'all' as meaning the complete class of liquid and non-liquid sour things. For, from context, the designation 'all' may apply even to a part, as in 'one should feed all.' Or else the word 'all' is meant to include rice and other substances whose <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive transformation) is sour.

children.text: payaseti tṛtīyayeva sahārthe labdhe punaḥ sahetyabhidhānaṃ kevalāmlādiyuktasyaiva virodhitopadarśanārthaṃ tena amlapayaḥsaṃyoge guḍādisaṃyoge sati viruddhatvaṃ na dugdhāmrādīnām ||
children.translated_text: Since the sense of 'together with' is already obtained by the instrumental in 'with milk,' the further statement 'together with' is made to show incompatibility only when milk is joined with sour things and the like by themselves. Thus, when a sour-and-milk combination also has a combination with jaggery and the like, milk with mango and such things is not incompatible.
<s>Vanaka</s> is <s>vanakodrava</s>.
<s>Padmottarikā</s> is <s>kusumbha</s>.
'<s>Śārkara</s>' qualifies a particular kind of <s>maireya</s> liquor.

children.text: vātaṃ cātikopayatīti vacanena pittakaphāv alpaṃ kopayatīti bodhayati evaṃ pittaṃ cātikopayati kaphaṃ cātikopayatītyetayorapi vācyam ||
children.translated_text: By saying 'and it greatly provokes <s>vāta</s>,' he makes one understand that it provokes <s>pitta</s> and <s>kapha</s> only slightly. The same should also be said of the two statements 'it greatly provokes <s>pitta</s>' and 'it greatly provokes <s>kapha</s>.'
<s>Hāridraka</s> is the bird known as <s>haritāla</s>.

children.text: balākā vāruṇyā saha viruddhā tathā kulmāṣaiśca balākā viruddhā ||
children.translated_text: The <s>balākā</s> bird is incompatible together with <s>vāruṇī</s> liquor; likewise the <s>balākā</s> is incompatible with <s>kulmāṣa</s>.

children.text: eraṇḍasīsakāvasaktamiti eraṇḍakāṣṭhāvasaktaṃ sīsako hi bhaṭitrakaraṇakāṣṭham ucyate ||
children.translated_text: 'Suspended on castor-wood <s>sīsaka</s>' means suspended on castor wood; for <s>sīsaka</s> is the name for wood used in constructing a furnace or still.
'That very thing' means the meat of the <s>hāridraka</s> bird.

children.text: matsyā nistālyante pacyante yasmin tanmatsyanistālanaṃ kiṃvā nistālanaṃ vasā jatūkarṇe'pyuktaṃ matsyavasā siddhāḥ pippalyaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: <s>Matsyanistālana</s> is that in which fish are boiled, that is, cooked. Or <s>nistālana</s> means fat; it is also stated in <s>Jātūkarṇa</s>: 'long peppers cooked in fish fat.'
<s>Kākamācī</s> together with honey is incompatible by combination.
<s>Bhāsa</s> is a henhouse fowl.
In order to include unstated cases of incompatibility, he says the passage beginning 'whatever.'
It is called <s>āhāra</s> (intake) because it is brought in; medicine too is included.
'Having caused the <s>doṣa</s> to flow' means that, after producing the <s>doṣas</s> in an unagitated form, it does not expel them.

children.text: anena vamanavirecanadravyāṇi nirākaroti tāni hi doṣānāsrāvya nirharanti ||
children.translated_text: By this he rules out emetic and purgative substances, for they expel the <s>doṣas</s> after causing them to flow.

children.text: yaccāpi deśakālāgnītyādigranthaṃ kecit paṭhanti sa ca vyakta eva ||
children.translated_text: Some read the passage beginning 'and whatever also, with regard to place, time, and digestive fire'; that too is quite clear.
<s>Ṣāṇḍhya</s> means impotence.
A defect of progeny is such things as the condition of having dead offspring.
