children.text: yatra vārtāke kaṭutiktatvena vātakaratvaṃ prāptamapi ca vikṛtiviṣamasamavāyāttanna bhavati tatrācāryeṇa vārtākaṃ vātaghnam ityuktam eva ||
children.translated_text: Where, in <s>vārtāka</s>, the state of producing <s>vāta</s> would be expected because of pungency and bitterness, but because of <s>vikṛtiviṣamasamavāya</s> that does not occur, there the teacher has indeed said, "<s>vārtāka</s> removes <s>vāta</s>."
Thus, and so on: the respective examples current in the treatise should be followed.

children.text: yattu prakṛtisamasamavāyakṛtarasadoṣaguṇadvārā prāptamapi dravyaguṇaṃ vikāralakṣaṇaṃ ca brūte tat prakarṣārthaṃ spaṣṭārthaṃ ceti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: But when it states a property of a substance or a characteristic of a disorder that is already obtained through the qualities of taste and <s>doṣa</s> produced by <s>prakṛtisamasamavāya</s>, that should be understood as being for the sake of emphasis and clarity.
He concludes with the passage beginning "therefore."
"The true nature" means the true nature of the <s>prabhāva</s> (specific efficacy) of <s>rasa</s> and the others.

children.text: yattu pūrvaṃ tatrādau rasadravyadoṣavikāraprabhāvān upadekṣyāmaḥ ityanena rasādiprabhāvavyākhyānapratijñānaṃ kṛtaṃ tattu rasaprabhāvānumānenaiva dravyaprabhāvakathanāt tathā doṣaprabhāveṇa ca vikāraprabhāvakathanāc caritārthaṃ syāt ||
children.translated_text: But earlier, by the statement "There, at the beginning, we shall teach the <s>prabhāva</s>s of <s>rasa</s>, substance, <s>doṣa</s>, and disorder," a promise was made to explain the <s>prabhāva</s>s beginning with <s>rasa</s>. That, however, would be fulfilled simply by stating the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance through inference from the <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>rasa</s>, and likewise by stating the <s>prabhāva</s> of disorder through the <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>doṣa</s>.

children.text: iha tu vikṛtiviṣamasamavāyātmake dravye vikāre vā rasadoṣaprabhāvānumānena na dravyavikāraprabhāvānumānam astīti kṛtvā pṛthak pṛthagrasādiprabhāvatattvābhidhānapratijñānam iti na paunaruktyam ||
children.translated_text: Here, however, because in a substance or disorder whose nature is an abnormal and uneven conjunction there is no inference of the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance or disorder by inference from the <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>rasa</s> or <s>doṣa</s>, the promise to state separately the true nature of the <s>prabhāva</s>s of <s>rasa</s> and the others is not repetition.

children.text: iha dravyāṇāṃ vīryaprabhāvavipākaprabhāvau ca dravyaprabhāve rasaprabhāve vāntarbhāvanīyau ||
children.translated_text: Here the <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>vīrya</s> (potency) and the <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>vipāka</s> (post-digestive effect) belonging to substances are to be included under the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance or under the <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>rasa</s>.

children.text: tatra yau rasānuguṇau vīryavipākaprabhāvau tau rase yau tu rasakramoktavīryavipākaviparītau vīryavipākau tau dravyaprabhāve boddhavyau ||
children.translated_text: Of these, those <s>prabhāva</s>s of <s>vīrya</s> and <s>vipāka</s> that accord with <s>rasa</s> should be understood under <s>rasa</s>; but those <s>vīrya</s> and <s>vipāka</s> effects that are contrary to the <s>vīrya</s> and <s>vipāka</s> stated in the sequence of the <s>rasa</s>s should be understood under the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance.

children.text: upadekṣyāma iti nikhilena tantreṇa rasādiprabhāvatattvaṃ pṛthag upadekṣyāma ityarthaḥ rasādiprabhāvaḥ prapañcena nikhile tantra eva vaktavyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "We shall teach" means: we shall teach separately, by means of the entire treatise, the true nature of the <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>rasa</s> and the others. The <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>rasa</s> and the rest is to be stated at length only in the whole treatise.
Showing that this alone is the concise statement, he says the passage beginning "there this."

children.text: eṣa iti rasāḥ ṣaḍ ityādinā tattvamupadekṣyāmaḥ ityantena granthenokta ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "This" means: it has been stated by the text beginning "the <s>rasa</s>s are six" and ending with "we shall teach the true nature."
"Has been taught" means: has been stated concisely.

children.text: anye tu tatraiṣa rasaprabhāva uddiṣṭo bhavati iti paṭhanti ||
children.translated_text: Others, however, read: "There this <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>rasa</s> has been indicated."

children.text: asmin pakṣe dravyadoṣavikāraprabhāvo 'pi 'tra uddiṣṭaḥ so 'pi rasadvārā tena rasasyaiva prapañcābhihitatvāt tasyaivābhidhānam upasaṃharati na dravyādīnāmiti jñeyam dravyaprabhāvamityādau punariti sāmānyena dravyaprabhāvakathanāt punaḥ śṛṅgagrāhikayā tailādidravyaprabhāvaṃ kathayiṣyāma ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: On this interpretation, the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance, <s>doṣa</s>, and disorder has also been indicated here, but that too is through <s>rasa</s>. Therefore, because only <s>rasa</s> has been explained in detail, he concludes only its statement, not that of substance and the others. This should be understood. In the phrase beginning "the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance," the word "again" means that, after stating the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance in general, he will again state specifically, as though grasping it by the horns, the <s>prabhāva</s> of substances such as oil.
"For the purpose of pacification" means having pacification as their purpose.
"Practiced constantly" means used without interruption.
"Having contrary qualities" means having qualities opposite to the qualities of oil.
"When contrary qualities come together" means when two contrary qualities meet.

children.text: nanu viruddhaguṇayor madhye bhūyasālpaṃ jīyate tat kathaṃ tailaṃ vātaṃ jayati na hy asya vātaṃ prati bhūyastvaṃ yuktamityāha satatam abhyasyamānam iti ||
children.translated_text: But, one may object, among two things with contrary qualities the smaller is overcome by the greater. How, then, does oil overcome <s>vāta</s>? For it is not reasonable that it has greater quantity in relation to <s>vāta</s>. He answers with "practiced constantly."

children.text: satatopayogena hi tailaṃ vātād adhikaṃ bhavati tena vātaṃ jayatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For by constant use oil becomes stronger than <s>vāta</s>; therefore it overcomes <s>vāta</s>. This is the meaning.

children.text: sarpiḥ khalvevameveti sarpirapi satatam abhyasyamānam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Ghee indeed is just so" means: ghee also, when practiced constantly.
"Not sweet" means pungent in taste, being contrary to sweet by dryness, lightness, non-aphrodisiac quality, and the like.

children.text: iha ca prabhāvaśabdena sāmānyena dravyaśaktir ucyate nācintyaśaktiḥ tena tailādīnāṃ snehauṣṇyādiguṇādapi vātādiśamanaṃ dravyaprabhāvādeva bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And here the word <s>prabhāva</s> denotes, in a general sense, the power of a substance, not an inconceivable power. Therefore the pacification of <s>vāta</s> and the others by oil and the like, even through qualities such as unctuousness and heat, occurs precisely from the <s>prabhāva</s> of the substance.

children.text: sarpiṣi ca yadyapi madhuro rasaḥ pittapraśame vyāpriyate tathāpi mādhuryaśaityamandatvaiḥ pittaśamanaṃ sarpiḥkāryameva tena dravyaprabhāva eva vācyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And in the case of ghee, although sweet taste operates in the pacification of <s>pitta</s>, still the pacification of <s>pitta</s> through sweetness, coldness, and mildness is the very action of ghee. Therefore the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance alone is to be stated.

children.text: yadā tu rasadvārā kāryaṃ dravyasya cintyate tadā rasaprabhāva iti vyapadeśo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: But when the action of a substance is considered through the channel of <s>rasa</s>, then the designation is "the <s>prabhāva</s> of <s>rasa</s>."

children.text: evaṃ kaṣāyānurase madhuni ca samādhānaṃ vācyam ||
children.translated_text: In the same way the explanation should be stated also with regard to honey, whose secondary taste is astringent.

children.text: anye tu bruvate yattailādīnāṃ vātādiśamanatvaṃ pratyacintya eva prabhāvo 'yamucyate tatra ca tailavātayor viruddhaguṇayor melake tailameva vātaṃ jayati na tu vātas tailam iti tailasyācintyaprabhāvaḥ evaṃ sarpirmadhunor api pittaśleṣmaharaṇe prabhāvājjñeye ||
children.translated_text: Others, however, say that the pacification of <s>vāta</s> and the others by oil and the like is here called precisely an inconceivable <s>prabhāva</s>. In this case, when oil and <s>vāta</s>, which have contrary qualities, come together, oil alone overcomes <s>vāta</s>, while <s>vāta</s> does not overcome oil; thus oil has an inconceivable <s>prabhāva</s>. Likewise, ghee and honey too should be understood to remove <s>pitta</s> and <s>śleṣman</s> through <s>prabhāva</s>.

children.text: etaccānye necchanti yatas tailādīnāṃ satatam abhyasyamānamiti padenādhikyameva vātādijayakāraṇamuktaṃ tathā yaccānyad api kiṃcid dravyam ityādigranthena dravyācintyaprabhāvaṃ parityajya sāmānyena guṇavaiparītyam evābhyāsād vātādijayahetur ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Others do not accept this, because by the phrase "when practiced constantly" it is stated that the very superiority of oil and the like is the cause of conquering <s>vāta</s> and the others; and because by the text beginning "and any other substance whatsoever" an inconceivable <s>prabhāva</s> of substance is set aside, and the contrariety of qualities in general, through practice, is said to be the cause of conquering <s>vāta</s> and the others.
After describing substances that are to be practiced as examples of <s>prabhāva</s>, he describes those that are not to be practiced, with the passage beginning "now."

children.text: adhikamanyebhya iti vacanādanyadapi citrakabhallātakādyevaṃjātīyaṃ nātyupayoktavyaṃ pippalyādidravyaṃ tv anyebhyo 'pyadhikam atyupayoge varjanīyamiti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By the statement "more than others," he shows that other substances too of this kind, such as <s>citraka</s> and <s>bhallātaka</s>, are not to be used excessively, but that substances such as <s>pippalī</s> are to be avoided in excessive use even more than the others.

children.text: kaṭukāḥ satyo madhuravipākāḥ ityādi pippalīguṇakathanam anabhyāsaprayoge doṣavaiparītyena doṣapraśamanopadarśanārthaṃ tathā atyabhyāse guruprakleditvācchleṣmāṇam utkleśayanti ityādigranthavaktavyadoṣakaraṇayogyatopadarśanārthaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: The statement of the qualities of <s>pippalī</s>, beginning "though pungent, they have a sweet <s>vipāka</s>," is for the purpose of showing, in occasional use, the pacification of <s>doṣa</s>s by opposition to those <s>doṣa</s>s, and also for the purpose of showing its capacity to produce the faults that will be stated in the text beginning "when overused, because they are heavy and moistening, they excite <s>śleṣman</s>."
The division is: "and they are considered medicines, immediately."
"Immediately" means when they are not practiced habitually.

children.text: śubhāśubhakāriṇyo bhavantīti sadyaḥ śubhakāriṇyaḥ atyabhyāsaprayoge tv aśubhakāriṇyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: They become productive of good and bad effects: immediately they produce good, but when applied through excessive habituation they produce bad.
He shows this very production of good and bad effects with the passage beginning "good at first contact."

children.text: prayogasamasādguṇyād iti samasya prayogasya sadguṇatvāt same 'lpakāle alpamātre ca pippalyādiprayoge sadguṇā bhavantītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Because of the excellence of an even application" means because the even application is good in character; in an even use of <s>pippalī</s> and the like, with little time and small quantity, they possess good qualities.
Those whose excessive use is connected with the accumulation of <s>doṣas</s> are called connected with the accumulation of <s>doṣas</s>.
He explains this very connection with the accumulation of <s>doṣas</s> with the passage beginning "constantly."

children.text: pippalīdharmakathanaprastāvād guṇāntaram āha yogavāhinyas tv ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Since the discussion has turned to the statement of the properties of <s>pippalī</s>, he states another quality with the words beginning "but they are carriers of the regimen."

children.text: yogavāhitvena kaṭukānāmapi pippalīnāṃ vṛṣyaprayogeṣu yogaḥ tathā jvaragulmakuṣṭhaharādiprayogeṣu jvarādīn hanti pippalī ||
children.translated_text: Because they are <s>yogavāhin</s> (carriers of a therapeutic regimen), even pungent <s>pippalīs</s> are included in aphrodisiac applications; likewise, in applications for removing fever, <s>gulma</s>, skin disease, and the like, <s>pippalī</s> destroys fever and the rest.
And this prohibition against excessive use of <s>pippalī</s> should be understood after setting aside exceptions.

children.text: tena pippalīrasāyanaprayogas tathā gulmādiṣu ca pippalīvardhamānakaprayogo na virodham āvahati ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the <s>pippalī-rasāyana</s> application, and also the increasing-dose application of <s>pippalī</s> for <s>gulma</s> and the like, do not entail contradiction.

children.text: ukte hi viṣaye yathoktavidhānena nirdoṣā eva pippalya iti ṛṣivacanād unnīyate
children.translated_text: For, in the stated matter, it is inferred from the statement of the seer that <s>pippalīs</s>, when used according to the prescribed method, are entirely faultless.

children.text: anye tu annasaṃskaraṇe pippalyādīnām atiprayogo na tu svātantryeṇeti bruvate
children.translated_text: Others, however, say that the excessive use of <s>pippalī</s> and the like is in the seasoning of food, not independently.

children.text: satatam upayujyamānā iti atimātratvena tathā satataprayogeṇa ceti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: "Being used constantly" should be understood as meaning both in excessive measure and through continual application.
"Injuring the heart" means accompanied by a pain in the form of cutting around the heart.
<s>Glāni</s> is wasting of flesh, or loss of delight.

children.text: na kevalaṃ lavaṇātiyogaḥ śarīropaghātakaraḥ kiṃtu bhūmer apyupaghātakara ityāha ye 'pīhetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Not only is excessive use of salt injurious to the body, but it is injurious even to the ground; he states this with the passage beginning "those too here."
"Barren" means dominated by salt.

children.text: lavaṇaṃ nātyupayuñjīteti nātimātraṃ lavaṇaṃ satatam upayuñjīta annadravyasaṃskārakaṃ tu stokamātram abhyāsenāpyupayojanīyam eva ||
children.translated_text: "One should not use salt excessively" means one should not constantly use salt in excessive quantity; but a small amount that seasons food substances is certainly to be used even habitually.

children.text: vāhlīkādivyatirikte 'pi deśe ye 'tilavaṇam aśnanti teṣāmapi doṣānāha ye hītyādi ||
children.translated_text: Even in regions other than <s>Vāhlīka</s>, he states the faults of those who eat too much salt with the passage beginning "for those who."

children.text: etena cānyatrāpi deśe 'timātralavaṇasātmyānāṃ lavaṇātyupayogakṛta eva śaithilyādidoṣa unnīyate na deśasvabhāvakṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By this, even in another region, the faults such as looseness, produced by excessive use of salt in those habituated to an excessive measure of salt, are inferred to be caused by overuse of salt, not by the nature of the region.
"Of them" means of those habituated to excessive alkali and salt.

children.text: tatsātmyata iti atimātrakṣārād atimātralavaṇāc ca sātmyāt ||
children.translated_text: "Because of habituation to that" means because of habituation to excessive alkali and excessive salt.
"Gradually" means according to the gradual procedure for abandoning habituation taught in the section <s>Na vegān dhāraṇīya</s>.
And here, by the word <s>sātmya</s>, <s>okasātmya</s> (habituation through practice) is intended.

children.text: alpadoṣam adoṣaṃ veti pakṣadvaye 'tyarthasātmyam alpadoṣaṃ bhavati anyattvadoṣam iti vyavasthā ||
children.translated_text: In the two alternatives, "slightly faulty" or "faultless," very strong habituation is slightly faulty, while the other is faultless; such is the rule.
"<s>Sātmya</s> is called" means "<s>okasātmya</s> is called."
"From <s>oka</s>" means from habituation.
"For the meaning of <s>upaśaya</s>" means that which is denoted by the word <s>upaśaya</s>.
"That" means <s>okasātmya</s>.
"Threefold" means by the division into superior, inferior, and middling.

children.text: saptavidhaṃ tu ekaikarasena ṣaṭ saṃsṛṣṭarasopayogāccaikam evaṃ saptavidham ||
children.translated_text: But it is sevenfold: six by the use of each single taste, and one by the use of combined tastes; thus it is sevenfold.
By the word "combined," two-taste combinations and so on up to the full set of six tastes are included.
"Standing between the superior and the inferior" means from two tastes and so on up to five tastes.
A person is characterized by the inferior and the middling.
"Superior" means possessing all tastes.
"One should establish <s>sātmya</s>" means one should habituate oneself.
"Gradually" means according to the previously stated order of habituation.

children.text: upapāditasarvarasasātmyenāpi cāhāraḥ praśastaprakṛtyādisampanna eva kartavya ityāha sarvarasam ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Even for one whose habituation to all tastes has been established, food should be endowed with a praiseworthy nature and the like; he states this with the passage beginning "all-tasted."
"Having examined" means having considered in terms of wholesomeness and unwholesomeness.

children.text: hitameveti padena yadeva prakṛtyādinā hitaṃ tad evānurudhyeta sevetetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: By the phrase "only what is wholesome," he means that one should attend to and use only that which is wholesome by nature and the other factors.

children.text: āhārasya vidhiḥ prakāro vidhānaṃ vā ityāhāravidhiḥ tasya viśeṣo hitatvamahitatvaṃ ca tasyāyatanāni hetūn ity āhāravidhiviśeṣāyatanāni ||
children.translated_text: The method, kind, or procedure of food is <s>āhāravidhi</s>; the specific condition of that, namely wholesomeness and unwholesomeness, and its bases or causes are called <s>āhāravidhiviśeṣāyatanāni</s>.
The meaning is that the wholesomeness and unwholesomeness of a kind of food have causes such as its nature.
Those of which the consumer is the eighth are called "having the consumer as the eighth."
What has been stated, he analyzes by nature and the other factors with the passage beginning "there."
"Natural" means not produced by processing and the like.

children.text: māṣamudgayor iti prakṛtyā māṣe gurutvaṃ mudge ca laghutvaṃ śūkare gurutvam eṇe ca laghutvam ||
children.translated_text: In the case of black gram and mung bean: by nature black gram has heaviness and mung bean has lightness; a pig has heaviness and an antelope has lightness.

children.text: dravyāṇām iti vaktavye svābhāvikānām iti yat karoti tenotpattikāle janakabhūtaiḥ svaguṇāropaṇaṃ saṃskārastūtpannasyaiva toyādinā guṇāntarādhānamiti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: Although he could have said "of substances," he says "of natural things"; by that he shows that at the time of origination the generative elements impose their own qualities, whereas <s>saṃskāra</s> is the placing of another quality by water and the like into something already produced.

children.text: tacca prākṛtaguṇopamardenaiva kriyate yathā toyāgnisaṃnikarṣaśaucais taṇḍulasthaṃ gauravam upahatya lāghavam anne kriyate ||
children.translated_text: And that is done only by suppressing the natural quality: for example, by contact with water and fire and by washing, the heaviness present in rice grains is overcome and lightness is produced in cooked rice.

children.text: yaduktaṃ sudhautaḥ prasrutaḥ svinnaḥ saṃtaptaś caudano laghuḥ ||
children.translated_text: As it has been said: cooked rice that is well washed, drained, boiled, and heated is light.
Likewise, even in red <s>śāli</s> and the like, which are light, lightness increases through contact with fire and so on.

children.text: manthanādguṇādhānaṃ yathā śothakṛd dadhi śothaghnaṃ sasnehamapi manthanāt iti ||
children.translated_text: The addition of a quality by churning is as in the statement, "curd that causes swelling becomes swelling-curing from churning, even though it still contains fat."

children.text: deśena yathā bhasmarāśer adhaḥ sthāpayet ityādau ||
children.translated_text: Through place, as in the statement "one should place it beneath a heap of ashes," and so on.
By perfuming, there is the imparting of qualities, as in water's imitation of fragrance through being perfumed with blue lotus and the like.

children.text: bhāvanayā ca svarasādikṛtayā sthitasyaivāmalakāder guṇasyotkarṣo bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And by <s>bhāvanā</s> (impregnation or trituration) performed with fresh juice and so on, there is an intensification of a quality already present in <s>āmalaka</s> and the like.
By increase of time and so forth, as in statements such as, "One should drink it when its taste has arisen after a fortnight."

children.text: bhājanena yathā traiphalenāyasīṃ pātrīṃ kalkenālepayet ityādau ||
children.translated_text: By the vessel, as in passages such as, "One should smear an iron bowl with a paste of <s>triphala</s>."
Because of the word "and so on," grinding, consecration by mantra, and the like are included.

children.text: nanu saṃskārādheyena guṇena kathaṃ svābhāvikaguṇanāśaḥ kriyate yataḥ svabhāvo niṣpratikriyaḥ ityuktaṃ yadi hi saṃskāreṇa svābhāvikagurutvaṃ pratikriyate tadā svabhāvo niṣpratikriyaḥ iti kathaṃ brūmaḥ svabhāvo niṣpratikriyaḥ iti svabhāvo bhāvānām utpattau nānyathā kriyate ||
children.translated_text: But, one may object: how is the destruction of a natural quality produced by a quality imparted through <s>saṃskāra</s> (processing), since it has been said that nature admits no counteraction? If natural heaviness is counteracted by processing, how can we say, "nature admits no counteraction"? "Nature admits no counteraction" means that the nature of things, at their origination, is not made otherwise.

children.text: tena jātipratibaddhaṃ māṣādīnāṃ gurutvaṃ na tajjātau sphoṭayituṃ pāryate saṃskāreṇa tu tadanyathākaraṇamanumatameva dṛṣṭatvāt ||
children.translated_text: Therefore the heaviness of <s>māṣa</s> and the like, bound to their class, cannot be eliminated in that class; but alteration of it by processing is certainly accepted, because it is observed.

children.text: kaścit tu guṇo dravyāṇāṃ saṃskārādināpi nānyathā kriyate yathā vahner auṣṇyaṃ vāyoścalatvaṃ tailasya sneha ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Still, some quality of substances is not altered even by processing and the like, as heat in fire, mobility in wind, and unctuousness in oil.
For these are qualities that last as long as the substance itself.
But heaviness and the like, since their disappearance is observed even in old grain and similar cases, are not qualities that last as long as the substance itself.

children.text: uktaṃ hi guṇo dravyavināśād vā vināśam upagacchati ||
children.translated_text: For it has been said: a quality undergoes destruction either from the destruction of the substance,
or from the introduction of another quality.

children.text: yatra tu saṃskāreṇa vrīherlājalakṣaṇaṃ dravyāntarameva janyate tatra guṇāntarotpādaḥ suṣṭhveva ||
children.translated_text: But where, by processing, another substance altogether is produced from rice, namely parched grain, there the production of another quality is entirely proper.
He states <s>saṃyoga</s> (combination) with the passage beginning "but combination."

children.text: sa viśeṣamārabhata iti saṃyujyamānadravyaikadeśe 'dṛṣṭaṃ kāryam ārabhata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "It produces a specific effect" means that it produces an effect not seen in any single part of the substances being combined.

children.text: yaṃ naikaikaśa iti yaṃ viśeṣaṃ pratyekasaṃyujyamānāni dravyāṇi nārabhanta ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Which not singly" means: the substances being combined, taken individually, do not produce that specific effect.

children.text: madhusarpiṣī hi pratyekamamārake milite tu mārake bhavataḥ kṣīramatsyādisaṃyogaśca kuṣṭhādikaro bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Honey and ghee, taken individually, are not fatal, but when mixed they become fatal; and the combination of milk and fish produces skin disease and the like.

children.text: saṃyogas tv iha prādhānyenaivopalabhyamānadravyamelako vivakṣitas tena bhāvanādiṣvapi yadyapi saṃyogo 'sti tathāpi tatra bhāvanādravyāṇāṃ prādhānyenānupalabdher na saṃyogena grahaṇam ||
children.translated_text: Here <s>saṃyoga</s> is intended as a mixture of substances that are perceived as principal. Therefore, although there is combination even in <s>bhāvanā</s> and the like, because the substances used for <s>bhāvanā</s> are not perceived there as principal, it is not included under combination.
<s>Rāśi</s> is quantity.

children.text: mātrāmātraphalaviniścayārtha iti mātrāvadāhārauṣadhasya ca yat phalaṃ śubham amātrasya hīnasyātiriktasya vā yat phalam aśubham ||
children.translated_text: "For determining the result of proper and improper measure" means: the auspicious result of food and medicine taken in proper measure, and the inauspicious result of what is unmeasured, whether deficient or excessive.

children.text: yaduktaṃ tasya jñānārtham ucitapramāṇam anucitapramāṇaṃ ca rāśisaṃjñaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: For the sake of knowing what has been stated, proper measure and improper measure are given the name <s>rāśi</s>.
He explains <s>sarvagraha</s> (taking as a whole) with the passage beginning "there."
"Of all" means the measuring, as one lump, of mixed food, meat, soup, and the like.
He explains <s>parigraha</s> (taking separately) with the passage beginning "but parigraha."

children.text: ekaikaśyeneti annasya kuḍavaḥ sūpasya palaṃ māṃsasya dvipalamityādyavayavamānapūrvakaṃ samudāyamānam ||
children.translated_text: "One by one" means a total measure preceded by the measure of each part, such as one <s>kuḍava</s> of rice, one <s>pala</s> of soup, two <s>palas</s> of meat, and so on.

children.text: sarvagrahe pratyavayavamānaniyamo nāsti tena yena kenacid āhāreṇa pratyekamaniyatamānena sampūrṇāhāramātrāniyamanaṃ sarvagrahaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In <s>sarvagraha</s> there is no fixed measure for each individual component; thus <s>sarvagraha</s> is the regulation of the total meal-measure by food of any kind, with each component being of unspecified measure.
He shows this very point through the derivation of the word, with the passage beginning "for of all."
"From all sides" means from each individual component.
He divides <s>deśa</s> (place) with the passage beginning "place."
By the mention of <s>sthāna</s> (location), he indicates both the place of the food-substance and the place of the eater.
"It teaches" means that it becomes a cause for knowing the qualities of a substance produced by its origin, range of movement, and so on.

children.text: tatrotpattyā himavati jātaṃ guṇavadbhavati marau jātaṃ laghu bhavati ityādi ||
children.translated_text: There, with respect to origin: what is born in the Himalaya is possessed of good qualities; what is born in a desert region is light, and so forth.

children.text: pracāreṇa laghu bhakṣyāṇāṃ prāṇināṃ tathā dhanvapracāriṇāṃ bahukriyāṇāṃ ca lāghavaṃ viparyaye ca gauravaṃ gṛhyate ||
children.translated_text: With respect to range of movement, lightness is understood in edible animals, and likewise in animals that move in arid country and perform much activity; in the contrary case, heaviness is understood.

children.text: deśasāmyena ca deśaviparītaguṇaṃ sātmyaṃ gṛhyate yathānūpe uṣṇarūkṣādi dhanvani ca śītasnigdhādi ||
children.translated_text: And by similarity of place, suitability to qualities opposite to the place is understood, as hot and dry qualities in marshy country, and cold and unctuous qualities in arid country.
But <s>okasātmya</s> (suitability through habituation) is included by the mention of the user.
"Constantly occurring" means time in the form of day and night and the like.
"Occasional" means qualified by particular states such as illness and childhood.

children.text: vikāramapekṣata iti bālyādikṛtaṃ tu śleṣmavikāraṃ jvarādikaṃ cāhāraniyamārthamapekṣata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "It depends on disorder" means that, for regulating diet, it takes into account disorders of <s>śleṣman</s> produced by childhood and the like, as well as fever and other conditions.
Since seasonal suitability depends on the season, it is dependent on <s>ṛtusātmya</s> (seasonal suitability).

children.text: evamāhāropayogaḥ kartavya evaṃ na kartavya ityupayoganiyamaḥ sa jīrṇalakṣaṇāpekṣa iti prādhānyenoktaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The rule of use, namely "food should be used in this way, and not in that way," has been stated principally as depending on the signs of digestion.

children.text: teneha ajalpann ahasan nātidrutaṃ nātivilambitam ityādyupayoganiyamamapyapekṣata eva ajīrṇabhojane tu mahāṃstridoṣakopalakṣaṇo doṣo bhavatītyayam evodāhṛtaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore here it also takes into account rules of use such as "not speaking, not laughing, neither too quickly nor too slowly"; but in eating during indigestion there is a great fault characterized by the aggravation of the three <s>doṣas</s>, and so this very example was cited.

children.text: yadāyattam okasātmyam iti bhoktṛpuruṣāpekṣaṃ hy abhyāsasātmyaṃ bhavati kasyaciddhi kiṃcid evābhyāsāt pathyamapathyaṃ vā sātmyaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: "On which <s>okasātmya</s> depends" means that suitability through habituation depends on the eating person; for, in the case of someone, some particular thing, whether wholesome or unwholesome, becomes suitable through habit.

children.text: eṣāmityādau śubhaphalā viśeṣā aśubhaphalāśca parasparopakārakā bhavantīti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: In the passage beginning 'eṣām', it should be understood that the distinctions having auspicious results and those having inauspicious results are mutually auxiliary.

children.text: tatra prakṛtyā lāghavādiḥ śubhaphalaḥ gurvādiś cāśubhaphalaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Among these, by nature lightness and the like have an auspicious result, while heaviness and the like have an inauspicious result.
A distinction imposed by processing and the like, too, is auspicious when taught by the treatise, but inauspicious when prohibited.
Unsuitability to a region, being produced in a censured region, and so on are inauspicious results of a substance.

children.text: evaṃ kālāsātmyamaśubhaphalaṃ cājīrṇabhojanādi tathā okāsātmyaṃ cāśubhamaśubhaphalamiti jñeyaṃ viparītaṃ tu śubhaphalam ||
children.translated_text: Similarly, unsuitability with respect to time is an inauspicious result, as are eating during indigestion and the like; likewise unsuitability with respect to habitual residence is inauspicious and has an inauspicious result. The opposite should be understood as an auspicious result.

children.text: mohāditi ajñānāt pramādāditi jñātvāpi rāgād ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Through delusion' means through ignorance; 'through negligence' means through passion and the like even after knowing.
'Pleasant' means pleasant only for that present moment.
The explanation of 'unwholesome' is 'having an unhappy sequel'.

children.text: asukhaṃ duḥkharūpam udarka uttarakālīnaṃ phalaṃ yasya sa tathā ||
children.translated_text: That whose later result, its sequel, is unpleasant, being of the nature of suffering, is such.
'Or something else' means medicine, regimen, and the like.
In the passage beginning 'there', 'this' means what is about to be stated.
The rule of food, by which food is prescribed through the hot, unctuous, and other qualities to be stated, is the prescribing of the rule of food.

children.text: āturāṇāṃ ca keṣāṃciditi padena raktapittināṃ śītameva kapharogiṇāṃ rūkṣameva hitamityādiviparyayaṃ darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By the phrase 'and of some sick persons' he shows exceptions such as that only cold food is beneficial for those with <s>raktapitta</s>, and only dry food for those with a <s>kapha</s> disorder.

children.text: keṣāṃcidbhuñjānānām idam āhāravidhividhānaṃ hitatamaṃ bhavatīti yojanā ||
children.translated_text: The construction is: for some persons who are eating, this prescription of the rule of food becomes most beneficial.

children.text: prakṛtyaiveti svabhāvenaiva hitatamaṃ hitatamam ityuktaṃ tena yat prakṛtyā hitaṃ tat kadācideva kaṃcideva puruṣam āsādyāhitaṃ bhavati tacca kādācitkatvād anādṛtaṃ tena prāyikatvādenaṃ hitatamaṃ vakṣyāma iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'By nature itself' means by its own nature. By saying 'most beneficial, most beneficial', he implies this: what is beneficial by nature sometimes becomes unbeneficial only when it meets some particular person; but because that is occasional, it is disregarded. Therefore, since it is generally so, we shall call this most beneficial.
In the passage beginning 'hot', the division is 'properly'.
'Of that' means of food furnished with hot and the other qualities.
'Good quality' means possession of excellent qualities.
'It loosens' means it makes the mass separate.

children.text: mātrāvaditi praśaṃsāyāṃ matup tena praśastamātram ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'In proper measure' has the suffix <s>matup</s> in a laudatory sense; therefore it means 'with an excellent measure'.

children.text: apīḍayaditi anatimātratvena svasthānasthitaṃ sadvātādīn sthānāpīḍanād aprakopayat ||
children.translated_text: 'Without oppressing' means that, because it is not excessive in quantity, while <s>vāta</s> and the others remain in their own places, it does not provoke them by compressing their sites.
'It passes along to the anus' means that, when transformed, it exits in a suitable manner.
'Heat' means the digestive fire.
'Of the previous' means of what was done on another day.
'Untransformed' means not properly produced.

children.text: āhāraraseneti āhārapariṇāmagatena madhurādinā kiṃvā āhārajena rasena ||
children.translated_text: 'By the food-<s>rasa</s>' means by the sweet and other tastes involved in the transformation of food, or by the <s>rasa</s> produced from food.
The passage beginning 'when the <s>doṣas</s> are situated in their own places' gives the sign of digested food.
'Produced by foods of incompatible potency' means by such diseases as <s>kuṣṭha</s>, blindness, and <s>visarpa</s>, which are mentioned in the <s>Ātreyabhadrakāpyīya</s>.

children.text: manovighātakarairbhāvairiti trividhakukṣīye vakṣyamāṇaiḥ kāmādibhiś cittopatāpakaraiś cittavikārair ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'By states that obstruct the mind' means by mental alterations such as desire and the like, which torment the mind and are to be stated in the <s>Trividhakukṣīya</s>.

children.text: tatheṣṭaiśca sarvopakaraṇair bhuñjāno manovighātaṃ na prāpnotīti yojanā aniṣṭabhojanāder manovighāto bhavati ||
children.translated_text: The construction is: one who eats with all desired utensils likewise does not incur mental obstruction. Mental obstruction arises from disliked food and the like.
'Moistening upward' means going on a wrong path.
'Depression' means sinking down.
'Non-establishment' means non-entry into the abdomen because it remains in the heart.

children.text: bhojyagatānāṃ doṣāṇāṃ keśādīnāṃ sādguṇyasya ca svādutvādeḥ upalabdhir na niyatā bhavati kadācidupalabhyate kadācin neti ||
children.translated_text: The perception of faults in the food to be eaten, such as hairs, and also of its good qualities, such as sweetness, is not fixed: sometimes they are perceived and sometimes not.

children.text: tatra doṣānupalabdhyā sadoṣasyaiva bhakṣaṇaṃ sādguṇyānupalabdhyā ca prītyabhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There, through non-perception of the faults, one eats what is in fact faulty; and through non-perception of the good qualities, there is absence of pleasure.

children.text: viṣamaṃ ca pacyata iti cirakālabhojanenāgnisambandhasya vaiṣamyāditi bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And it is digested unevenly; the idea is that, because eating takes a long time, the connection with the digestive fire becomes uneven.

children.text: ya evātidrutam aśnato doṣā iti utsnehanādayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The faults of one who eats too quickly are just those beginning with moistening upward.

children.text: nopaśeta itītyatra itiśabdena sātmyāsātmyavidhānopadarśakena vicāraphalamokasātmyasevanaṃ darśayati ||
children.translated_text: In the expression 'one should not resort to it', by the word 'iti', which points to the rule of suitability and unsuitability, he indicates that the result of reflection is resorting to what is suitable by habit.

children.text: ātmana iti padenātmanaivātmasātmyaṃ pratipuruṣaṃ jñāyate na śāstropadeśeneti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By the word 'of oneself' he shows that one's own habitual suitability is known by oneself for each individual person, not by instruction from the treatise.
With the passage beginning 'the <s>rasa</s>s', he praises knowledge of the <s>rasa</s>, <s>prabhāva</s>, and the rest stated in the chapter.

children.text: sa no bhiṣagiti no 'smākaṃ saṃmata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'He is our physician' means: he is accepted by us.

children.text: doṣavikārau ca yadyapi trividhakukṣīye prabhāvavistāreṇa vaktavyau tathāpīha saṃkṣepeṇoktāv eva tena doṣavikāraprabhāvāv apyuktāv iti yaducyate saṃgrahe tat sādhu ||
children.translated_text: Although <s>doṣa</s> and disorder are to be discussed later in the <s>Trividhakukṣīya</s> through an extensive treatment of <s>prabhāva</s>, still they have indeed been stated here in brief. Therefore what is said in the summary, that the <s>prabhāvas</s> of <s>doṣa</s> and disorder too have been stated, is correct.

children.text: tailādidravyatrayakathanaṃ ca dravyaprabhāvagṛhītamiti kṛtvā na pṛthak saṃgrahe paṭhitam ||
children.translated_text: And the mention of the triad of substances beginning with oil is included under the <s>prabhāva</s> of substance; therefore it is not read separately in the summary.
'Of the two excellent ones' means of the two that are highest because they are excellent.

children.text: dīrghasyeti rasāyanādinā śatādapi dīrghasya sukhasyeti nīrogatvena niyatasyeti yuganiyatasya kalau varṣaśatapramāṇasyety arthaḥ śatād arvāṅ niniyatam apīha niyataśabdenocyate tena na tatra tasya daivapuruṣakārajanyatvaṃ ghaṭate tathāpi tasyāpraśastadaivapuruṣakārajanyatvāt daivapuruṣakārajanyatvaṃ bhavatīti yuktaṃ kiṃcāniyatāyuṣa eva puruṣā rasāyanādhikāriṇo bhavanti niyatāyuṣaṃ prati rasāyanasyākiṃcitkaratvāt rasāyanādikṛtaṃ cāyuraniyataṃ praśastatvena praśastadaivapuruṣakārajanyaṃ bhavatīti yuktam ||
children.translated_text: 'Of long' means of life longer even than a hundred years through <s>rasāyana</s> and the like. 'Pleasant' means certain because of being free from disease. 'Fixed' means fixed by the age, that is, measuring one hundred years in the Kali age. Even what is fixed below a hundred is here called 'fixed'; therefore in that case its being produced by fate and human effort is not tenable. Nevertheless, because it is produced by inferior fate and human effort, it is proper that it is produced by fate and human effort. Moreover, only persons with indeterminate lifespan are eligible for <s>rasāyana</s>, since <s>rasāyana</s> does nothing for one with fixed lifespan; and the lifespan produced by <s>rasāyana</s> and the like is indeterminate, and because it is excellent, it is properly produced by excellent fate and human effort.

children.text: kiṃvā dīrghatve sati niyatasyāyuṣo hetur iti yojanā tena yuganiyate ca śatavarṣaṃ tathā tadadhikaṃ cāniyataṃ mahatā karmaṇaiva kriyate puruṣakāreṇa tu mahatāsya sukhitvaṃ rogānupaghātāt kriyate rasāyanena ca jarādivyādhipratighātaḥ kriyate rasāyanalabhyam apyāyurbalavatkarmaniyatam eveti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or the construction is: when there is long life, it is the cause of a fixed lifespan. Thus, when an age fixed by the era is one hundred years, and likewise when what exceeds that is unfixed, it is produced only by great <s>karma</s>; but through great <s>puruṣakāra</s> (human effort) its happiness is produced, because disease does not injure it, and through <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenative therapy) resistance to diseases such as old age is produced. The intended sense is that even the lifespan obtainable by <s>rasāyana</s> is fixed by powerful <s>karma</s>.
Of the opposite case: of what is unfixed with regard to length, and likewise, when it is accompanied by disease, of what is not happy.
By the word 'the other' is meant the conjunction of the two when <s>daiva</s> (fate, past action) and <s>puruṣakāra</s> are deficient.

children.text: madhyamā madhyamasya dīrghatvenādīrghatvenāniyatasya tathā sukhāsukhatvenāniyatasyāyuṣo madhyamayoḥ karmaṇor yuktirityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'The middle' means the conjunction of the two middle forms of action for a middle lifespan: one unfixed as to being long or not long, and likewise unfixed as to being happy or unhappy.
By 'cause' he means the rationale for the mutual obstruction of <s>daiva</s> and <s>puruṣakāra</s>.
The passage beginning with '<s>daiva</s>' is to be understood.

children.text: durbalam āyurjananaṃ daivaṃ balavatā mārakeṇa dṛṣṭāpathyabhojanādinā viparītamaraṇakāryajananād upahanyate viśiṣṭena balavatā itarat karma dṛṣṭaṃ puruṣakārākhyam upahanyate parābhūyate ||
children.translated_text: A weak <s>daiva</s> that produces lifespan is impaired by a strong death-producing visible cause, such as eating what is unwholesome, because that produces the opposite effect, death. Conversely, the other action, the visible action called <s>puruṣakāra</s>, is impaired, that is, overcome, by a specific and powerful <s>karma</s>.

children.text: etaddaivakartṛkadṛṣṭaparābhavadarśanād daivaniyatameva sarvamāyur iti kecinmanyanta ityāha dṛṣṭvetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Because they observe this defeat of the visible cause brought about by <s>daiva</s>, some think that every lifespan is fixed only by <s>daiva</s>. He states this with the passage beginning 'having seen'.

children.text: yadi dṛṣṭamāyuḥ kāraṇaṃ syāt na tadā bheṣajaiḥ samyagupapāditānāṃ mṛtyuḥ syāt yataśca satyapi cikitsite karmavaśāttu mṛtyur bhavati tena yatrāpi cikitsā jīvayatīti manyante tatrāpi karmaivāsti jīvanakāraṇamiti dṛṣṭaśaktitvād avadhārayāma iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If the visible cause were the cause of lifespan, then those who have been properly provided with medicines would not die. But since death occurs, even when treatment exists, through the force of <s>karma</s>, therefore even where people think that treatment keeps one alive, <s>karma</s> itself is present as the cause of living. This is the sense: because its power is observed, we determine this to be so.

children.text: daivapuruṣakārayor ubhayorapi bādhyatvaṃ darśayannekāntena niyatāyuḥpakṣaṃ vyudasyati karmetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Showing that both <s>daiva</s> and <s>puruṣakāra</s> can be obstructed, he rejects the position that lifespan is invariably fixed, with the passage beginning '<s>karma</s>'.

children.text: na kvacit karma na bhavati yaducyate
children.translated_text: There is nowhere that <s>karma</s> does not exist, as is said:
<s>Karma</s> that has not been experienced is not exhausted, even by hundreds of crores of aeons;
the good or bad <s>karma</s> that has been done must necessarily be experienced.
Thus.

children.text: kiṃcittvakālaniyatamiti yathā idaṃ mārakaṃ karma na tu kvacitkāle pañcaviṃśavarṣādau niyataṃ tena yasmin kāle puruṣakārākhyaṃ dṛṣṭakarmānuguṇaṃ prāpnoti tasmin kāle sahakārisāṃnidhyopabṛṃhitabalaṃ mārayati yadā tu dṛṣṭam apathyasevādi na prāpnoti na tadā mārayati pratyayaiḥ pratibodhyata iti dṛṣṭakāraṇair udriktaṃ kriyate ||
children.translated_text: But some <s>karma</s> is not fixed with respect to time. For example, this is death-causing <s>karma</s>, but it is not fixed to some particular time, such as the twenty-fifth year. Therefore, at whatever time the visible action called <s>puruṣakāra</s> occurs in conformity with it, then, strengthened in power by the presence of an assisting cause, it kills. But when the visible cause, such as the use of unwholesome things, does not occur, then it does not kill. 'It is awakened by conditions' means that it is made intense by visible causes.

children.text: ye tu bruvate kiṃcit karma kālaniyataṃ yadā pacyate tasmin kāle pacyata eveti kālaniyamaḥ vipākaniyataṃ tu idaṃ karma vipacyata eva na tu vipacyata iti na kālavipākaniyataṃ tu yathedaṃ karma asminneva kāle vipacyata eveti etacca kālavipākaniyatatvād balavad ucyate etadeva dṛṣṭābādhanīyamiti teṣāṃ mate abhuktam api kṣīyate durbalakarma prāyaścittādineti boddhavyaṃ paraṃ viparyaye'pi tadā kiṃcittvavipākakālaniyatamiti vaktavyaṃ syāt kiṃcittvakālaniyatamiti vacanāttu kālaniyatamapi ||
children.translated_text: But those who say, 'Some <s>karma</s> is fixed in time; when it ripens, it ripens at that very time,' define this as restriction by time. As for what is fixed in ripening: this <s>karma</s> certainly ripens, and it is not the case that it does not ripen. What is fixed in both time and ripening is such as this: this <s>karma</s> ripens only at this very time. And this, because it is fixed in time and ripening, is called powerful; this alone is not obstructed by visible causes. According to their view, it should be understood that weak <s>karma</s> may be exhausted even without being experienced, through expiation and the like. But then, even in the contrary case, one would have to say, 'some is fixed with regard to ripening and time'; yet because the statement says, 'some is fixed with regard to time,' what is fixed in time is included as well.
'There' means in matters such as firmness in the treatise.
'<s>Tadvidyasaṃbhāṣā</s>' means conversation with one who studies that same science.
'<s>Kalya</s>' means free from disease.
'<s>Kṛtakṣaṇa</s>' means one who has set aside a period of time for study, with no other occupation.

children.text: prātarvā utthāya upavyūṣaṃ vā utthāyeti yojanā ||
children.translated_text: The construction is: having risen in the morning, or having risen before dawn.
'<s>Upavyūṣa</s>' means when a little of the night remains.
'Led by the mind' means guided by a concentrated mind.

children.text: svadoṣaparihāraparadoṣapramāṇārtham iti svakīyādhyayanadoṣaparihārārthaṃ parakīyādhyayanadoṣapramāṇārthaṃ parakīyādhyayanadoṣajñānārtham ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'For the sake of removing one's own faults and measuring another's faults' means for the sake of removing faults in one's own study, and for the sake of measuring faults in another's study, that is, for the sake of knowing the faults in another's study.
That by which something is measured is <s>pramāṇa</s>; here mere knowledge is intended.

children.text: samyag buddhvārthatattvaṃ buddhvā cādhīyāno nirdoṣādhyayano bhavati samyagadhyayanajñānācca parasya sadoṣamadhyayanaṃ pratipadyate ||
children.translated_text: One who studies after properly understanding the truth of the meaning has faultless study; and from knowledge of proper study he recognizes defective study in another person.
'Thus is the rule of study' is the conclusion.
Study performed according to the rule as stated becomes well grasped.

children.text: dṛṣṭādṛṣṭasaṃpattyādhyayanakālavarjanaṃ vedādhyayane niṣiddhamevātrāpi tajjñeyamiti na viśeṣeṇoktam ||
children.translated_text: Avoidance of study at times lacking visible and invisible auspiciousness and the like is already forbidden in Vedic study; here too that should be understood, and so it is not stated specifically.

children.text: nidānasthāne jñātahetvādinā tathā vimāne pratītarasadoṣādimānena kartavyacikitsāyā adhikaraṇaṃ śarīraṃ jñātavyaṃ bhavati yato'pratipanne 'śeṣāviśeṣataḥ śarīre na śarīravijñānādhīnā cikitsā sādhvī bhavati ataḥ śarīraṃ kāraṇotpattisthitivṛddhyādiviśeṣaiḥ pratipādayituṃ śārīraṃ sthānamucyate ||
children.translated_text: In the <s>Nidānasthāna</s>, through the causes and other matters already known, and likewise in the <s>Vimāna</s>, through the measure of tastes, <s>doṣas</s>, and the like already understood, the body, which is the locus of the treatment to be performed, becomes knowable. For when the body has not been understood in its entirety and in its particulars, treatment that depends on knowledge of the body is not sound. Therefore, in order to explain the body through particulars such as causes, origination, maintenance, and growth, the section called <s>Śārīra</s> is stated.

Here too, because it primarily teaches distinctions of the person and related topics useful for treatment that is a cause of liberation, the cessation of absolute suffering, the chapter called <s>Katidhāpuruṣīya</s> is taught.
Of how many kinds?
'How manyfold?' Thus.

children.text: puruṣa ityanena cāviśeṣeṇa puruṣaśabdābhidheyo 'rtho 'bhidhīyate yataḥ khādayaścetanāṣaṣṭhā ityādinā tathā caturviṃśatikabhedabhinnaśca karmapuruṣa eva śarīrī vācyaḥ tathā cetanādhāturapyekaḥ smṛtaḥ puruṣasaṃjñakaḥ ityanenātmaiva śarīrarahitaḥ puruṣaśabdārthatvena vācyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And by the word <s>puruṣa</s>, without distinction, the object denoted by the word <s>puruṣa</s> is expressed. For in the passage beginning "the elements beginning with ether, with consciousness as the sixth," and likewise in the statement that it is divided into twenty-four distinctions, the embodied being, namely the <s>karmapuruṣa</s>, is meant. Likewise, in "the single conscious element is remembered as called <s>puruṣa</s>," the self alone, apart from the body, is to be meant as the meaning of the word <s>puruṣa</s>.
It is a <s>dhātu</s> because it supports the <s>puruṣa</s>; therefore "by a distinction of <s>dhātu</s>" means by a distinction in the sense of supporting the <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: dhīmanniti viśeṣaṇena ya eva dhīmān sa eva puruṣabhedādikam imaṃ vakṣyamāṇaṃ susūkṣmaṃ vaktuṃ samartha iti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By the qualifier "wise," he shows that only one who is wise is able to explain this extremely subtle matter, beginning with the distinctions of <s>puruṣa</s>, which is about to be stated.

children.text: puruṣaḥ kāraṇaṃ kasmād iti kasmāddhetoḥ puruṣaḥ saṃsāre pradhānaṃ sthāyikāraṇam ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Why is <s>puruṣa</s> the cause?" means: for what reason is <s>puruṣa</s> the chief enduring cause in transmigration?
"Source" means cause, because something arises from it.
"In wombs" means in births or species.
"All" means even those belonging to another person.
The <s>kṣetrajña</s> is the self.
The <s>kṣetra</s> is everything that will be stated, excluding the unmanifest.
The passage begins with "to be known."

children.text: asati kṣetre kṣetrajñānābhāvānna kṣetrajñatvamupapadyate iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The idea is that, if there is no <s>kṣetra</s>, since there is no cognition of a field, the status of being <s>kṣetrajña</s> is not possible.
"As a witness" means similar to a witness.

children.text: viśeṣo vedanākṛta iti putrādijñānarūpavedanājanito harṣādiviśeṣa ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "The distinction is produced by feeling" means a special state such as joy, produced by feeling in the form of cognition of a son and the like.

children.text: tisṛṇāmiti atītānāgatavartamānānāṃ duḥkharūpāṇāṃ madhye kāṃ cikitsati ||
children.translated_text: "Of the three" means: among the sufferings that are past, future, and present, which one does he treat?

children.text: atītāmityādau kiṃśabdo'dhyāhāryaḥ tena kim atītāṃ cikitsati kiṃ vartamānāṃ kiṃvā bhaviṣyatīmiti yojyam ||
children.translated_text: In the passage beginning "the past," the word "which?" is to be supplied. Thus it should be construed: does he treat the past one, the present one, or the future one?

children.text: sthānaṃ nāstīti kṣaṇikatvena cikitsāyāḥ pravṛttiyogyakālāvasthānaṃ nāsti ||
children.translated_text: "There is no standing" means that, because it is momentary, there is no persistence in a time-state suitable for the activity of treatment.

children.text: vedanānāṃ kāraṇam adhiṣṭhānaṃ ca yadyapi dīrghaṃjīvitīye 'pyuktaṃ tathāpīha prakaraṇavaśād viśeṣapratītyākāṅkṣayā ca viśiṣṭaḥ punaḥ praśnāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Although the cause and basis of feelings have also been stated in the <s>Dīrghajīvitīya</s>, nevertheless here, because of the context and because there is an expectation of knowing something specific, the questions are asked again in a specific form.

children.text: praśnārthāścāmī uttaragranthe ācāryeṇa prapañcanīyā iti neha vyākaraṇīyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: And the meanings of these questions are to be elaborated by the teacher in the following text; therefore they are not to be explained here.
The passage begins with "the elements beginning with ether."

children.text: khādayaḥ khaṃ vāyur agnir āpaḥ kṣitistathā iti vakṣyamāṇāḥ cetanāṣaṣṭhā ityatra cetanāśabdena cetanādhāraḥ samanaskaṃ ātmā gṛhyate khādigrahaṇena cendriyāṇi khādimayānyavaruddhāni ||
children.translated_text: "The elements beginning with ether" are those about to be stated as ether, air, fire, water, and earth. In "with consciousness as the sixth," the word "consciousness" means the bearer of consciousness, namely the self together with the mind. And by mentioning ether and the rest, the senses, which are made of ether and the other elements, are included.

children.text: ayaṃ ca vaiśeṣikadarśanaparigṛhītaś cikitsāśāstraviṣayaḥ puruṣaḥ ayameva pañcamahābhūtaśarīrisamavāyaḥ puruṣaḥ ityanena suśrutenāpyuktaḥ ||
children.translated_text: This <s>puruṣa</s>, accepted in the <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> system and forming the subject matter of medical science, is also what <s>Suśruta</s> has stated with the words: "This very conjunction of the body made of the five great elements and the embodied self is <s>puruṣa</s>."

children.text: smṛta iti bhāṣayā pūrvācāryāṇām apyayaṃ puruṣaśabdavācyo'bhipreto nāsmatkalpita iti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By the expression "is remembered," he shows through ordinary language that earlier teachers too intended this as denoted by the word <s>puruṣa</s>, and that it is not invented by us.

children.text: puri śarīre śete iti vyutpattyā ya ātmā puruṣaśabdenocyate tamāha cetanetyādi ||
children.translated_text: By the derivation "he lies in the city, the body," the self is called by the word <s>puruṣa</s>; he states that with the passage beginning "consciousness."

children.text: atra puruṣa iti kartavye yat puruṣasaṃjñaka iti karoti tena na cetanādhāturūpaḥ puruṣaścikitsāyam abhipretaḥ kiṃtu śāstrāntaravyavahārānurodhād ihāpyayaṃ puruṣaśabdena saṃjñita iti darśayati cikitsāviṣayastu ṣaḍdhātuka eva puruṣaḥ ata eva tatra saṃjñitagrahaṇaṃ na kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: Here, although one might expect simply "<s>puruṣa</s>," he says "called by the name <s>puruṣa</s>." By this he shows that the <s>puruṣa</s> in the form of the conscious element is not intended in medical treatment; rather, in conformity with the usage of other treatises, this too is designated here by the word <s>puruṣa</s>. But the <s>puruṣa</s> that is the object of treatment is only the six-element <s>puruṣa</s>; for that very reason the word "called" was not used there.

children.text: ayaṃ ca puruṣaśabdo gavādāvapi ṣaḍdhātusamudāye yadyapi vartate tathāpi sarvapradhāne nara eva viśeṣeṇa vartate tena nātiprasiddhe gavādau puruṣaśabdaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And although this word <s>puruṣa</s> also applies to an aggregate of six elements in a cow and the like, still it applies especially to a human being, who is foremost among all. Therefore the word <s>puruṣa</s> is not used for the less well-known case of a cow and the like.

children.text: ṣaḍdhāturūpameva puruṣaṃ punaḥ sāṃkhyadarśanabhedāc caturviṃśatikabhedenāha punaścetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Again, because of a distinction from the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> system, he describes the same <s>puruṣa</s> consisting of six elements as having twenty-four divisions, with the passage beginning "again."
He divides the twenty-fourfold entity itself with the passage beginning "mind."

children.text: yadyapi pañcaviṃśatitattvamayo'yaṃ puruṣaḥ sāṃkhyairucyate yadāha mūlaprakṛtiravikṛtirmahadādyāḥ prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ sapta
children.translated_text: Although this <s>puruṣa</s> is said by the <s>Sāṃkhya</s>s to consist of twenty-five principles, as it is said: "Root nature is unevolved; the seven beginning with <s>mahat</s> are both evolvents and evolutes;

children.text: ṣoḍaśakastu vikāro na prakṛtir na vikṛtiḥ puruṣaḥ iti tathāpīha prakṛtivyatiriktaṃ codāsīnaṃ puruṣamavyaktatvasādharmyād avyaktāyāṃ prakṛtāveva prakṣipya avyaktaśabdenaiva gṛhṇāti tena caturviṃśatikaḥ puruṣaḥ ityaviruddham ||
children.translated_text: "the group of sixteen is an evolute; <s>puruṣa</s> is neither evolvent nor evolute," still here the indifferent <s>puruṣa</s>, separate from <s>prakṛti</s>, is inserted into unmanifest <s>prakṛti</s> itself because of its similarity to the unmanifest, and is included by the word "unmanifest" alone. Therefore the statement that <s>puruṣa</s> is twenty-fourfold is not contradictory.

children.text: udāsīnasya hi sūkṣmasya bhedapratipādanam ihānatiprayojanam iti na kṛtam ||
children.translated_text: For the explanation of a distinction belonging to the indifferent and subtle one has no great purpose here, and so it has not been made.

children.text: daśendriyāṇīti pañca karmendriyāṇi pañca buddhīndriyāṇi ca ||
children.translated_text: "The ten senses" means the five organs of action and the five organs of cognition.

children.text: aṣṭadhātukīti khādipañcakabuddhyavyaktāhaṃkārarūpā vakṣyati hi khādīni buddhiravyaktam ahaṅkārastathāṣṭamaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: "Consisting of eight <s>dhātu</s>s" means consisting of the five beginning with ether, <s>buddhi</s>, the unmanifest, and <s>ahaṃkāra</s>. For he will say: "The elements beginning with ether, <s>buddhi</s>, the unmanifest, and <s>ahaṃkāra</s> as the eighth."

children.text: atra caturviṃśatike prathamoddiṣṭaṃ mano lakṣayitumāha lakṣaṇam ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Here, in the twenty-fourfold entity, in order to define mind, which was first mentioned, he speaks with the passage beginning "definition."

children.text: yathā jñānasyābhāvo jñānasya bhāvaśca manogamako bhavati tadāha satītyādi ||
children.translated_text: He states how the absence of cognition and the presence of cognition become indicators of mind, with the passage beginning "when present."

children.text: vaivṛttyānmanasa iti indriyeṇāsaṃyogāt sānnidhyāditi indriyeṇa manasaḥ saṃbandhāt ||
children.translated_text: "Through the turning away of the mind" means because there is no conjunction with the sense faculty; "through proximity" means because the mind is connected with the sense faculty.

children.text: evaṃ manyate yadā yugapad indriyārthā indriyaiḥ saṃyujyante tadā kvacid indriyārthe jñānaṃ bhavati kvacinna bhavatīti dṛṣṭaṃ tenemau jñānabhāvābhāvau jñānakāraṇāntaraṃ darśayataḥ yacca tat kāraṇāntaraṃ tanmanaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He thinks as follows: when sense objects are simultaneously joined with the senses, it is observed that cognition occurs with respect to some sense object and does not occur with respect to another. Therefore these two, the presence and absence of cognition, point to some further cause of cognition; and that further cause is the mind.

children.text: tacca kāraṇaṃ manorūpaṃ yadyātmavadyugapat sarvendriyavyāpakaṃ svīkriyate kiṃvā anekasaṃkhyam indriyavat svīkriyate tadā punarapi yugapad indriyārthasaṃbandhe pañcabhir jñānair bhavitavyaṃ vibhunā vā manasā anekair vā manobhir yugapad adhiṣṭhitatvād indriyāṇāṃ na ca bhavanti yugapajjñānāni tasmādyugapajjñānānudayāl liṅgānmano'ṇurūpamekaṃ ca sidhyatītyāha aṇutvamityādi ||
children.translated_text: And if that cause, in the form of <s>manas</s> (mind), is accepted either as pervading all the sense faculties simultaneously, like the self, or as many in number, like the sense faculties, then again, when the sense faculties and their objects are in simultaneous contact, there would have to be five cognitions, because the faculties would be simultaneously governed either by an all-pervading mind or by many minds. But simultaneous cognitions do not occur. Therefore, from the sign that simultaneous cognitions do not arise, it is established that mind is atomic in form and single. He states this with the words beginning 'atomicity'.
Having described the quality of mind, he states the object of mind with the words beginning 'the thinkable'.

children.text: cintyaṃ kartavyatayā akartavyatayā vā yanmanasā cintyate ||
children.translated_text: The thinkable is what is thought by the mind as something to be done or not to be done.
The investigable is what is examined in terms of logical fitness and unfitness.

children.text: ūhyaṃ ca yat sambhāvanayā ūhyate evametadbhaviṣyati iti ||
children.translated_text: The conjecturable is what is conjectured by supposition: 'This will be so.'
The meditatable is the object of cognition through sustained contemplation.
The determinable is the object of ascertainment as possessing good qualities or defects.
By the phrase 'anything whatever,' he includes unstated objects such as pleasure and the rest.
'Knowable to the mind' means grasped by the mind independently of the senses.

children.text: ete ca mano'rthāḥ śabdādirūpā eva tena ṣaṣṭhārthakalpanayā na caturviṃśatisaṃkhyātirekaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And these objects of mind are themselves forms such as sound and the rest; therefore, by positing a sixth object, there is no increase beyond the number twenty-four.

children.text: sukhādayas tu śabdādivyatiriktā mano'rthā buddhibhedagrahaṇenaiva grāhyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: But pleasure and the others, being objects of mind distinct from sound and the rest, are to be grasped simply by taking account of distinctions in cognition.
Having described the object of mind, he states the action of mind with the words beginning 'of the senses'.

children.text: indriyābhigrahaḥ indriyādhiṣṭhānaṃ manasaḥ karma tathā svasya nigraho manasaḥ karma mano hy aniṣṭaviṣayaprasṛtaṃ manasaiva niyamyate manaśca guṇāntarayuktaṃ sadviṣayāntarān niyamayati ityāhureke ||
children.translated_text: The taking hold of the senses, that is, the governing of the senses, is an action of mind. Likewise, restraint of itself is an action of mind, for mind that has turned toward an undesirable object is restrained by the mind itself. And some say that mind, when endowed with another quality, restrains itself from other objects.
As has been said: 'The mind inclined toward its object cannot, because of a lapse of firmness,

children.text: niyantum ahitād arthād dhṛtirhi niyamātmikā iti ||
children.translated_text: be restrained from a harmful object; for <s>dhṛti</s> (steadfastness) has restraint as its nature.'

children.text: tena dhṛtyā kāraṇabhūtayā ātmānaṃ niyamayatīti na svātmani kriyāvirodhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, since one restrains oneself by <s>dhṛti</s> as the causal factor, there is no contradiction of an action being directed toward oneself.
He states another action of mind: conjecture and investigation.

children.text: atroha ālocanajñānaṃ nirvikalpakam vicāro heyopādeyatayā vikalpanam ||
children.translated_text: Here conjecture is indeterminate cognition through mere observation, while investigation is conceptual determination in terms of what is to be rejected or accepted.

children.text: caturvidhaṃ hi vikalpakāraṇaṃ sāṃkhyā manyante tatra bāhyam indriyarūpam ābhyantaraṃ tu mano'haṃkāro buddhiśceti tritayam ||
children.translated_text: The <s>Sāṃkhyas</s> hold that the causes of conceptual determination are fourfold: among them the external one has the form of a sense faculty, while the internal set is the triad of mind, <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-maker), and <s>buddhi</s> (intellect).

children.text: tatrendriyāṇyālocayanti nirvikalpena gṛhṇantītyarthaḥ manastu saṃkalpayati heyopādeyatayā kalpayatītyarthaḥ ahaṃkāro 'bhimanyate mamedamahamatrādhikṛta iti manyata ityarthaḥ buddhir adhyavasyati tyajāmyenaṃ doṣavantam upādadāmyenaṃ guṇavantam ityadhyavasāyaṃ karotītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: There the sense faculties observe, meaning that they grasp indeterminately. The mind forms intentions, meaning that it conceptualizes in terms of what is to be rejected or accepted. <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> appropriates, meaning that it thinks, 'This is mine; I am responsible here.' <s>Buddhi</s> determines, meaning that it makes the decision, 'I abandon this as defective; I take up this as possessing good qualities.'

children.text: ūhas tu yadyapi bāhyacakṣurādikarma tathāpi tatrāpi mano'dhiṣṭhānam astīti manaḥkarmatayoktaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Although conjecture is the action of an external faculty such as the eye, still even there the mind is the governing factor; therefore it is stated as an action of mind.

children.text: vacanaṃ hi sāntaḥkaraṇā buddhiḥ sarvaṃ viṣayam avagāhate yasmāt ||
children.translated_text: For the statement says: '<s>Buddhi</s>, together with the inner organ, enters into every object, since

children.text: tasmāt trividhaṃ karaṇaṃ dvāri dvārāṇi śeṣāṇi iti ||
children.translated_text: therefore the instrument is threefold at the doorway, and the remaining instruments are doors.'

children.text: tataḥ paraṃ buddhiḥ pravartata iti ūhavicārānantaraṃ buddhir adhyavasāyaṃ karotītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'After that, <s>buddhi</s> proceeds' means that after conjecture and investigation, intellect makes a determination.

children.text: ahaṃkāravyāpāraś cābhimananam ihānukto 'pi buddhivyāpāreṇaiva sūcito jñeyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The operation of <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, namely appropriation, though not stated here, should be understood as indicated by the very operation of <s>buddhi</s>.

children.text: buddhirhi tyajāmyenamupādadāmīti vādhyavasāyaṃ kurvatī ahaṃkārābhimata eva viṣaye bhavati tena buddhivyāpāreṇaivāhaṃkāravyāpāro 'pi gṛhyate ||
children.translated_text: For <s>buddhi</s>, when it makes the determination 'I abandon this; I take this up,' occurs only with respect to an object already appropriated by <s>ahaṃkāra</s>. Thus the operation of <s>ahaṃkāra</s> too is grasped through the operation of <s>buddhi</s> itself.
For in <s>buddhi</s> there is the assignment of the operations of all the instruments.
As has been said: 'These special qualities, like lamps and mutually distinct,
illuminate the whole object of the <s>puruṣa</s> and present it to <s>buddhi</s>.'
He explains this very point, that <s>buddhi</s> is preceded by conjecture and investigation, with the words beginning 'by the sense faculty'.
'It is grasped' means that it is grasped indeterminately by mere conjecture.
'By good quality' means as something to be accepted.
'By defect' means as something to be rejected.
He explains the determination of <s>buddhi</s> with the words beginning 'arises'.
'In that object' means in the object conceived by the mind.
'Having certainty as its nature' means steady in character, that is, having the form of determination.

children.text: vyavasyatīti anuṣṭhānaṃ karoti udyukto bhavatītyarthaḥ buddhyadhyavasitamarthaṃ vaktuṃ kartuṃ vānutiṣṭhatīti yāvat ||
children.translated_text: 'It decides' means that it performs an action, that it becomes intent. That is to say, one undertakes to speak or do the matter determined by <s>buddhi</s>.

children.text: buddhipūrvakamityanena yadeva buddhipūrvakam anuṣṭhānaṃ tad evaivaṃvidhaṃ bhavati nonmattādyanuṣṭhānamiti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By the phrase 'preceded by <s>buddhi</s>,' he shows that only an undertaking preceded by intellect is of this kind, not the undertaking of a mad person and the like.

children.text: mano'bhidhāyendriyāṇyabhidhatte tatrāpi jyāyastvād buddhīndriyāṇi prāgāha ekaiketyādi ||
children.translated_text: Having described mind, he describes the sense faculties. Among them too, because the cognitive sense faculties are more important, he first states them with the words beginning 'each'.

children.text: khādīnāṃ madhye ekaikenādhikena bhūtena yuktānīndriyāṇi pañca cakṣurādīni ekaikādhikapadena pañcāpi pāñcabhautikāni paraṃ cakṣuṣi tejo'dhikamityādyuktaṃ sūcayati ||
children.translated_text: Among space and the other elements, the five sense faculties, the eye and the rest, are each joined with one predominant element. By the word 'each predominant,' he indicates that all five are composed of the five elements, while in the eye fire is predominant, and so on.
'Inferable from their actions' means inferable from their effects; the effect is visual cognition and the like.

children.text: yebhyo buddhiḥ pravartata iti yāni buddhīndriyāṇi tānīmāni pañceti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: 'From which cognition proceeds' means that he shows: these are those five cognitive sense faculties.

children.text: yadyapi ca sāṃkhye āhaṃkārikāṇīndriyāṇi yaduktaṃ sāttvika ekādaśakaḥ pravartate vaikṛtād ahaṃkārād iti tathāpi matabhedādbhautikatvam indriyāṇāṃ jñeyaṃ kiṃvā aupacārikam etadbhautikatvam indriyāṇāṃ jñeyam upacārabījaṃ ca yad guṇabhūyiṣṭhaṃ yad indriyaṃ gṛhṇāti tattadbhūyiṣṭham ityucyate cakṣustejo gṛhṇāti tena taijasam ucyate ityādi jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: And although in <s>Sāṃkhya</s> the sense faculties are said to arise from <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, as in the statement, 'the sāttvika set of eleven proceeds from the modified <s>ahaṃkāra</s>,' still, because of a difference of doctrine, the material nature of the sense faculties should be understood. Or else this material nature of the sense faculties should be understood as figurative. The basis of the figurative usage is this: whichever sense faculty apprehends a quality that is predominant in a given element, that faculty is said to be predominant in that element. The eye apprehends light, and therefore it is called fiery; and so on should be understood.
Now he states the organs of action, with 'the hands' and so on.
The two hands are one organ, and the two feet are one organ, because each performs an action of a single kind.
The anus and the generative organ are each a separate one.
For the purpose of including and excluding speech, he states a distinction with 'and speech' and so on.

children.text: jyotiriva jyotiḥ dharmakartṛtvenobhayalokaprakāśakāritvāt etadviparyayeṇa tamaḥ anṛtā ||
children.translated_text: 'Light' is like light, because, by producing <s>dharma</s>, it illumines both worlds. By the opposite of this, false speech is darkness.

children.text: sampratyuddeśakramānurodhādarthe 'bhidhātavye 'rthānāṃ prakṛtigrahaṇagṛhītapañcabhūtaguṇatayā parādhīnatvād aṣṭadhātuprakṛtigṛhītāni bhūtānyeva tāvadāha mahābhūtānītyādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, in accordance with the order of enumeration, when the objects are to be explained, because the objects are dependent, since they possess the qualities of the five elements already included by the mention of <s>prakṛti</s>, he first states the elements included in the eightfold elemental <s>prakṛti</s>, with 'the great elements' and so on.

children.text: śabdādayo yathāsaṃkhyaṃ khādīnāṃ naisargikā guṇā jñeyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Sound and the rest, in their proper order, are to be understood as the natural qualities of ether and the other elements.

children.text: yastu guṇotkarṣo 'bhidhātavyaḥ sa hi anupraviṣṭabhūtasambandhād eva ||
children.translated_text: But the excellence of qualities that is to be explained comes only from the connection with elements that have entered into one another.

children.text: tena pṛthivyāṃ caturbhūtapraveśāt pañcaguṇatvam evaṃ jalādāv api caturguṇatvādi jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore earth has five qualities because the four elements enter into it; in the same way water and the rest should be understood as having four qualities and so forth.

children.text: naisargikaṃ guṇamabhidhāya bhūtāntarapraveśakṛtaṃ guṇam āha teṣām ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Having stated the natural quality, he states the quality produced by the entry of other elements, with 'of them' and so on.

children.text: ekaguṇaḥ pūrva iti pūrvo dhātuḥ kharūpaḥ śabdaikaguṇaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'The prior one has one quality' means: the prior element, whose form is ether, has sound as its single quality.

children.text: puṃliṅgatā ca khādīnāṃ dhāturūpatābuddhisthīkṛtatvāt uktaṃ hi khādayaś cetanāṣaṣṭhā dhātavaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: And the masculine gender of ether and the other elements is because they have been fixed in thought as <s>dhātu</s>s. For it has been said, 'Ether and the rest, with consciousness as the sixth, are the <s>dhātu</s>s.'

children.text: yathā yathā ca paratvaṃ tathā tathā ca guṇavṛddhir yathāsaṃkhyam ||
children.translated_text: And in proportion as there is posteriority, in that same proportion there is an increase of qualities, according to the order.

children.text: nanu etāvatā 'py ekaguṇatvadviguṇatvādi na niyamena jñāyate ko guṇaḥ kva bhūte ityāha pūrva ityādi ||
children.translated_text: But one might object: even by this much it is not definitely known that there is one quality, two qualities, and so on, nor which quality belongs to which element. He explains this with 'the prior' and so on.

children.text: guṇiṣu khādiṣu dhātuṣu pūrvo guṇaḥ krameṇa yathāsaṃkhyaṃ vartate na kevalaṃ pūrvaḥ kiṃtu pūrvasyāpi yo guṇaḥ sa ca pūrvaguṇa uttare bhūte vartate ||
children.translated_text: Among the quality-bearing elements, ether and the rest, the prior quality occurs successively in due order. Not only the prior quality, but also whatever is the quality of that prior one, namely the prior quality, occurs in the later element.

children.text: tena khe pūrve pūrvaḥ śabdaguṇo vartate vāyau tu sparśaḥ kramaprāptaḥ pūrvo bhavati pūrvaguṇaśca śabda iti dviguṇatvam evamagnyādau ca jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in ether, which is prior, the prior quality sound occurs. In air, touch, obtained by sequence, is prior, and sound is the prior quality; therefore air has two qualities. The same should be understood for fire and the rest.

children.text: gandhas tūttaraguṇāntarābhāvānna pūrvo bhavati tathāpi gandhaś ca tadguṇāḥ iti granthe tadguṇā itipadāpekṣayā gandhasya pūrvatvaṃ kalpanīyaṃ kiṃvā pūrva iti chattriṇo gacchantīti nyāyenoktaṃ tenāpūrvo 'pi gandhaḥ kramāgataḥ pṛthivyāṃ jñeyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Smell, however, does not become prior, because there is no further later quality. Nevertheless, in the textual phrase 'and smell and its qualities,' the priority of smell must be imagined with reference to the word 'its qualities.' Or else 'prior' is stated by the maxim 'the umbrella-bearers are going'; therefore even smell, though not prior, should be understood as occurring by sequence in earth.
He states the distinctive definition of the elements, with 'rough' and so on.

children.text: apratīghātaḥ apratihananam asparśatvam iti yāvat sparśavaddhi gativighātakaṃ bhavati nākāśaḥ asparśavattvāt ||
children.translated_text: 'Non-obstruction' means non-impeding, that is to say, absence of touch. For what has touch obstructs motion; ether does not, because it lacks touch.
'All this' means roughness and the rest.
'Within the range of the tactile sense faculty' means knowable by the tactile sense faculty.
How is all this knowable by the tactile sense faculty? He explains this with 'by the tactile' and so on.
'Together with its opposite' means with the absence of touch.

children.text: yad indriyaṃ yadgṛhṇāti tattasyābhāvamapi gṛhṇāti tena ākāśasyāsparśatvam api sparśanendriyagrāhyam iti yuktam ||
children.translated_text: Whatever a sense faculty apprehends, it also apprehends the absence of that thing. Therefore it is reasonable that even the absence of touch in ether is graspable by the tactile sense faculty.

children.text: dravatvaṃ calatvaṃ ca sāṃkhyamate sparśanagrāhyatvāt sthūlabhūtavātadharmaḥ sparśa eva yaddhi sparśanena gṛhyate tat sarvaṃ mahābhūtavātapariṇāma eva ||
children.translated_text: In the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> doctrine, fluidity and mobility, because they are grasped by touch, are simply touch, the property of the gross element air. For whatever is grasped by touch is entirely a transformation of the great element air.

children.text: etāni ca khādīni sūkṣmāṇi tanmātrarūpāṇi jñeyāni sthūlabhūtāni tu khādīni vikāratayā tatroktāni ||
children.translated_text: And these elements, ether and the rest, are to be understood as subtle, having the form of <s>tanmātra</s>s; but the gross elements, ether and the rest, have been mentioned there as products.
In the class of <s>prakṛti</s>s, the <s>tanmātra</s>s were stated as subtle in form.

children.text: vacanaṃ hi tanmātrāṇyaviśeṣās tebhyo bhūtāni pañca pañcabhyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For the statement is: 'The <s>tanmātra</s>s are the undifferentiated ones; from them come the five elements, and from the five,'

children.text: ete smṛtā viśeṣāḥ śāntā ghorāśca mūḍhāśca iti tenehāpi khādīni tanmātraśabdoktāni sūkṣmāṇi boddhavyāni ||
children.translated_text: 'these are remembered as the differentiated ones, peaceful, fierce, and dull.' Therefore here too ether and the rest, denoted by the word <s>tanmātra</s>, are to be understood as subtle.

children.text: bhūtānāṃ sūkṣmāṇāṃ śarīrasthānāṃ liṅgāntarāṇyāha guṇā ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states other marks of the subtle elements situated in the body, with 'the qualities' and so on.
The qualities are sound and the rest.
'Of the quality-bearers' means of the elements in subtle form.

children.text: evacagrahaṇāt śabdādayaśca vyaktāḥ sūkṣmāṇāṃ śarīrasthānāṃ bhūtānāṃ lakṣaṇaṃ bhavantīti vākyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because of the word 'and,' the meaning of the sentence is that sound and the rest too, when manifest, become the marks of the subtle elements situated in the body.
He states the objects, with 'the objects' and so on.

children.text: arthaśabdena tu ye śabdādayo'bhidhīyante te sthūlakhādirūpā eva jñeyāḥ yenākāśapariṇāma eva śabdaḥ vātapariṇāmaḥ sparśa ityādi darśanam ||
children.translated_text: But the sound and the rest that are denoted by the word 'object' should be understood as being simply the gross forms of ether and the other elements. Thus the view is that sound is precisely a transformation of ether, touch a transformation of air, and so on.

children.text: śabdādigrahaṇaṃ nātrākāśādigrahaṇaṃ yat tadākāśādipariṇāma eva śabdādaya iti yuktameva ||
children.translated_text: The mention of sound and the rest here is not a mention of ether and the rest; yet it is quite reasonable that sound and the rest are precisely transformations of ether and the other elements.

children.text: etena yacchrotragrāhyaṃ tat sarvam ākāśaṃ śabdaśca yat sparśena gṛhyate tat sarvaṃ vāyuḥ sparśaścetyādi jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: By this it should be understood that whatever is grasped by hearing is all ether, and sound too; and whatever is grasped by touch is all air, and touch too; and so on.

children.text: saṃprati prakṛtigaṇapraviṣṭāyā buddher upadarśanārthaṃ tasyā buddhervṛttibhedāt jñānaviśeṣarūpāṇyāha yetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, in order to indicate buddhi as included within the group of prakṛti, he states the particular forms of cognition that arise from the different functions of that buddhi, with the passage beginning 'ya'.
