children.text: yadindriyamāśrityeti yadindriyapraṇālikām āśritya mahacchabdākhyasya buddhitattvasya vṛttiviśeṣarūpāṇi jñānānīndriyapraṇālikayā bhavanti tadindriyajanyatvenaiva tāni vyapadiśyante cakṣurbuddhiḥ śrotrabuddhirityādivyapadeśena ||
children.translated_text: 'Depending on whatever sense organ' means: depending on the channel of whatever sense organ. Cognitions that are special forms of activity of the principle called buddhi, denoted by the word mahat, arise through the channel of the senses; they are therefore designated precisely as produced by that sense, by expressions such as eye-cognition and ear-cognition.

children.text: manobhavā ca buddhiścintyādiviṣayā manasā nirdiśyate manobuddhiriti vyapadiśyata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And buddhi that arises from the mind, having objects such as what is to be thought about, is indicated by the mind and is designated as mental cognition; this is the meaning.

children.text: indriyamanobhedena ṣaṭtvaṃ buddhīnāṃ pratipādya buddhibahutvaṃ prāha bhedādityādi ||
children.translated_text: Having established that cognitions are sixfold because of the distinction between the senses and the mind, he states the multiplicity of buddhi with the passage beginning 'because of difference'.

children.text: kāryasya indriyārthasya ca bhedāt tatsaṃbandhena bhidyamānā bahvyo buddhayo bhavanti kāryaṃ sukhaduḥkhabhedāḥ sukhaduḥkhaprapañcena hi tatkāryeṇa kāraṇaṃ jñānamapi bahu bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Because of difference in the effect and in the object of the senses, the buddhis, being differentiated by relation to these, become many. The effect consists of distinctions of pleasure and pain; for by the manifold expansion of pleasure and pain, cognition too, which is their cause, becomes manifold.
Now he states the means for all external cognition, with the passage beginning 'ātman'.
'Ātman' means the unmanifest.
'One by one' means each individually.
To show that buddhi is produced by the conjunction of the ātman and the other factors, he gives an example with the passage beginning 'finger'.

children.text: anena dṛṣṭāntena śabdadvayamāha aṅgulyaṅguṣṭhatalajaśabda ekaḥ ayaṃ cāṅguṣṭhayantritamadhyamāṅgulyāḥ karatalasaṃyogājjāyamānatalaśabda ucyate tantrīvīṇānakhodbhavaśca vīṇāśabda ekaḥ anye tvekam evāṅgulyādijaṃ vīṇāśabdaṃ varṇayanti ||
children.translated_text: By this example he states two kinds of sound: one is the sound produced by finger, thumb, and palm, namely the palm-sound that arises when the middle finger, controlled by the thumb, contacts the palm; and one is the lute-sound produced by the nail and the strings of a vīṇā. Others, however, explain only a single vīṇā-sound as produced from the finger and the other factors.

children.text: etena yathā śabdo'ṅgulādyanyatamavaikalye'pi na bhavati tathā buddhir apyātmādīnām anyatamavaikalye'pi na bhavatīti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By this he shows that, just as sound does not occur if any one among the finger and the other factors is absent, so too buddhi does not arise if any one among the ātman and the other factors is absent.

children.text: atra ca buddhivṛttīnāṃ jñānānāṃ kathanenaivāhaṃkāro'pi sūcita eva yato'haṅkāropajīvitaivātmādisaṃvaliteyaṃ buddhiḥ ahaṃ paśyāmi ityādirūpā bhavati tena buddherahaṅkārasya coktatvād avaśiṣṭam avyaktaṃ kāryadvārā brūte buddhītyādi ||
children.translated_text: Here, merely by speaking of the cognitive functions of buddhi, ahaṃkāra too is implicitly indicated, since this buddhi, conjoined with the ātman and the other factors, is dependent on ahaṃkāra and takes such forms as 'I see.' Therefore, since buddhi and ahaṃkāra have been stated, he speaks of the remaining unmanifest through its effects, with the passage beginning 'buddhi'.
'The higher' means the unmanifest.

children.text: buddhyādīnāṃ yogaṃ melakaṃ dharatīti yogadharam avyaktaṃ hi prakṛtirūpaṃ puruṣārthapravṛttaṃ buddhyādimelakaṃ bhogasaṃpādakaṃ sṛjati ||
children.translated_text: It is called 'holder of conjunction' because it holds, that is, maintains the conjunction or aggregate of buddhi and the other principles. For the unmanifest, being prakṛti and acting for the purpose of puruṣa, produces the aggregate of buddhi and the rest, which accomplishes experience.

children.text: evaṃ vyutpāditaṃ caturviṃśatikam upasaṃharati caturviṃśatika ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Thus he sums up the twenty-fourfold set that has been explained, with the passage beginning 'twenty-fourfold'.

children.text: yadi vā karmendriyāṇyabhidhāya mahābhūtānītyādinā arthā evāśrayabhūtakhādikathanenocyante yā yad indriyam āśrityetyādinā tu sphuṭopalabhyamānā buddhivṛttibhedā ucyante buddhyahaṃkāratanmātrāṇyavyaktāni tu sūkṣmāṇi noktāni tāni sarvāṇyeva buddhīndriyamano'rthānām ityādigranthe paraśabdenocyante tena yogadharaṃ paramityanena mūlaprakṛtistathā prakṛtivikṛtayaśca mahadādayaḥ saptocyante evaṃ caturviṃśatiko rāśirbhavati ||
children.translated_text: Or else, after mentioning the organs of action, the passage beginning 'the great elements' refers only to the objects by naming their supports, such as space and the rest; and the passage beginning 'depending on whatever sense organ' refers to the clearly perceptible differences in the functions of buddhi. But buddhi, ahaṃkāra, the subtle elements, and the unmanifest are subtle and are not directly stated. All those are referred to by the word 'higher' in the passage beginning 'of the cognitive senses, the mind, and the objects.' Thus, by 'the higher, holder of conjunction,' root-prakṛti is stated, and likewise the seven prakṛtis-cum-modifications beginning with mahat are stated. In this way the aggregate becomes twenty-fourfold.
And the higher status of the prakṛtis is entirely appropriate in relation to their modifications.

children.text: saṃpratyevaṃrūpapuruṣasya sakāraṇaṃ saṃsaraṇaṃ mokṣahetuṃ cāha raja ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, of the puruṣa of this kind, he states transmigration together with its cause and also the cause of mokṣa, with the passage beginning 'rajas'.
'This conjunction' means the aggregate consisting of the twenty-fourfold set.
'By those two' means by rajas and tamas.

children.text: sattvavṛddhyā kāraṇabhūtayā rajastamonivṛttyā puruṣarūpaḥ saṃyogo nivartate mokṣo bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Through the increase of sattva as the cause, and through the cessation of rajas and tamas, the conjunction constituting puruṣa ceases; mokṣa comes about. This is the meaning.

children.text: sattvaṃ vṛddhaṃ viśuddhajñānajananād rajastamasī saṃsārakāraṇe vijitya prakṛtipuruṣavivekajñānānmokṣamāvahati ||
children.translated_text: When sattva has increased, because it produces pure knowledge, it overcomes rajas and tamas, the causes of saṃsāra, and brings mokṣa through discriminative knowledge of prakṛti and puruṣa.

children.text: punaścaturviṃśatike puruṣe karmaphalādi darśayan doṣahīne puruṣe karmaphalādyabhāvamarthāddarśayati atretyādi ||
children.translated_text: Again, while showing karma, its fruit, and the rest in the twenty-fourfold puruṣa, he indicates by implication that in a puruṣa free from faults there is no karma, fruit, and so on, with the passage beginning 'here'.
'The fruit is here' means in the aggregate-puruṣa described above.
'Karma' means the unseen potency.
'Fruit' means the fruit of the unseen potency.
'Ownness' means mineness.

children.text: jñānaṃ ca yadyapi caturviṃśatitattvātiriktasyodāsīnasyaiva tathāpi taccetanayā prakṛtirapi cetanāmāpadya cetanaiva bhavatīti yuktam atra jñānam iti ||
children.translated_text: Although knowledge belongs to the inactive principle that is distinct from the twenty-four principles, still, through its consciousness, prakṛti too takes on consciousness and becomes as if conscious; therefore it is proper to say that knowledge is present here.

children.text: vacanaṃ hi tasmāt tatsaṃyogād acetanaṃ cetanāvadiva liṅgam iti ||
children.translated_text: For there is the statement: therefore, because of conjunction with that, the unconscious liṅga is as if conscious.
'Dissolution and arising' means life and death.
'Continuity' means the continuity of bodies.

children.text: cikitsāṃ ceti naiṣṭhikī ātyantikaduḥkhacikitsā mokṣasādhanā jñātavyā ||
children.translated_text: 'And treatment' means that the final treatment, the treatment of absolute suffering, is to be understood as the means to mokṣa.
By the words 'and whatever else,' he includes everything knowable, even if it has not been specifically stated.

children.text: puruṣaḥ kāraṇaṃ kasmāditi praśnasyottaraṃ bhāstama ityādi ||
children.translated_text: The answer to the question 'Why is puruṣa the cause?' is given with the passage beginning 'light and darkness'.
'Light' means insight.
'Darkness' means delusion.
In this context, by 'puruṣa' the ātman is intended.
'Support' means the body.
Movement occurs from attention to a purpose; arrival too is the same.

children.text: kāraṇaṃ puruṣastasmāditi bhāstamaḥsatyādau kāraṇaṃ puruṣa ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Therefore puruṣa is the cause' means that puruṣa is the cause in matters such as insight, darkness, and truth.

children.text: etadeva bhādikāraṇatvam ātmana āha na cedityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states precisely this causal status of the ātman with respect to insight and the rest, with the passage beginning 'if not'.

children.text: evaṃ manyate bhāstamasī dharmādharmajanye dharmādharmau cāsatyātmani nirāśrayau na bhavitumarhataḥ tathā satyaṃ dharmajanakatayā upādeyam anṛtaṃ cādharmajanakatayānupādeyam etaccātmani sthire'sati dharmādharmajanakatvaṃ nāsti tataśca satyāsatyabhedo 'pyakiṃcitkaratvānnāsti evaṃ śubhāśubhakarmaṇyapi vācyaṃ tathā kartā ca kāraṇapratisaṃdhātā na bhavati pratisaṃdhātur ātmano 'bhāvād ityarthaḥ tathā boddhā ca pūrvāparāvasthāpratisaṃdhātaiva bhavati śarīraṃ cātmano bhogāyatanaṃ nātmānaṃ vinā bhavati evaṃ sukhādāvapyātmanaḥ kāraṇatvamunneyam vijñānaṃ śāstrārthajñānaṃ śāstrāṇi pratisaṃdhātrātmanaiva kṛtāni ||
children.translated_text: He understands it thus: <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, which are produced by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, cannot exist without a support when the self is not real. Likewise truth is to be adopted because it produces <s>dharma</s>, and untruth is not to be adopted because it produces <s>adharma</s>; but when there is no stable self, their capacity to produce <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> does not exist. Therefore the distinction between truth and falsehood too does not exist, since it accomplishes nothing. The same should be said of auspicious and inauspicious actions. And the agent is not one who connects cause and result, because there is no self that connects them: this is the meaning. Likewise the knower too is precisely one who connects earlier and later states. And the body, as the abode of the self's experience, does not exist apart from the self. In this way the causal role of the self should also be inferred with regard to pleasure and the like. Knowledge is knowledge of the meaning of the treatise; the treatises were composed only by a self that connects experience.

children.text: na caiṣu sambhavejjñānamiti ātmānaṃ jñātāraṃ vinā na bhādiṣu jñānaṃ sambhavet jñāturātmano'bhāvādityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'And among these knowledge could not arise' means: without the self as knower, knowledge could not arise in entities beginning with 'bhā', because there is no self as knower: this is the meaning.

children.text: na ca taiḥ syāt prayojanam iti bhādīnām ātmārthatvenāsatyātmani bhādyutpatteḥ prayojanaṃ na syāt prayojanābhāvāccotpādo na syāt sarveṣāmeva hi bhāvānām ātmasthau dharmādharmau puruṣabhogārthamutpādakau asati bhoktari bhojyenāpi na bhavitavyaṃ kāraṇābhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: 'And there would be no purpose in them' means: since the entities beginning with 'bhā' exist for the sake of the self, if the self were unreal there would be no purpose in the arising of those entities; and, because there is no purpose, there would be no arising. For in the case of all beings, <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, located in the self, produce them for the sake of the person's experience. If there is no experiencer, there should also be no object of experience, because the cause is absent.

children.text: ātmānaṃ vinā śarīrānutpāde dṛṣṭāntadvayaṃ prameyagauravād āha kṛtaṃ mṛddaṇḍetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Because the point to be proved is weighty, he gives two examples for the non-production of the body without the self, with the words beginning 'made of clay, stick, and so on'.
'Made by the instruments in combination' means: made by the elements without dependence on a self.

children.text: yuktyā anumānarūpayā āgamena ca rahito yuktyāgamabahiṣkṛtaḥ pratyakṣaṃ cātra noktaṃ tasyātmānaṃ prati prāyo'yogyatvāt ||
children.translated_text: 'Devoid of reasoning and scripture' means devoid of reasoning in the form of inference and of <s>āgama</s> (authoritative testimony). Perception is not mentioned here, since for the self it is generally unsuitable.
'By all <s>pramāṇa</s>s' means by perception and the rest.
In 'from which', the fifth case ending is used with the intended sense of an ablative in relation to the instrument itself.

children.text: āgamayanti bodhayantīti āgamāḥ pramāṇānyeva anye tvāgamapramāṇābhyāṃ śāstrāṇyeva bruvate ||
children.translated_text: They are <s>āgama</s>s because they make one understand, they teach; they are simply <s>pramāṇa</s>s. Others, however, say that by <s>āgama</s> and <s>pramāṇa</s> the treatises themselves are meant.
He raises the doctrine of those who deny the self with the words beginning 'they are not'.

children.text: asmiñśarīre te ka eva pṛthivījalādayo bhāvāḥ ye ta eveti vyapadiśyante te na bhavanti pūrvānubhūtā nānubhavantītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: In this body, what exactly are those entities such as earth and water which are designated as 'the same'? They are not the same; what was formerly experienced does not experience now: this is the meaning.

children.text: yadi te na bhavanti kathaṃ tarhi te ityabhijñānamityāha tatsadṛśāstvanye pūrvasadṛśā ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: If they are not the same, how then is there recognition as 'the same'? He answers: 'but others similar to them', meaning similar to the former ones.
'Arisen in succession' means established as a continuum of similar things.
'Because of similarity of form' means because they have a similar form.

children.text: teṣāṃ samudaya iti kṣaṇabhaṅgināṃ melaka ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Their aggregate' means a collection of things that perish moment by moment.
'Without a lord' means without a permanent self.
'Called sattva' means called a living being.
'Some' means the Buddhists.

children.text: bauddhā hi nirātmakaṃ kṣaṇikajñānādisamudāyamātraṃ śarīram icchanti pratisaṃdhānaṃ ca kṣaṇikānām api jñānādīnāṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvād ekaphalasaṃtatāvicchanti ||
children.translated_text: For the Buddhists hold that the body is only a selfless aggregate of momentary cognitions and the like; and they hold that continuity exists even for momentary cognitions and the like because of the relation of cause and effect and the continuity of a single result.
He refutes this with the words beginning 'of them'.

children.text: teṣāṃ jñānasantānavādinām anyena kṛtasyaudanapākādeḥ phalamannādi anye bhuñjata iti prāpnoti ||
children.translated_text: For those who teach a continuum of cognitions, it follows that other people eat the result, namely the food and so on, of rice-cooking and the like performed by someone else.

children.text: etaccāsaṃgataṃ yataḥ phalaṃ bhokṣyāmīti kṛtvā bhāviphalapratyāśayā pravṛttiryuktā na tvanyasya bhogyatāṃ phalasya paśyan kaścit pravartate yo'pi sūpakārādiḥ parārthaṃ pravartate so 'parārthena svārthaṃ sādhayitukāma eveti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And this is incoherent, because activity undertaken in expectation of a future result is reasonable when one thinks, 'I shall enjoy the result'; but no one acts while seeing that the result is to be enjoyed by another. Even a cook and the like who acts for another's sake really wishes to accomplish his own interest through the interest of another: this is the purport.
Having refuted the opposing view, he states his own view with the words beginning 'the instrument'.
The otherness and non-otherness of the changing instrument, the body, is observed.

children.text: kartā cātmā sa eva na vināśītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And the agent, the self, is just the same; that is, it is not perishable.
He gives an example for this very point with the words beginning 'for an agent'.

children.text: yathānekaśilpavit kartā karaṇairvāṃśīsaṃdaṃśayantrādibhiḥ kāṣṭhapāṭanalauhaghaṭanādi karoti tathātmāpītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Just as an agent skilled in many crafts performs such actions as cutting wood and joining iron with instruments such as a saw, tongs, and machines, so too does the self: this is the meaning.

children.text: athāyamātmasadbhāvaḥ sthiro'stu śarīrārambhakāṇāṃ bhūtānāṃ kā vā gatirityāha nimeṣetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, let this existence of the self be stable; but what is the fate of the elements that begin the body? He answers with the words beginning 'in the time of a blink'.
'Of entities' means of entities such as the body.

children.text: atyaya iti vināśe śarīrasya svāgnipacyamānasya nimeṣakālādapi śīghraṃ vināśo bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'At destruction' means at perishing: the body, being cooked by its own fire, perishes even more quickly than the time of a blink; this is the meaning.

children.text: amīṣāṃ ca bhāvānāṃ bhagnānāṃ na punarbhāvaḥ punarāgamanaṃ nāstītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And of these entities, once broken apart, there is no re-becoming, no coming back again: this is the meaning.

children.text: tena yena śarīreṇa yat kṛtaṃ taccharīraṃ tatphalaṃ na prāpnotītyuktaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: By this it is said that whatever was done by that body, that body does not obtain its result.

children.text: atha mā bhavatvevaṃ tataḥ kimityāha kṛtamityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, if it should not be so, what follows from that? He states this with the words beginning 'what has been done'.

children.text: kṛtaṃ karma yāgādi na phalarūpatayānyamupaiti evaṃ sati devadattakṛtena śubhakarmaṇā yajñadattādayo'pi sukhabhājaḥ syuḥ tasmāt kṣaṇabhaṅgiśarīrād atiriktaḥ karmakartā tatphalabhoktā cāstīti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: An action that has been done, such as a sacrifice, does not go to another in the form of its result. If this were so, then <s>Yajñadatta</s> and others would also become enjoyers of happiness through the good action done by <s>Devadatta</s>. Therefore there exists an agent of action and experiencer of its result distinct from the momentarily perishing body: this is the purport.
'Action and enjoyment' means in action and in the enjoyment of its result.
'Of beings' means of living creatures.
He gives another reason for the existence of the self with the words beginning 'I-making'.

children.text: ete'haṅkārādayaḥ sthira eva paramātmani bhavanti pūrvāparakālāvasthāyivastudharmatvād iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: These, beginning with <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego-maker), exist only in the stable <s>paramātman</s> (supreme self), because they are properties of a thing that remains through earlier and later times; this is the sense.

children.text: dehamantareti dehaṃ vinā dehātirikte kāraṇe satyahaṅkāro bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "Apart from the body" means: without the body, when there is a cause distinct from the body, <s>ahaṃkāra</s> arises.

children.text: prabhavaḥ puruṣasya kaḥ ityasyottaraṃ prabhava ityādi ||
children.translated_text: The answer to "What is the origin of <s>puruṣa</s> (person)?" is the passage beginning "origin."
"Origin" means cause.
"Called a mass" means either having the form of an aggregate of six <s>dhātu</s>s (constituents), or having the form of a twenty-fourfold aggregate.
"Born from action produced by delusion, desire, and aversion" is equivalent to "born from delusion, desire, aversion, and action."

children.text: mohāddhi bhāveṣu icchā dveṣaśca bhavati tataḥ pravṛttiḥ pravṛtterdharmādharmau tau ca śarīraṃ janayato bhogārtham ||
children.translated_text: For from delusion, with respect to things, desire and aversion arise; from that comes activity; from activity come <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>; and those two generate the body for the sake of experience.
The answer to "Is it ignorant or knowing?" is the passage beginning "the self."
The instruments here are mind, <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), and the sense faculties.
The construction is: "knowledge does not occur."

children.text: nanu yadyayam ātmā jñaḥ tat kimityasya sarvadā jñānaṃ na bhavatītyāha paśyato'pītyādi ||
children.translated_text: But if this <s>ātman</s> (self) is knowing, then why does knowledge not belong to it at all times? To this he replies with the passage beginning "even for one who sees."
"Even for one who sees" means even for one who has eyesight.
"True" is a qualifier of seeing.

children.text: tena mlāne darpaṇe jale vā darśanaṃ bhavadapyayathārthagrāhitayā na tattvarūpaṃ bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in a tarnished mirror or in water, even when seeing occurs, because it grasps inaccurately it is not true in form; this is the meaning.
"In the mind" is illustrative; by it one should understand that, when the eye and the rest too are impaired, this is also so.

children.text: karaṇaprastāvājū jñāne karmaṇi vedanāyāṃ ca yāvat karaṇam ātmanastadāha karaṇānītyādi ||
children.translated_text: Because the topic is the instruments, he states, with the passage beginning "the instruments," whatever instrument belongs to the self in knowledge, action, and sensation.

children.text: saṃyogajamiti karmaṇā vedanayā buddhyā ca yojyam ||
children.translated_text: "Born from conjunction" is to be connected with action, sensation, and <s>buddhi</s>.
It should be construed: "alone, it does not obtain the fruit."
"Alone" means without instruments.
"It operates from conjunction" means that it arises from the aggregate of instruments.
"Without that" means without conjunction.

children.text: atraiva sāmagrījanyatve sarvakāryāṇāmupapattimāha na hyeka ityādi ||
children.translated_text: On this very point, that all effects are intelligible as produced by a complete causal assemblage, he says the passage beginning "for not one."

children.text: eko bhāvaḥ kāraṇarūpaḥ sahakārikāraṇāntararahito na kāryakaraṇe vartata ityarthaḥ evaṃ tāvadekaṃ kāraṇaṃ kārye na vartate kāryaṃ ca hetuṃ vinā na bhavatītyāha vartate nāpyahetuka iti hetuṃ vinā bhāva utpattidharmā na vartate na bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: A single entity in the form of a cause, without another assisting cause, does not operate in producing an effect; this is the meaning. Thus, first, a single cause does not operate with respect to an effect; and an effect does not exist without a cause. To state this he says, "nor does it occur without a cause": an entity whose nature is to arise does not occur, does not come to be, without a cause.

children.text: tena karaṇayuktātmajanyaṃ kāryaṃ na kevalādātmano heturūpād bhavatītyuktaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Therefore it is said that an effect produced by the self furnished with instruments does not arise from the self alone as the cause.

children.text: atha hetuṃ vinā cedbhāvo na bhavati tat kimabhāve'pi śārīrāṇāṃ bhāvānāṃ hetvapekṣā na vetyāha śīghragatvādityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, if an entity does not come to be without a cause, does the nonexistence of bodily states also require a cause or not? To address this he says the passage beginning "because of rapid passing."

children.text: śīghragatvāt svabhāvāllakṣito'bhāvo na svabhāvaṃ vyativartate śīghragatvasvabhāvaṃ na tyajatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nonexistence, marked by nature as having rapid passing, does not transgress its own nature; the meaning is that it does not abandon its nature of rapid passing.

children.text: tena ahetuka evābhāvo bhavati bhāvastu sahetukaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore nonexistence is indeed without a cause, while an existent thing has a cause.

children.text: uktaṃ hi utpattihetur bhāvānāṃ na nirodhe'sti kāraṇam iti ||
children.translated_text: For it has been said: "There is a cause for the production of existent things; there is no cause for cessation."

children.text: kiṃvā śīghragatvād asthiratvād abhāvo nāvasthāntaramātmanāśaṃ pratigacchatīti granthārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Or rather, because of rapid passing, that is, because of instability, nonexistence does not undergo another state, namely the destruction of itself; this is the meaning of the text.
The answer to "Is it eternal or non-eternal?" is the passage beginning "beginningless."
And the beginningless <s>puruṣa</s>, whose form is unmanifest, is denoted by the word <s>ātman</s>.

children.text: viparīta iti ādimān rāśirūpaḥ puruṣa ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "The opposite" means <s>puruṣa</s> that has a beginning and has the form of an aggregate.
On this very point, that what is beginningless is eternal, he also cites agreement from another śāstra with the passage beginning "existent."
"Existent" means something in the form of an existent entity, accessible to <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid cognition), in the threefold time.
By this, the impermanence of prior nonexistence, though it has no cause, is not a counterexample, because it is of the nature of nonexistence.
In the phrase "otherwise, produced from a cause," here too "of the nature of an existent entity" is to be supplied.
Thus the indestructibility of destruction, even though it is produced from a cause, is ruled out.
What is that eternality? He says the passage beginning "that very."
From an entity whose nature is production.

children.text: tannityatvaṃ na kuto'pi bhāvādbhavati nityaṃ hi na kuto'pi bhavati ||
children.translated_text: That eternality does not arise from any entity at all, for what is eternal does not arise from anything at all.

children.text: tataścātmā bhāvaṃ prati nirapekṣatvāt sarvebhyo bhāvebhyo'pyagre nityaṃ sadeva ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, since the self is independent with respect to becoming, it is eternally existent even before all entities.
And this eternal thing of such a kind should be understood as unmanifest.
"Inconceivable" is a qualifier of the unmanifest.
And the unmanifest is root <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature).

children.text: vyaktam anyatheti prakṛteranyatamakāryaṃ mahadādikamanityam ākāśamapi vikārarūpatayānityameva udāsīnapuruṣastu nitya evāvyaktaśabdenaiva lakṣita ityuktameva ||
children.translated_text: "The manifest is otherwise" means: any product of <s>prakṛti</s>, such as <s>mahat</s> and the rest, is impermanent; even ether, because it has the form of an evolute, is certainly impermanent. But the indifferent <s>puruṣa</s> is eternal, and it has already been said that it is indicated by the word "unmanifest" alone.
He states the synonyms that encompass further properties of the unmanifest with the passage beginning "unmanifest."

children.text: punaḥ prakārāntareṇa vyaktāvyaktārtham āha vakṣyata ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Again, in another way, he explains the meaning of manifest and unmanifest with the passage beginning "it will be stated."
"The other pair" means the pair of manifest and unmanifest established by another mode of explanation.
"Grasped by a mark" means grasped by inference.

children.text: atīndriyam ityanena cendriyagrahaṇāyogyaṃ yat kenāpi śabdādiliṅgena gṛhyate na tadavyaktaṃ kiṃtu yannityānumeyaṃ mano'haṅkārādi tadevāvyaktam ||
children.translated_text: By saying "beyond the senses," he means that what is not fit to be grasped by the senses, yet is grasped through some mark such as sound and the like, is not the unmanifest; rather, only what is always to be inferred, such as mind and <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, is unmanifest.

children.text: prakṛtiḥ kā vikārāḥ ke ityasyottaraṃ khādīnītyādi ||
children.translated_text: The answer to "What is <s>prakṛti</s>, and which are the evolutes?" is the passage beginning "ether and the rest."
"Ether and the rest" means the subtle elements beginning with ether, denoted by the word <s>tanmātra</s> (subtle element).
<s>Buddhi</s> is denoted by the word <s>mahat</s>.
The unmanifest is root <s>prakṛti</s>.

children.text: ahaṅkāraḥ buddhivikāraḥ sa ca trividhaḥ bhūtādiḥ taijasaḥ vaikārikaśca ||
children.translated_text: <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> is an evolute of <s>buddhi</s>; and it is threefold: <s>bhūtādi</s>, <s>taijasa</s>, and <s>vaikārika</s>.
The nature of beings, both stationary and moving, is the elemental nature of beings.

children.text: atra cāvyaktaṃ prakṛtireva paraṃ buddhyādayastu svakāraṇavikṛtirūpā api svakāryāpekṣayā prakṛtirūpā iha prakṛtitvenoktāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here the unmanifest alone is <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) in the primary sense; but <s>buddhi</s> and the rest, although they are transformations of their own causes, are here called <s>prakṛti</s>s with reference to their own effects.

children.text: yaduktaṃ mūlaprakṛtir avikṛtirmahadādyāḥ prakṛtivikṛtayaḥ sapta iti ||
children.translated_text: For it has been said: 'The root <s>prakṛti</s> is not a transformation; the seven beginning with <s>mahat</s> are both <s>prakṛti</s>s and transformations.'
He states the transformations with 'the transformations' and so on.

children.text: evaśabdo bhinnakrame'vadhāraṇe tena vikārā eva ṣoḍaśa paraṃ na prakṛtayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The word 'eva' is used out of sequence for restriction; therefore the transformations are only sixteen, and are not <s>prakṛti</s>s in the higher sense.
The senses belonging to cognition are the <s>buddhīndriya</s>s (cognitive sense faculties).

children.text: pañcārthā iti sthūlā ākāśādayaḥ śabdādirūpāḥ guṇaguṇinorhi paramārthato bhedo nāstyevāsmin darśane ||
children.translated_text: 'The five objects' means the gross elements, ether and the rest, in the form of sound and so on; for in this doctrine there is in truth no difference at all between qualities and their bearers.

children.text: enam eva prakṛtivikārasamūhaṃ kṣetrakṣetrajñabhedena vibhajate itītyādi ||
children.translated_text: He divides this very aggregate of <s>prakṛti</s>s and transformations according to the distinction between field and knower of the field, with 'iti' and so on.
'Excluding the unmanifest' means excluding <s>prakṛti</s> and the inactive one; and indeed <s>prakṛti</s> has consciousness through the consciousness of the inactive <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: saṃprati mahāpralayāntaraṃ yathādisarge buddhyādyutpādo bhavati tadāha jāyata ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now he explains how, after the great dissolution, the arising of <s>buddhi</s> and the rest takes place at the first creation, with 'is born' and so on.

children.text: buddhyāhamiti manyata iti buddherjāte nāhaṅkāreṇāhamiti manyata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Through <s>buddhi</s> he thinks, I am' means that, once <s>buddhi</s> has arisen, he does not think 'I am' through <s>ahaṃkāra</s>.
'Ether and the rest' means the subtle ether and the rest, in the form of <s>tanmātra</s>s, and likewise the eleven senses.

children.text: vacanaṃ hi prakṛter mahāṃstato 'haṅkārastasmād gaṇaśca ṣoḍaśakaḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: For the statement is: 'From <s>prakṛti</s> comes <s>mahat</s>; from that, <s>ahaṃkāra</s>; from that, the group of sixteen.'

children.text: yathākramamiti yasmādahaṅkārādutpadyate tena krameṇa tatra vaikṛtāt sāttvikādahaṅkārāttaijasasahāyād ekādaśendriyāṇi bhavanti bhūtādestvahaṅkārāttāmasāttaijasasahāyāt pañcatanmātrāṇi ||
children.translated_text: 'In due order' means according to the sequence in which they arise from <s>ahaṃkāra</s>: from modified, sāttvika <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, assisted by the taijasa form, arise the eleven senses; but from elemental-origin, tāmasa <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, assisted by the taijasa form, arise the five <s>tanmātra</s>s.
For it has been said: 'The set of eleven, sāttvika, proceeds from the modified <s>ahaṃkāra</s>;'
'From the elemental origin comes the <s>tanmātra</s>; that is tāmasa; from the taijasa comes both.'
'From that' means after the effect belonging to <s>ahaṃkāra</s>, because of connection with the gross elements produced from the <s>tanmātra</s>s.
'Born complete in all limbs' means born at the first creation.

children.text: evamādisarge prakṛter mahadādisargaṃ darśayitvā mahāpralaye prakṛtāvavyaktarūpāyāṃ buddhyādīnāṃ layamāha puruṣa ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Having thus shown, in the first creation, the creation from <s>prakṛti</s> beginning with <s>mahat</s>, he states the dissolution of <s>buddhi</s> and the rest into <s>prakṛti</s>, which has the form of the unmanifest, at the great dissolution, with 'the <s>puruṣa</s>' and so on.
'With desired states' means with <s>buddhi</s> and the rest, which are desired for the sake of the <s>puruṣa</s>'s experience.

children.text: anye tu evaṃbhūtasaṅgaṃ janmani buddhyādiviyogaṃ ca maraṇe bruvate ||
children.translated_text: But others say that association with such elements occurs at birth, and separation from <s>buddhi</s> and the rest at death.
That is not so, because <s>buddhi</s> and the rest are present at birth and death.

children.text: uktaṃ hi atīndriyaistair atisūkṣmarūpair ātmā kadācinna vimuktapūrvaḥ
children.translated_text: For it has been said: 'The self has never before been freed at any time from those supersensory things of exceedingly subtle form,'

children.text: naivendriyair naiva manomatibhyāṃ na cāpyahaṅkāravikāradoṣaiḥ iti ||
children.translated_text: 'nor indeed from the senses, nor from mind and intellect, nor from the faults that are transformations of <s>ahaṃkāra</s>.'
So too it is said elsewhere: 'The subtle body, produced before, unattached, fixed, extending down to the subtle state beginning with <s>mahat</s>,'
'transmigrates without experience, conditioned by states.'

children.text: tasmānmahāpralaya eva prakṛtau layaḥ tathādisarga eva prakṛtermahadādisṛṣṭiriti ||
children.translated_text: Therefore dissolution into <s>prakṛti</s> occurs only at the great dissolution, and the creation from <s>prakṛti</s> beginning with <s>mahat</s> occurs only at the first creation.

children.text: etadeva prapañcaṃ layaṃ ca prakṛterāha avyaktād ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states this very expansion and dissolution from <s>prakṛti</s> with 'from the unmanifest' and so on.
'From the unmanifest' means from <s>prakṛti</s>; 'to manifestness' means that it goes to the condition of being an expansion beginning with <s>mahat</s> and ending with the great elements.

children.text: avyaktād iti mahābhūtaprapañcādyavasthātaḥ punaravyaktarūpatāṃ yāti gacchati mahāpralaye hi mahābhūtāni tanmātreṣu layaṃ yānti tanmātrāṇi tathendriyāṇi cāhaṅkāre layaṃ yānti ahaṅkāro buddhau buddhiśca prakṛtāviti layakramaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'From the unmanifest' means that, from the state beginning with the expansion of the great elements, it again goes to, reaches, the state of the unmanifest. For at the great dissolution the great elements dissolve into the <s>tanmātra</s>s; the <s>tanmātra</s>s, and likewise the senses, dissolve into <s>ahaṃkāra</s>; <s>ahaṃkāra</s> into <s>buddhi</s>; and <s>buddhi</s> into <s>prakṛti</s>. This is the order of dissolution.
And this order of dissolution also occurs in liberation.

children.text: paraṃ tu tatra taṃ puruṣaṃ prati punaḥ sargaṃ nārabhate prakṛtiḥ ||
children.translated_text: Only, in that case <s>prakṛti</s> does not begin creation again with respect to that <s>puruṣa</s>.

children.text: ayaṃ saṃsāraḥ kuto bhavatītyāha raja ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He explains whence this <s>saṃsāra</s> arises, with 'rajas' and so on.
'Entered' means connected with.

children.text: cakravat parivartata iti punaḥ punar layasargābhyāṃ yujyate ||
children.translated_text: 'It revolves like a wheel' means that it is joined again and again with dissolution and creation.
'Pair' means the couple in the form of <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>.
'Devoted to egoity' means intent on false knowledge such as 'from egoity this is mine.'
'Arising and dissolution' mean birth and death, or else dissolution and creation.

children.text: ato'nyatheti ye rāgadveṣavimuktā nirahaṃkārāśca teṣāṃ nodayapralayau bhavataḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Otherwise than this' means that for those who are free from passion and aversion and are without egoity, there is no arising and dissolution.

children.text: kiṃ liṅgaṃ puruṣasya ca ityasyottaraṃ prāṇāpānāvityādi ||
children.translated_text: The answer to 'And what is the sign of the <s>puruṣa</s>?' is given with 'breath and downward breath' and so on.
<s>Prāṇa</s> and <s>apāna</s> are exhalation and inhalation.

children.text: nimeṣādyā iti ādyaśabdagrahaṇena unmeṣādyāḥ prekṣaṇaviśeṣā gṛhyante ||
children.translated_text: 'Blinking and the rest' means that, by taking the word 'and the rest,' opening of the eyes and other special forms of seeing are included.
'The motion of the mind' means such things as going to <s>Pāṭaliputra</s> by means of the mind.

children.text: indriyāntarasaṃcāro'pi manasa eva yathā cakṣuḥ parityajya manaḥ sparśanamadhitiṣṭhatītyādi ||
children.translated_text: Movement to another sense faculty also belongs to the mind, as in: 'having left the eye, the mind occupies touch,' and so on.

children.text: preraṇaṃ ca tathā dhāraṇaṃ ca manasa eveti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: And impulse, likewise, and retention too should be understood as belonging to the mind alone.
The division is: 'movement to another place in dream.'
The mention of coming to the fivefold state is knowledge of death.

children.text: savyenāvagama iti savyenākṣṇā sa evāyaṃ dakṣiṇākṣidṛṣṭo ghaṭa ityavagama ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Recognition with the left' means recognition with the left eye, as in: 'this pot is the very same one that was seen with the right eye.'
Consciousness is mere knowing.
But <s>buddhi</s> is knowledge through consideration and exclusion.
Now, as to how these make the self known, he explains with 'because' and so on.
'Of one living' means of one connected with a self distinct from the five elements.

children.text: pañcatvaṃ tu yadyapi jīvato na bhavati kiṃtu mṛtasyaiva tathāpi pañcatvaṃ mṛtaśarīre dṛśyamānaṃ viparyayāt pañcatvābhāvājjīvaccharīraliṅgaṃ bhavatīti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: Although dissolution into the five elements does not occur for a living person, but only for one who is dead, nevertheless dissolution into the five elements, seen in a dead body, should be understood as a mark of a living body by contrary inference, because in it that dissolution into the five elements is absent.

children.text: atraivodāhṛtāśca prāṇāpānādayo na bhūtamātre bhavanti nirātmakeṣviṣṭakāmṛtaśarīrādiṣvadarśanāt ||
children.translated_text: And the examples mentioned here, breath, downward breath, and the rest, do not occur in mere elements, because they are not seen in things without self, such as bricks and dead bodies.

children.text: na ca mana eva bhūtātiriktam ātmā bhavitumarhati yatastasyāpi karaṇarūpasya preraṇādyātmanā kartrā kartavyam ||
children.translated_text: Nor can the mind itself, as something distinct from the elements, be the self, because it too, having the nature of an instrument, must be impelled by an agent, the self, through acts such as prompting.

children.text: nāpīndriyāṇyātmatvena svīkartuṃ pāryante yatastathā sati indriyāntaropalabdham arthaṃ nendriyāṇi yajñadattopalabdham arthaṃ devadatta iva pratisaṃdhātuṃ samarthāni bhaveyuḥ asti cendriyāntaropalabdhārthapratisaṃdhānaṃ yathā surabhicandanaṃ spṛśāmītyatra ||
children.translated_text: Nor can the senses be accepted as the self, because, if that were so, the senses would not be able to connect an object perceived by another sense, just as <s>Devadatta</s> cannot connect an object perceived by <s>Yajñadatta</s>. But there is connection of an object perceived by another sense, as in the statement, 'I touch fragrant sandalwood.'

children.text: tasmān mana indriyabhūtātirikta ātmā tiṣṭhatīti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: Therefore it should be understood that there exists a self distinct from mind, senses, and elements.

children.text: atra yadyapi buddhiśabdena cetanādhṛtismṛtyahaṅkārāḥ prāpyanta eva buddhiprakāratvena tathāpi pṛthakpṛthagarthagamakatvena punaḥ pṛthagupāttāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here, although consciousness, firmness, memory, and egoity are indeed included by the word intellect, since they are forms of intellect, still they are again taken up separately because each conveys a distinct meaning.

children.text: tathāhi cetanā guṇatvena acetanakhādibhūtātiriktadharmeṇātmānaṃ gamayati dhṛtistu niyamātmikā niyantāramātmānaṃ gamayati buddhistu ūhāpohayorekaṃ kāraṇaṃ gamayatyātmānaṃ smṛtistu pūrvānubhūtārthasmartāraṃ sthāyinamātmānaṃ gamayatītyādyanusaraṇīyam ||
children.translated_text: Thus consciousness, as a quality, indicates the self through a property distinct from unconscious elements such as ether; firmness, being regulatory in nature, indicates the self as regulator; intellect indicates the self as the single cause of supposition and exclusion; and memory indicates the self as a stable rememberer of an object previously experienced. This line of reasoning should be followed in the same way for the rest.
When the self is absent as the substratum, he states the absence of breath and the rest in the body with the words beginning 'the body'.

children.text: śūnyāgāramiva śūnyāgāraṃ yathā adhiṣṭhātṛśūnyam evaṃ mṛtaśarīramapi ||
children.translated_text: 'Like an empty house' means: just as an empty house is without an occupant, so too is a dead body.

children.text: ṣaḍdhātukaṃ śarīraṃ tatra ṣaṣṭhe ātmani gate pañcabhūtātmakaṃ śarīraṃ bhavati tena pañcatvaṃ gatamucyate ||
children.translated_text: The body is made of six constituents. When the sixth, the self, has departed, the body becomes one whose nature is the five elements; therefore it is said to have gone to the five-element state.

children.text: niṣkriyasya kriyā tasya katham ityasyottaram acetanamityādi ||
children.translated_text: To the question, 'How can there be action of what is inactive?', the answer is given with the words beginning 'unconscious'.

children.text: cetayitā para iti para ātmā cetayitā paraṃ na tu sākṣāt kriyāvān ||
children.translated_text: 'The one who causes consciousness is another' means that the other, the self, is the one who causes consciousness, but is not directly active.

children.text: nanu yadyevaṃ kathaṃ tasya kriyetyāha yuktasyetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, if this is so, how can action belong to it? He states the answer with the words beginning 'when joined'.

children.text: ātmādhiṣṭhitasyaiva manasaḥ kriyā upacārād ātmanaḥ kriyetyucyata ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The action of the mind only when governed by the self is, by figurative usage, called the action of the self: this is the meaning.
He establishes this very point with the words beginning 'possessed of consciousness'.

children.text: cetanena hyātmanādhiṣṭhitaṃ manaḥ kriyāsu pravartate cetanānadhiṣṭhitaṃ tu manaḥ kriyāsu na pravartate tena yatkṛtā sā kriyā sa eva kriyāvāniti vyapadeṣṭuṃ yujyate natvacetanaṃ manaḥ tat parādhīnakriyatvena paramārthataḥ kriyāvad api kartṛtvena nocyata iti vākyārthaḥ nocyate iti kartṛ iti śeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For the mind, when governed by the conscious self, engages in actions; but the mind, when not governed by consciousness, does not engage in actions. Therefore it is proper to designate as active the very one by whom that action is caused, and not the unconscious mind. Even if in the highest sense it possesses action, since its action depends on another, it is not called an agent. This is the meaning of the sentence. In 'it is not called', the word 'agent' is to be supplied.
He resolves the objection that, even if the self is independent, it is made to go to an undesired womb, with the words beginning 'according to its own'.
'Now' means at the present point.
'In all' means in all wombs or births, such as those of hell-beings, cows, elephants, and insects.

children.text: prāṇaistantrayate prāṇairyojayati ātmanaivāyaṃ dharmādharmasahāyenātmānaṃ sarvayoniṣu nayati na paraprerito yāti yato nānyaḥ puruṣo'sya prerako'sti īśvarābhāvāt kiṃvā satyapi īśvare tasyāpi karmaparādhīnatvāt ||
children.translated_text: 'He connects by the breaths' means he joins with the vital breaths. This self itself, assisted by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, leads itself into all wombs; it does not go impelled by another, since there is no other person who impels it, because there is no <s>Īśvara</s>; or, even if <s>Īśvara</s> exists, because he too is dependent on karma.

children.text: idameva cāsyāniṣṭayonigamane svātantryaṃ yad aniṣṭayonigamanahetvadharmakaraṇe svātantryam adharmakaraṇārabdhasvakarmaṇaivāyam anicchannapi nīyata ityaniṣṭayonigamanaṃ bhavati svātantryaṃ ca yathoktaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: And this is precisely its independence in going to an undesired womb: it has independence in performing the <s>adharma</s> that is the cause of going to an undesired womb. By its own karma begun through the performance of <s>adharma</s>, it is led even unwillingly; thus there is going to an undesired womb, and independence too exists in the way stated.

children.text: vaśī yadyasukhaiḥ kasmādbhāvair ākramyate ityasyottaraṃ vaśītyādi ||
children.translated_text: To the question, 'If he is in control, why is he overwhelmed by unpleasant states?', the answer is given with the words beginning 'being in control'.

children.text: vaśī svecchādhīnapravṛttiḥ iṣṭe'niṣṭe vātmā tena vaśī sannayaṃ tāni karmāṇi karoti śubhānyaśubhāni vā āpātaphalarāgāt yāni kṛtvā tatkarmaprabhāvācchubhenāśubhena vā phalena yogamāpnoti ||
children.translated_text: 'Being in control' means having activity dependent on one's own will, whether with regard to what is desired or undesired. Therefore, being in control, this self performs those actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious, because of attachment to their immediate result; and, after performing them, through the force of that karma it comes into conjunction with a result, whether auspicious or inauspicious.

children.text: etena kartavye karmaṇyasya vaśitvaṃ kṛtakarmaphalaṃ tvasyānicchato'pi bhavati tena tatprati nāsya vaśitvam ||
children.translated_text: By this it is said that it has control over the action to be performed, but the result of the action already performed occurs even when it does not wish it; therefore it has no control over that.

children.text: anyadapi vaśitvaphalamāha vaśī cetaḥ samādhatta iti ||
children.translated_text: He states another result of being in control: 'being in control, he steadies the mind.'

children.text: aniṣṭe'rthe vaśī sannayaṃ mano nivartayati yadi hyayaṃ vaśī na syāt na mano nivartayituṃ śaknuyāt ||
children.translated_text: Being in control, this self withdraws the mind from an undesired object. For if it were not in control, it would not be able to withdraw the mind.

children.text: aparamapi vaśitvagamakaṃ karmāha vaśī sarvaṃ nirasyatīti ||
children.translated_text: He states another action that indicates control: 'being in control, he casts off everything.'

children.text: vaśī sannayaṃ mokṣārthaṃ pravṛttaḥ sarvārambhaṃ śubhāśubhaphalaṃ tyajatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning is that, being in control and having undertaken action for the sake of <s>mokṣa</s>, this self abandons every undertaking that has an auspicious or inauspicious result.

children.text: iha svatantraḥ parātmanā īśvarādinā preritapravṛttir ucyate vaśī tu svayamapi pravartamāna icchāvaśāt pravartate na preritapravṛttirūpatvenepsite'nīpsite ca vartate iti svātantryavaśitvayorbhedaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Here 'independent' is used of one whose activity is not impelled by another self such as <s>Īśvara</s>; but one who is in control, even while acting by himself, acts under the power of his own wish, and does not operate toward what is desired or undesired merely as one whose activity is impelled. This is the distinction between independence and control.

children.text: sarvāḥ sarvagatatvācca vedanāḥ kiṃ na vetti saḥ ityasyottaramāha dehītyādi ||
children.translated_text: To the question, 'Since he is all-pervading, why does he not know all sensations?', he gives the answer with the words beginning 'the embodied one'.

children.text: sarvagata iti sarvagato'pi san saṃsparśanendriya iti saṃsparśanayukte śarīre vedanāḥ sukhaduḥkharūpā vetti sarvāśrayasthāstu na vettīti yojanā ||
children.translated_text: "All-pervading" means: although he is all-pervading, as one connected with the tactile faculty he knows sensations, whose form is pleasure and pain, in a body furnished with touch; but he does not know those located in all supports. This is the construction.

children.text: yasmāt sarvagato'pyātmā svakīya eva sparśanavati śarīre paraṃ vedanā vetti tena sarvāśrayasthāḥ sarvavedanā na vettīti vākyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since, although the <s>ātman</s> is all-pervading, it knows only the sensation in its own body that has the sense of touch, therefore it does not know all sensations located in all supports: this is the meaning of the sentence.
"Located in all supports" means located in all other bodies.

children.text: paraśarīre cātmā svakarmopārjitendriyābhāvād vidyamāno'pi nopalabhate sukhaduḥkhe ||
children.translated_text: And in another body, although the <s>ātman</s> is present, it does not perceive pleasure and pain, because the senses acquired by its own karma are absent there.

children.text: sve sve śarīra iti vaktavye yatra saṃsparśanendriye iti karoti tena svaśarīre'pi yatra keśanakhādau sparśanendriyaṃ nāsti tatra nātmā kiṃcidupalabhata iti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: Where one might have said "in each and every body," he says "where there is the tactile faculty"; by this he shows that even in one's own body, where there is no sense of touch, as in hair and nails, the <s>ātman</s> perceives nothing.

children.text: na paśyati vibhuḥ kasmāt ityādipraśnasyottaraṃ vaktuṃ pravṛtto vibhutvasādhakārthaguṇahetuprāptyā vibhutvam eva tāvadātmanaḥ sādhayati vibhutvam ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Having begun to state the answer to the question beginning "Why does the all-pervading one not see?", he first establishes the all-pervasiveness of the <s>ātman</s> itself, by adducing the meaning, quality, and reason that prove all-pervasiveness, with the words beginning "all-pervasiveness."
All-pervasiveness is possession of a measure that extends everywhere.
"For this very reason" means because of the all-pervasiveness just stated.

children.text: etadeva spaṣṭārthaṃ sākṣād brūte yasmād ityādi ||
children.translated_text: He states this very point directly, for the sake of making the meaning clear, with the words beginning "because."

children.text: sarvagatatvaṃ sarvato'pyupalabhyamānatvena sarvagatākāśādiparimāṇasyāpyasti tena tadvyavacchedārthaṃ mahān iti padaṃ tena sarvatropalabhyamānaṃ mahāparimāṇayogidravyaṃ vibhurucyata iti phalati ||
children.translated_text: All-pervasiveness also belongs to the measure of all-pervading entities such as space, inasmuch as they are apprehended everywhere; therefore, in order to exclude that, the word "great" is used. Thus the result is that a substance which is apprehended everywhere and possesses great measure is called all-pervading.

children.text: vibhutvaṃ vyutpādya kuḍyatirohitajñānaṃ naikāntena bhavatīti darśayannāha manasa ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Having explained all-pervasiveness, he says, while showing that knowledge of what is hidden by a wall does not occur invariably, the words beginning "of the mind."
Complete concentration is <s>samādhi</s>.

children.text: anena yoginaḥ samādhibalāt tirohitamapi paśyatīti darśayati ||
children.translated_text: By this he shows that a yogin sees even what is hidden, through the power of <s>samādhi</s>.

children.text: ye tu tirohitaṃ na paśyanti tatrāpyupapattimāha nityetyādi ||
children.translated_text: With regard to those who do not see what is hidden, he states the explanation with the words beginning "constant."

children.text: sarvayonigatamapyātmānaṃ manasānubandhagatam ekayonāvavasthitaṃ vidyād iti yojyam ||
children.translated_text: It should be construed thus: one should know the <s>ātman</s>, though present in all wombs or bodies, as connected with the mind and established in a single body.

children.text: dehanirvartakena karmaṇā anupāta ātmani saṃbandho yasya tena manasā dehakarmānupātinā ||
children.translated_text: "With the mind that follows the karma of the body" means: with the mind whose attachment, that is, connection, to the <s>ātman</s> is through the karma that produces the body.

children.text: etena yadyapyātmā kuḍyādibhir atirohitas tathāpi yad asyopalabdhisādhanaṃ manastasyaikasminneva śarīre vyavasthitasya vyavadhānānna paśyatyayaṃ tiraskṛtam ityuktaṃ bhavati ||
children.translated_text: By this it is said that, although the <s>ātman</s> is not hidden by walls and the like, still this person does not see what is concealed, because his instrument of perception, the mind, is fixed in one body alone and is obstructed.
The answer to the question beginning "Is it the knower of the field or the field?" is given with the words beginning "beginning."

children.text: kṣetrapāraṃparyamiti kṣetrasyāvyaktavarjitasya mahadāditrayoviṃśatikasya paramparasaṃtater anāditvenaiva kṣetrakṣetrajñayor idaṃ prathamamiti vyapadeśo naiva bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: "The succession of fields" means that, since the continuous succession of the <s>kṣetra</s> (field), excluding the unmanifest and consisting of the twenty-three principles beginning with <s>mahat</s>, is beginningless, no designation such as "this is the first" can apply to the field and the knower of the field. This is the meaning.

children.text: nanu yadi kṣetraparaṃparāpyanādis tadā tasyātmavad ucchedo na prāpnoti yadanādi tannityaṃ bhavati yathātmeti dṛṣṭaṃ brūmaḥ anāditve'pi yat svarūpenaivānādi tannocchidyate yathātmā yattu ucchittidharmakaṃ buddhyādi taducchidyata eva saṃtānastu paramārthataḥ saṃtānibhyo 'tirikto nāstyeva yadanādiḥ syāt tena saṃtānasyānāditvaṃ bhāktameva ||
children.translated_text: Objection: if the succession of fields too is beginningless, then its cessation, as in the case of the <s>ātman</s>, should not occur; for what is beginningless is eternal, as is seen in the <s>ātman</s>. We reply: even when something is beginningless, that which is beginningless by its very own nature is not destroyed, as the <s>ātman</s> is; but what has the nature of being cut off, such as intellect and the rest, is indeed cut off. A continuum, however, in the highest sense is not something different from the things that form the continuum, such that it would itself be beginningless. Therefore the beginninglessness of the continuum is only figurative.

children.text: kiṃcaivaṃbhūtasya buddhyādisaṃtānasyocchede mokṣapratipādaka āgama eva pramāṇatvena jñeyaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, in the cessation of such a continuum of intellect and the rest, the authoritative tradition that teaches liberation should itself be known as the means of proof.
The answer to "And of whom is he the witness?" is given with the words beginning "knower."

children.text: jño jñānavān sākṣīti loke kathyate natvajñaḥ pāṣāṇādiḥ ||
children.translated_text: A knower, one possessed of knowledge, is called a witness in ordinary speech, not an unknowing thing such as a stone.

children.text: tena jñatvenāsatyapyanyasmin kartari sākṣītyucyate iti vākyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore, because he is knowing, even when there is no other agent, he is called a witness: this is the meaning of the sentence.
"Of all" means of the elements beginning with space.

children.text: sarve bhāvā iti sarve bhūtadharmā darśanayogyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: "All entities" means all properties of the elements that are fit to be seen.
"Having the <s>ātman</s> as witness" means being apprehended by the <s>ātman</s>.
The answer to the question beginning "How could there be, for what is unchanging?" is given with the words beginning "not one."

children.text: avikārasya paramātmano vedanākṛto viśeṣo nāstyeva yatra tu vedanākṛto viśeṣaḥ sa rāśirūpaḥ paramātmavyatirikta eveti vākyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For the unchanging <s>paramātman</s> (supreme self), there is no distinction produced by sensation at all; but where there is a distinction produced by sensation, that is in the form of an aggregate and is distinct from the <s>paramātman</s>: this is the meaning of the sentence.

children.text: bhūtānāmadhiṣṭhātā ātmā bhūtātmā ayaṃ bhūtātmā eko bhūtavyatirikto na lakṣaṇaiḥ prāṇāpānādibhiruktair upalabhyate ||
children.translated_text: The <s>ātman</s>, the presiding ruler of the elements, is the <s>bhūtātman</s> (elemental self). This <s>bhūtātman</s>, being one and distinct from the elements, is not apprehended by the stated marks such as inhalation and exhalation.
Why is it not apprehended? He states this with the words beginning "distinction."

children.text: ekasya bhūtarahitasya yadātmano viśeṣo vedanādir nopalabhyata eva tenānupalabdhir evātra pramāṇamityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since no distinction, such as sensation, of the one <s>ātman</s> devoid of elements is apprehended at all, non-apprehension itself is the means of proof here. This is the meaning.
The conjunct person is the twenty-fourfold one.

children.text: nanvevamapi caturviṃśatyantarniviṣṭasya bhūtātmano'pi vedanākṛtaviśeṣeṇa bhavitavyaṃ yataḥ samudāyadharmaḥ samudāyināmeva bhavati yathā māṣarāśer gurutvaṃ pratyekaṃ māṣāṇāmeva gauraveṇa bhavatītyāha vedanetyādi ||
children.translated_text: Objection: even so, the <s>bhūtātman</s> included among the twenty-four must have a distinction produced by sensation, since a property of an aggregate belongs to the aggregated members themselves, just as the heaviness of a pile of beans exists through the heaviness of the individual beans. He answers this with the words beginning "sensation."
Sensation has the form of pleasure and pain.

children.text: yatra buddhyādisamūhe niyatā vyavasthitā vedanā tatraiva tatkṛto dainyaharṣādiviśeṣo'pi niyataḥ tatraiva buddhyādirāśau vartate nātmanīti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Where sensation is fixed and established in the aggregate of intellect and the rest, there too the distinction produced by it, such as dejection and joy, is fixed; it occurs in that very aggregate of intellect and the rest, not in the <s>ātman</s>. This is the purport.

children.text: buddhyādigatena guṇatrayapariṇāmarūpeṇa sukhaduḥkhādinā asukhaduḥkha evātmā tatsaṃbandhāt sukhaduḥkhādimān bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Because pleasure, pain, and the like are transformations of the three <s>guṇa</s>s belonging to intellect and the rest, the <s>ātman</s> itself is neither pleasure nor pain; but through connection with them it becomes possessed of pleasure, pain, and so on.
Alternatively, he gives the answer to the question beginning 'of one who is afflicted' with the words beginning 'he treats'.

children.text: atītavedanācikitsā na mukhyā kiṃtu lokaprasiddhopacāreṇocyata iti vākyārthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The meaning of the sentence is that treatment of pain that is past is not primary; rather, it is spoken of by a usage well known in the world.
'By well-known expressions' means by expressions well known in common usage.
'Counter-action' means treatment.
'Support' means in the body.
With the words beginning 'prodromal sign' he establishes the treatment of pain that has not yet come.

children.text: pūrvarūpaṃ yadyapi bhaviṣyatām eva bhavati rogāṇāṃ tathāpi bhaviṣyatāmiti padena bhūte'pi vyādhau yāni rūpāṇi bhavanti tāni nirākaroti ||
children.translated_text: Although a prodromal sign belongs only to diseases that are going to occur, still, by the word 'of future ones' he excludes those symptoms which occur even in a disease that has already arisen.

children.text: uktaṃ hi prāk saṃtāpāt api cainaṃ saṃtāpārtam anubadhnanti ityanena rogāvasthāyām api pūrvarūpasadbhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For it has been stated earlier, by the words 'before the heat, and they also follow him when he is afflicted by heat', that prodromal signs can exist even in the state of disease.
Thus the treatment of past and future pain has been explained.
Showing also the treatment of present pain, he states the ultimate view with the words beginning 'by successive connection'.
'Successive connection' means connection according to the principle of a continuum.
'Of pains' means of diseases.
'By resorting to the cause of pleasure' means by resorting to treatment that is the cause of health.
'Pleasure' means health.

children.text: evaṃ manyate yadā cikitsā sukhahetuḥ sevyate tadā duḥkhahetusevābhāvād duḥkhaṃ notpadyate utpannaṃ ca duḥkhaṃ rogarūpaṃ kṣaṇabhaṅgitvena svayameva naśyati sukhahetusānnidhyāt sukham ārogyam utpadyate tena cikitsayā anāgataṃ duḥkhaṃ hetupratibandhānnirudhyate sukhaṃ ca janyate iti siddhāntaḥ ||
children.translated_text: He means this: when treatment, which is a cause of pleasure, is resorted to, pain does not arise because there is no resorting to a cause of pain; and pain that has already arisen, in the form of disease, perishes by itself because it is momentary. Because of the presence of the cause of pleasure, pleasure, that is health, arises. Therefore the conclusion is that by treatment future pain is stopped through the obstruction of its cause, and pleasure is produced.
He states this very point with the words beginning 'not equal'.

children.text: samāśca viṣamāśca kṣaṇabhaṅgitvasvabhāvānna vaiṣamyāvasthāṃ sāmyāvasthāṃ vā yāntītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Equal and unequal states, because they are by nature momentarily perishing, do not pass into a state of inequality or a state of equality: this is the meaning.

children.text: hetubhiḥ sadṛśā iti samahetoḥ samāḥ tathā viṣamahetośca viṣamāḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Similar through causes' means: equal states arise from an equal cause, and likewise unequal states from an unequal cause.
And this has already been elaborated in the chapter <s>Cikitsāprābhṛtīya</s>.

children.text: cikitsāprastāvena sakaladuḥkhahāriṇīṃ cikitsāṃ mokṣaphalām āha cikitsā tvityādi ||
children.translated_text: On the occasion of discussing treatment, he speaks of the treatment that removes all suffering and has <s>mokṣa</s> as its fruit, with the words beginning 'but treatment'.
'Final end' means absolute release from suffering, in the form of <s>mokṣa</s>.
That which has come into being for that purpose is 'final'.

children.text: vinopadhāmiti tṛṣṇāṃ vinā tṛṣṇāśūnyā pravṛttirmokṣaphalā bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Without attachment' means without craving; activity empty of craving has <s>mokṣa</s> as its fruit: this is the meaning.
'The further cause' means the root cause.
The body is the support of pain precisely in the form of pain.

children.text: bhogatṛṣṇayā hi pravartamāno dharmādharmān duḥkhaśarīrotpādakān upādatte sarvopadhātyāgāttu na rāgadveṣābhyāṃ kvacit pravartate apravartamānaśca na dharmādharmānupādatte evam anāgatadharmādharmoparamaḥ upāttadharmādharmayostu rāgadveṣaśūnyasyopabhogād eva kṣayaḥ tena sarvathā karmakṣayād duḥkhaśarīrābhāva iti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For a person acting out of craving for enjoyment takes on <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>, which produce a body of suffering. But through abandoning all attachments he does not act anywhere through passion and aversion; and, not acting, he does not take on <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>. Thus future <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> cease. As for the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> already taken on, in one who is free from passion and aversion they are exhausted simply through experience. Therefore, because karma is exhausted in every way, there is no body of suffering: this is the intention.

children.text: atraiva tṛṣṇāyā duḥkhakāraṇatve dṛṣṭāntamāha kośakāra ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Here, regarding craving as the cause of suffering, he gives an example with the words beginning 'the cocoon-maker'.
The cocoon-maker is the insect known by that very name.
'Always afflicted' means always seized by the suffering of <s>saṃsāra</s>.
'Because of non-undertaking' means because of the absence of undertaking preceded by passion and aversion.

children.text: asaṃyogāditi ārambhaśūnyatvena dharmādharmocchedakṛtāccharīrāsaṃyogāt śarīrābhāve ca nirāśrayam akāraṇakaṃ duḥkhaṃ na bhavatīti bhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Because of non-connection' means because, since there is no undertaking, there is no connection with a body produced by the cutting off of <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>; and when the body is absent, pain, having no support and no cause, does not exist: this is the intention.
He gives the answer to 'What is the cause of sensations?' with the words beginning 'intellect, resolve'.
And this point, being stated because it belongs to the present topic, does not incur repetition.
Intellect, resolve, and memory are divisions of cognition.

children.text: ete ca śiṣyavyutpattyarthaṃ prajñābhedatvenānyathā vyutpādya ihocyante ||
children.translated_text: These too are explained elsewhere as divisions of cognition for the instruction of the student, and are mentioned here in that way.

children.text: saṃprāptiḥ kālakarmaṇāmiti kālasya saṃprāptistathā karmaṇaśca saṃprāptiḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'The occurrence of time and karma' means the occurrence of time, and likewise the occurrence of karma.
'The occurrence of karma' means conjunction with karma that is coming to fruition.

children.text: kālasaṃprāptigrahaṇena ceha ye kālavyaktāste gṛhyante nāvaśyaṃ kālajanyāḥ yataḥ svābhāvikānapi kālajanyān tathā tṛtīyakādīn apyasātmyendriyārthādijanyān kālajatvenaivehābhidhāsyati ||
children.translated_text: By the mention of the occurrence of time here, those things that are manifested by time are included, not necessarily those produced by time; for even natural ones are here described as time-born, as are tertian fevers and the like, though they are produced by unsuitable contact of the senses with their objects and other causes.

children.text: karmajāstu prajñāparādhajanyā eveha karmajanyatvena viśeṣeṇa śiṣyavyutpattyarthaṃ pṛthagucyante kālavyañjyatvena ca karmajā iha kālasaṃprāptijanyeṣvavaroddhavyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: But things born from karma, here produced specifically by <s>prajñāparādha</s> (failure of judgment), are separately stated as karma-born for the instruction of the student; and because they are manifested by time, karma-born conditions here should be included among those produced by the occurrence of time.

children.text: prajñāparādhāvarodhaśca yathā karmajānāṃ tathā prathamādhyāya evoktam ||
children.translated_text: And the inclusion of karma-born conditions under <s>prajñāparādha</s> has likewise been stated already in the first chapter.

children.text: kiṃcācāryeṇonmādanidāne svayamevoktaṃ prajñāparādhāt sambhūte vyādhau karmaja ātmanaḥ ityādi tathā janapadoddhvaṃsanīye ca vimāne punaruktaṃ vāyvādīnāṃ yadvai guṇyamutpadyate tasya mūlam adharmaḥ tanmūlaṃ vāsatkarma pūrvakṛtaṃ tayoryoniḥ prajñāparādha eva iti ||
children.translated_text: Moreover, in the <s>Unmādanidāna</s> the teacher himself has said, 'in a disease arising from <s>prajñāparādha</s>, karma-born, belonging to the self,' and so on; and in the <s>Janapadoddhvaṃsanīya Vimāna</s> it is again stated: 'The disturbance that arises in air and the rest has <s>adharma</s> as its root; that has bad action done previously as its root; and the source of both of them is precisely <s>prajñāparādha</s>.'

children.text: tasmādiha saṃprāptiḥ kālakarmaṇāmityanena na kālajanyā gadā ucyante kiṃtu kālavyañjyāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Therefore here, by the phrase 'the occurrence of time and karma', diseases produced by time are not meant; rather, diseases manifested by time are meant.
He explains the derangement of intellect with the words beginning 'wrongly'.

children.text: viṣamābhiniveśaḥ ayathābhūtatvenādhyavasānaṃ nitye'nityam iti evaṃ hite'hitam ahite vā hitamiti yā buddhiḥ sa buddhibhraṃśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Misapprehension is determination not in accordance with reality, as when one takes the impermanent to be permanent. The understanding that what is beneficial is harmful, or that what is harmful is beneficial, is that derangement of intellect.

children.text: atha kathamayaṃ buddhivibhraṃśaśabdenocyata ityāha samaṃ buddhir hi paśyati ucitā buddhiḥ samaṃ yathābhūtaṃ yasmāt paśyati tasmādasamadarśanaṃ buddhivibhraṃśa ucita evetyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Now, how is this expressed by the word <s>buddhivibhraṃśa</s> (derangement of intellect)? He explains: for intellect sees evenly. Proper intellect sees evenly, that is, according to reality; therefore uneven seeing is indeed rightly called derangement of intellect. This is the meaning.
He states derangement of firmness with the words beginning 'toward objects.'
'Inclined toward objects' means becoming attached to objects.
'To restrain' means to turn away.

children.text: dhṛtirhi niyamātmiketi yasmād dhṛtirakāryaprasaktaṃ mano nivartayati svarūpeṇa tasmānmanoniyamaṃ kartumaśaktā dhṛtiḥ svakarmabhraṣṭā bhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Since firmness has restraint as its nature, and since firmness by its own form turns back the mind when it is attached to what should not be done, firmness that is unable to restrain the mind has fallen from its own function. This is the meaning.
He distinguishes derangement of memory with the words beginning 'of truth.'
The construction is: one whose memory falls away with respect to knowledge of reality.

children.text: smartavyaṃ hi smṛtau sthitam iti smartavyatvena saṃmatasyārthasya smaraṇaṃ praśastasmṛtidharmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For what is to be remembered is established in memory: remembering an object accepted as something to be remembered is the proper property of sound memory.

children.text: tatra ca tattvajñānasya śiṣṭānāṃ smartavyatvena saṃmatasya yadasmaraṇaṃ tat smṛtyaparādhādbhavatītyarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: And there, when knowledge of reality, accepted by cultivated people as something to be remembered, is not remembered, that occurs because of an offense of memory. This is the meaning.

Thus, showing action produced by the threefold derangement of intellect and the rest, and so born of <s>prajñāparādha</s> (offense against wisdom), as itself <s>prajñāparādha</s>, he says the words beginning 'by intellect.'
By the word 'all <s>doṣas</s>' are included <s>vāta</s> and the others, and also <s>rajas</s> and <s>tamas</s>.
'Letting the proper time for action pass' means transgressing the proper time for treatment.
'Wrong undertaking' means one whose form is deficient application, excessive application, or wrong application.

children.text: vinayācāralopenaiva prāptamapi yat punaḥ pūjyānāmabhidharṣaṇādyabhidhīyate tad viśeṣeṇa prakopakatvakhyāpanārthamudāharaṇārthaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Although this is already implied by the mere lapse of discipline and conduct, the further mention of assaulting or insulting venerable persons is for showing that it is especially aggravating, and also for giving an example.
'With defiled actors' means with fallen persons.
'Afflicted' means censured.
He states the definition of <s>prajñāparādha</s> in brief with the words beginning 'by intellect.'

children.text: viṣamam iti anucitaṃ viṣamavijñānaṃ svarūpata eva prajñāparādhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'Uneven' means improper. Uneven cognition is, in its very nature, <s>prajñāparādha</s>.
And uneven activity is called <s>prajñāparādha</s> because it is the effect of <s>prajñāparādha</s>.

children.text: manaso gocaraṃ hi taditi tadviṣamapravartanaṃ viṣamajñānaṃ ca manaḥkāryaprajñāviṣayatvena manaso gocaramityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: For that is within the range of the mind: uneven activity and uneven cognition are within the range of the mind because they are objects of wisdom, which is a function of the mind. This is the meaning.

children.text: viṣamapravartanaṃ ca manogocarajanyatvenopacārād uktaṃ visadṛśamanoviṣayajñānād viṣamavāgdehapravṛttir api bhavati ||
children.translated_text: Uneven activity, too, is mentioned figuratively because it is produced from what is within the mind's range; from cognition of an incongruous mental object there also arises uneven activity of speech and body.
He states the occurrence of diseases in relation to time with the words beginning 'specified.'
'Collection of diseases' means in the <s>Kiyantaḥśirasīya</s> chapter.
The accumulation, aggravation, and pacification of <s>pitta</s> and the others, in due order,
occur one by one in the six times beginning with the coming of clouds.
By this statement, and also by the example beginning 'for thus,'

children.text: tena kālasaṃprāptir vyādhīnāṃ yathācayaprakopapraśamāḥ pittādīnāṃ purā nirdiṣṭā iti yojyam ||
children.translated_text: the construction should be: the time-occurrence of diseases was previously specified according to the accumulation, aggravation, and pacification of <s>pitta</s> and the others.
He gives another example with the words beginning 'wrongly.'

In the passage beginning 'digested,' the time of food is that of food qualified by the three states beginning with being digested; likewise, the improper time of food is characterized by the states beginning with being undigested.
'Fully digested' means over-digested or acidly digested.

children.text: rātreryāmāstrayaśca ya iti trayo bhāgāḥ pūrvarātramadhyarātrāpararātrarūpāḥ na tu yāmaḥ prahara iti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: 'And the three <s>yāmas</s> of the night' means the three parts, namely the first part of the night, the middle of the night, and the last part of the night; it should not be understood as a <s>yāma</s> in the sense of a watch.

children.text: anyatrāpi ca bhāgatraye yāmavibhāgaṃ kṛtvā abhidhānaśāstre triyāmā niśābhidhīyate ||
children.translated_text: Elsewhere too, after making a division into <s>yāmas</s> in the three parts, night is called <s>triyāmā</s> in lexical teaching.

children.text: teṣu kāleṣviti jīrṇānnakālādiṣu jīrṇe aparāhṇe rātriśeṣe ca vātikā gadāḥ bhuktamātre pūrvāhṇe pūrvarātre ca kaphajā gadāḥ prajīrṇe madhyāhne madhyarātre ca pittajā niyatā rogāḥ ||
children.translated_text: 'At those times' means at times such as that of digested food: diseases of <s>vāta</s> are fixed in the state of digested food, in the afternoon, and at the end of the night; diseases born of <s>kapha</s> are fixed immediately after eating, in the forenoon, and in the first part of the night; and diseases born of <s>pitta</s> are fixed when food is fully digested, at midday, and at midnight.

children.text: annākāle cājīrṇalakṣaṇe bhojanāt trayo'pi doṣā bhavantīti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: And one should know that at an improper food-time, characterized by indigestion, all three <s>doṣas</s> arise from eating.

children.text: kiṃvā jīrṇabhuktaprajīrṇānnakālā iti chedaḥ tena jīrṇādyavasthāyuktānnakālāḥ pūrvavad eva jñeyāḥ tathā kālasthitiśca yā iti yojanā kālasthitiśabdena bālyādivayastraividhyam ucyate ||
children.translated_text: Or the division is 'the times of food as digested, eaten, and fully digested'; thus the times of food possessing the states beginning with being digested should be understood as before. Likewise the construction is 'and the state of time'; by the term 'state of time' is meant the threefold division of age, beginning with childhood.

children.text: tatra bālye ślaiṣmikāḥ yauvane paittikāḥ vārdhakye vātikā gadā vardhante iti jñeyam ||
children.translated_text: There one should know that in childhood phlegmatic diseases, in youth bilious diseases, and in old age windy diseases increase.

children.text: viṣamajvarānapi kālaviśeṣapravartamānamātratvena kālaje darśayannāha anyedyuṣka ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Showing intermittent fevers also as time-born, merely because they proceed at particular times, he says the words beginning 'every other day.'
A fever that seizes on the second day is the reverse of a <s>caturthaka</s> fever.
For he will say in the section on intermittent fever: there is also another, the reverse of <s>caturthaka</s>,
which causes fever on the intervening day, and then releases at the beginning and the end.
Thus.

children.text: kathaṃ svakīya eva kāle pravartanta ityāha kāle hyeṣāṃ balāgama iti ||
children.translated_text: How do they proceed only at their own time? He explains: for at that time their strength arrives.

children.text: ukta eva kāle yasmād balavanto bhavanti tasmāttatraiva saṃjātabalāḥ santo vyajyanta ityarthaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because they become strong precisely at the time already stated, therefore, having acquired strength there, they become manifest. This is the meaning.
He states the order of treatment for these with the words beginning 'and these.'

children.text: anye cetyanenānyān api kālaviśeṣaprāptiprādurbhāvinaḥ śothakuṣṭhādīn sūcayati ||
children.translated_text: By the words 'and others' he indicates also other conditions, such as swelling and skin disease, that appear when a specific time arrives.
In order to include even natural conditions here among time-born diseases, since they are manifested by the transformation of time, he says the words beginning 'of time.'

children.text: jarāmṛtyurūpān nimittājjātā jarāmṛtyunimittajāḥ mṛtyuśabdeneha yugānurūpāyuḥparyavasānabhavakālamṛtyur grāhyaḥ kiṃvā jarāmṛtyvor yannimittaṃ tasmājjātā jarāmṛtyunimittajāḥ jarāmṛtyunimittaṃ ca prāṇināṃ sādhāraṇadehanivartakabhūtasvabhāvo'dṛṣṭaṃ ca ||
children.translated_text: Those born from causes in the form of old age and death are 'born from causes of old age and death.' Here, by the word 'death' one should understand death at the proper time, arising when the lifespan appropriate to the age has reached its end; or else, they are born from that which is the cause of old age and death. And the cause of old age and death is the inherent nature that terminates the common body of living beings, and also the unseen factor.

children.text: atha svābhāvikānāṃ kā cikitsetyāha svabhāva ityādi ||
children.translated_text: Now, to the question, 'What treatment is there for natural conditions?', he answers with the words beginning 'nature.'

children.text: niṣpratikriya iti sādhāraṇacikitsayā rasāyanavarjyayā na pratikriyate rasāyanena tu pratikriyata eva tena ||
children.translated_text: 'Without countermeasure' means that it is not counteracted by ordinary treatment, apart from <s>rasāyana</s> (rejuvenation therapy); but by <s>rasāyana</s> it is indeed counteracted. Therefore,

children.text: asya prayogāccyavanaḥ suvṛddho'bhūt punaryuvā ityādirasāyanaprayogeṇa samaṃ na virodhaḥ kiṃvā svābhāvikā jarādayo rasāyanajanitaprakarṣāduttarakālaṃ punaravaśyaṃ bhavantīti niṣpratikriyatvenoktāḥ ||
children.translated_text: there is no contradiction with statements about the use of <s>rasāyana</s>, such as 'through its use <s>Cyavana</s>, though extremely old, became young again.' Or else, natural conditions such as old age are said to be without countermeasure because, after an excellence produced by <s>rasāyana</s>, they necessarily arise again at a later time.
